abstract: The growing demand for load-bearing components operating in chloride-containing environments calls for high-strength titanium alloys with enhanced corrosion resistance. In β-Ti alloys, conventional strengthening by discrete second-phase precipitation often introduces sharp compositional and electrochemical discontinuities at precipitate/matrix interfaces, promoting micro-galvanic corrosion and destabilizing passive films. Here we show that this trade-off between strength and corrosion resistance can be mitigated in Ti-24Nb-4Zr-8Sn (wt.%) by exploiting aging-induced spinodal decomposition, which produces a compositionally modulated and spatially continuous β/α″ dual-phase microstructure with a characteristic wavelength of about 20 nm. This continuous modulation provides densely spaced barriers to dislocation glide and increases strength, while avoiding the sharp interfacial electrochemical contrast associated with conventional precipitate-strengthened microstructures. In addition, spinodal decomposition induces periodic compositional modulation within the β/α″ microstructure, affecting passivation behavior through coupled Ti-O and Nb partitioning. The nanoscale α″ domains are enriched in both Ti and O, providing favorable local chemical environments that can facilitate Ti-oxide formation and promote passivation. Concurrent nanoscale Nb modulation is associated with a greater relative contribution of Nb oxides to the passive film, helping stabilize the barrier layer. These effects contribute to a thicker, more laterally continuous, and less defective passive film, thereby reducing defect-assisted transport and improving corrosion resistance in chloride-containing media. Our findings highlight spinodal decomposition as a viable route to co-optimize strength and corrosion resistance in β-Ti alloys.

title: Dislocation velocity enhancement under electron irradiation in magnesium
abstract: The softening of materials subjected to irradiation in reactors is known for a long time but still difficult to interpret. One reason for such a situation is that post-irradiation microstructural observations mainly show different types of irradiation defects which are potential sources of hardening, not softening. Irradiation softening must accordingly be studied in situ, as a function of temperature, irradiation energy and flux. Simple sources of irradiating particles can be used, such as ions or electrons, but in situ experiments remain difficult to perform, and to combine with clear microstructural observations. For those reasons, and in order to measure irradiation effects at the scale of individual dislocations, a simple procedure has been used: straining magnesium micro-samples in a transmission electron microscope working between 80kV (the irradiation threshold of magnesium) and 180kV. The in situ observations reveal a huge effect of the electron beam corresponding to a 10000 times enhancement of the velocity of screw dislocations in the prismatic planes under a 160kV electron beam, and the dependence of this enhancement factor with the accelerating voltage. These results are interpreted in terms of something equivalent to a temperature increase of 100K or more, but clearly different from a true heating process.

title: Editorial Board
Dislocation-pinning and dynamic strain-aging in hydrogen-alloyed Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic steel at sub-ambient temperatures
abstract: The interaction between solute hydrogen (H) and mobile dislocations in Fe-24Cr-19Ni mass% (Type310S) austenitic steel charged with 8500 atomic ppm H was investigated by stress relaxation tests conducted over the temperature range 213–295 K. At ambient condition, H atoms form solute atmospheres that can migrate coordinately with moving dislocations. In contrast, the reduced H diffusivity at lower temperatures progressively impedes dislocation motion, leading to dynamic strain aging (DSA) during the relaxation process, manifested as a retardation of thermally activated deformation. As a direct consequence of this dislocation-pinning effect, a pronounced yield point emerged upon reloading after relaxation. The kinetics of solute atmosphere formation and DSA were further quantified by evaluating the exhaustion rate of mobile dislocation density as a function of relaxation time. The experimental trends were successfully described using a classical Cottrell atmosphere model based on size-misfit interaction, demonstrating that the fundamental role of H in governing dislocation mobility is essentially analogous to that of other interstitial solute elements.

title: The plasticity of single-crystal tin: insights from strain rate and deformation gradient under micro-mechanical experiments
abstract: The plastic deformation mechanisms of low-melting-point metals with low-symmetry structures at the microscale remain poorly understood. This study systematically investigates the plastic behavior and strain gradient effects of single-crystal β-Sn under different strain rates through in situ SEM micro-tensile and micro-cantilever bending experiments. The results show that β-Sn exhibits strong orientation dependence, with the (101)[-101] slip system activated under both loading modes. Crucially, the deformation mechanisms are sensitive to both strain rate and loading mode. At high strain rates, deformation is dominated by dislocation slip. At low strain rates, tensile specimens exhibit pronounced creep damage, whereas such damage is markedly suppressed in bending specimens due to the steep stress gradient and surface effects. Significant strengthening is observed under bending, attributed to the accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). Quantitative analysis of surface slip steps reveals that the back stress from dislocation pile-ups scales with the square of the step height. The strain rate sensitivity parameter m (0.043–0.046) and the activation volume confirm a dynamic transition from diffusion-assisted climb at low rates to thermally activated slip at high rates. The microscale plastic behavior of β-Sn lies between that of FCC and BCC metals, resulting from the combined effects of its BCT crystal structure anisotropy and low melting point. This study provides new theoretical insights into the interaction between diffusion-controlled damage, gradient-induced hardening, and loading-dependent stress distributions in the microscale plasticity of low-melting-point metals.

title: Suppression of dynamic recovery via localized solute pinning for superior high-temperature strength in a lightweight refractory medium-entropy alloy
abstract: The deployment of lightweight refractory high- and medium-entropy alloys in next-generation aerospace systems is critically hindered by an inadequate understanding of their dynamic softening mechanisms at elevated temperatures. Herein, we report an approach to control dynamic recovery and recrystallization in a single-phase BCC Ti–Zr–V–Nb system, achieving a 24% increase in 800 °C tensile strength (from 236 MPa to 292 MPa) while retaining substantial high-temperature plasticity (29.7% fracture strain) and comparable room-temperature ductility (18.2%). This enhancement is achieved not by second-phase formation, but by establishing a sluggish diffusion environment to control microstructural evolution. A niobium-mediated change in atomic diffusivity actively promotes the rapid formation of localized solute atmospheres at defects during deformation, which in turn exerts a potent pinning force to suppress dynamic recovery. This mechanism is reflected by the apparent retardation of dynamic recrystallization processes, characterized by a significant increase in low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) and kernel average misorientation (KAM). Furthermore, atomic-scale observations using Cs-corrected STEM and APT provide direct structural indications for the physical origin of these pinning forces, driven by the profound segregation of Nb-rich clusters at defects. Systematic interrupted tests quantitatively confirm that this intense solute pinning acts continuously throughout the entire deformation process, severely restricting the recrystallization fraction and driving the continuous accumulation of an unrecovered substructure network. Our work establishes the targeted suppression of dynamic recovery through localized solute-defect interactions, providing a robust pathway for creating lightweight refractory alloys with superior high-temperature performance.

title: An Arrhenius–hazard approach to strength additivity, dynamic strain aging, and yield surfaces
abstract: Predicting alloy strength requires superposing multiple strengthening mechanisms, yet classical p -norm rules ( σ 1 p + σ 2 p ) 1 / p , often lack physical justification and require refitting when conditions change. This work demonstrates that hazard analysis helps resolve this additivity problem by recasting mechanism superposition as rate competition. The framework is demonstrated across three distinct settings: (i) particle strengthening, where cutting (discrete barrier), Orowan looping (continuous work, cast in Arrhenius form via the Lambert- W function), and climb-assisted bypass compete through additive hazards and integrate with forest hardening into deformation mechanism maps; (ii) the Portevin–Le Chatelier (PLC) effect, where solute aging modifies the barrier in each hazard channel via a Prony series, producing the characteristic V-shaped PLC window and serrated flow without assumed negative rate sensitivity; and (iii) yield surfaces, where the scalar stress bias generalizes to a tensorial activation work W = σ : A , so iso-quantile yield loci correspond to iso-hazard contours whose geometry follows from the symmetry of the activation-work tensor, including von Mises, non-Schmid, and multimechanism envelopes. In all three cases, the competition rules emerge from rate physics rather than phenomenological rules.

title: High-throughput determination of tie-lines in multicomponent phase diagrams: a case of Ni–Co–Ti–Al quaternary alloy with γ/γ’ phase
abstract: Equilibrium phase diagrams are essential for understanding and controlling microstructures in multi-component alloys. However, the rapid and automatic determination of tie-line compositions—critical for constructing these diagrams—remains a challenge. We propose a high-throughput method for efficiently constructing phase diagrams, focusing on determining phase-boundary compositions in multi-component alloys. Using the Ni–Co–Ti–Al quaternary alloy as a case study, we demonstrated that the automatic measurement of 813 phase-boundary composition pairs from a single test sample encompasses the entire two-phase region of the γ and γ' phases at 900 °C. This was achieved by utilizing a diffusion multiple with a gradual compositional gradient introduced via a two-step diffusion method. Local average and tie-line compositions of 10 μm × 10 μm local micro-areas at 2110 selected locations from 60,000 locations in the diffusion multiple were quickly determined through characteristic X-ray intensities measured by automatic area analysis using electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images. Furthermore, we developed a technique for extracting tie-line compositions of the γ matrix and γ' precipitates with a precipitate size range of 0.8–2 μm using statistical analyses of EPMA maps and SEM images. This enables the determination of phase-boundary compositions even for submicron precipitates, and 813 γ-γ' phase-boundary pairs were successfully analyzed from 2110 points. The total dataset acquisition time was 1624 h, achieving a 130-fold increase in efficiency compared to conventional methods using a single composition sample. Utilizing this method will dramatically accelerate the construction of future phase diagram databases.

title: Sb-site substitution inducing stacking disorder in Na3Ni2SbO6 cathodes toward enhanced electrochemical performance
abstract: Na3Ni2SbO6 with a honeycomb superlattice exhibits improved air stability but suffers from rapid capacity decay due to severe lattice changes during phase transitions. Herein, we introduce trace Ru/Te substitution at Sb sites to induce transition metal (TM) layer stacking disorder and investigate its correlation with electrochemical performance. Powder XRD refinements, simulated XRD, SAED, and aberration-corrected STEM analyses confirm that Te doping (Na2.8Ni2Sb0.8Te0.2O6) introduces substantially more stacking faults along the c‑axis compared to Ru doping, while intralayer honeycomb ordering is retained. Hard X‑ray XAS measurements verify that the doped Te is present in the hexavalent state. Electrochemical tests demonstrate that Te-doped Na2.8Ni2Sb0.8Te0.2O6 delivers improved cycling stability and higher average voltage (3.33 V) compared to pristine and Ru-doped samples. The higher the current density, the more pronounced the long‑term cycling stability of Te0.2 becomes. The Te‑doped sample retains 52% of its capacity after 400 cycles at 2C (200 mA g–1), whereas the capacity retentions of pristine and Ru-doped are all below 33%. In situ XRD reveals that enhanced stacking disorder enables more gradual lattice parameter evolution, enhances structural stability and suppresses the formation of residual phase after cycling. Post-cycling characterizations, including SEM, XRD, HRTEM and EIS tests, confirm that Te doping effectively maintains particle integrity and minimizes impedance growth. This work demonstrates that modulating stacking disorder via trace substitution is an effective strategy for improving the electrochemical performance of layered oxide cathodes.

title: Decoupling dislocation multiplication and velocity effects in metals at extreme strain rates
abstract: The dynamic behavior of metals is governed by collective dislocation motion and interactions that strongly depend on the applied strain rate. Metals exhibit weak strain rate sensitivity (SRS) below a certain threshold, followed by a distinct SRS upturn at higher loading rates. While this upturn is typically attributed to increased glide resistance at high dislocation velocity due to mechanisms such as phonon drag, the role of strain-rate-dependent dislocation multiplication and microstructural evolution under these extreme conditions remains elusive. Here, we decouple these two strengthening effects and show that, while dislocation velocity primarily governs the SRS upturn, the hardening due to microstructure evolution depends strongly on the initial dislocation density. Our investigation of hardness evolution across ten decades of strain rates in a quenched and tempered martensitic low-carbon steel (LCS) using laser-induced projectile impact tests (LIPIT) and nanoindentation reveals SRS upturn around 10^7 1/s. By performing in situ re-indentation of the formed craters, we probe the contribution of dislocations generated during initial deformation at different strain rates. We show that while dislocation multiplication plays a negligible role in fine-grained LCS with high dislocation density, a pronounced dislocation multiplication contributes to the hardness increase in pure iron with lower initial dislocation density. Our results show that, depending on the initial microstructure of metals, dislocation multiplication significantly governs high-strain-rate plasticity, in addition to dislocation velocity effects.

title: Equilibrium vacancy concentrations and defect-driven homogeneity ranges in Ti–Al–C, Ti–Al–N, and Ti–Al–C–N MAX phases
abstract: A quantitative understanding of homogeneity ranges and the thermodynamic stability of vacancy formation in MAX phases is essential for tailoring their properties, yet a comprehensive link between atomic-scale energetics and macroscopic phase behavior has remained elusive. In this work, we bridge this gap by integrating density functional theory (DFT) calculations with the Calphad (Calculation of Phase Diagrams) approach to investigate the Ti–Al–C–N system. Our results demonstrate that the X-sublattice (C, N) in Tin+1AlXn phases (n = 1 - 3) can accommodate extensive vacancy solubility ranging from 13% to 30%, whereas vacancies on the Al-sublattice are energetically unfavorable under equilibrium conditions. By incorporating DFT-derived mixing enthalpies and vacancy formation energies into the thermodynamic model, we successfully reproduce experimental isothermal sections and quaternary phase equilibria, resolving long-standing literature discrepancies regarding the stoichiometry of carbonitride solid solutions. Furthermore, we apply the framework to describe constrained equilibria in nanoscale TiN/TiAl and Ti/AlN multilayers, accurately predicting phase evolution and defect concentrations in thin film systems where global equilibrium is kinetically hindered. This work provides a roadmap for defect engineering in MAX phases and establishes a predictive framework for designing parent materials to tailor the chemistry and active-site density of derived two-dimensional MXenes.

title: In-situ observation of the reverse martensitic transformation in a Ti–Pd shape memory alloy
abstract: Thermoelastic martensitic transformation governs the shape memory effect in shape memory alloys. In this study, in-situ digital holographic microscopy was employed to clarify the mechanism of thermoelastic martensitic transformation in a Ti–Pd high temperature shape memory alloy during reverse transformation. At the initial stage of the reverse transformation, a habit plane variant (HPV) pair satisfying favorable self-accommodation and kinematic compatibility (KC) conditions transformed simultaneously from within a grain interior. Subsequently, secondary reverse transformation occurred in HPVs located adjacent to the first-transformed HPV pair, selected by their KC compatibility with the initially transformed HPV. These results demonstrate that, at elevated temperature, the reverse transformation in Ti–Pd is governed by strain-reduction and interfacial compatibility, rather than by the release of stored elastic energy, as typically observed in low-temperature SMAs such as Ti–Ni.

title: Spontaneous sliding at copper-graphene interface: A new irradiation induced defect-interface interaction mechanism
abstract: Weakly bonded heterointerfaces, characterized by low interfacial energy and structural flexibility, can act as efficient sinks for irradiation-induced defects, however their dynamic processes and associated mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this work, we use atomistic simulations to investigate the irradiation-induced structural transformation of the weakly bonded van der Waals (vdW) copper/graphene (Cu/Gr) interface, in comparison with strongly bonded metallic interfaces including Cu/silver interface, Cu twin boundary and Cu high-angle grain boundary. In contrast to these metallic interfaces, which retain structural rigidity under irradiation cascades, the Cu/Gr interface undergoes spontaneous interfacial sliding, enabling metastable high-energy stacking fault (HESF) and intrinsic stacking fault (ISF) interfacial states to transform toward the lowest-energy face-centered cubic (FCC) configuration. Thermodynamic and kinetic analyses reveal that the observed interfacial transformation is driven by interfacial binding energy gradients and proceeds through low-barrier sliding pathways. Irradiation-induced defects further reduce the associated migration barriers, thereby facilitating the HESF/ISF-to-FCC interfacial transformation. Moreover, energetic analysis suggests that the resulting FCC interfacial structure exhibits strong interstitial-absorption capability due to its lower interstitial formation energy and migration barrier. Statistical analysis supports this conclusion, showing a 13.3% reduction in residual defect density relative to the corresponding non-sliding counterparts. These findings provide mechanistic insights into the role of irradiation-induced interfacial transformation in defect annihilation and suggest a potential interface design strategy for radiation-tolerant metal matrix composites.

title: Dual-modulation doping effects advance n-type Mg3(Sb, Bi)2 thermoelectrics
abstract: N-type Mg 3 (Sb, Bi) 2 compounds suffer from low carrier mobility at low to mid-range temperatures due to strong ionized impurity scattering from uniform doping. Here, we successfully synthesized compounds comprising by Zr, Zr-doped Mg 3( Sb, Bi) 2 , and intrinsic Mg 3( Sb, Bi) 2 by employing a dual-modulation doping strategy. This approach leverages Zr nanoparticles and Zr-doped Mg 3( Sb, Bi) 2 as electron donors, supplying charge carriers to the intrinsic Mg 3( Sb, Bi) 2 , which serves as electronic high-speed channels. By integrating the Zr-doped and intrinsic phases through a synergistic process, we construct an efficient transport network that facilitates rapid electron conduction along these channels. Such a process optimizes carrier concentration, enhances mobility, and shifts the main scattering mechanism to phonon scattering, leading to a significant increase in Hall mobility from 30.7 to 155.3 cm 2 V −1 s −1 . Consequently, the power factor at room temperature rises from 11.6 to 35.9 µW cm −1 K −2 , achieving a peak ZT value over 2.0 at 573 K and an exceptionally high average ZT of 1.7 over 323∼773 K, the highest reported to date. Device-level demonstrations confirm practical applicability, with a single-leg module reaching 13.6% efficiency under 467 K and a two-pair p-n module incorporating p-type GeTe achieving 7.5% at Δ T = 320 K. This dual-modulation doping strategy provides a generalizable design paradigm for optimizing transport and thermal management in n-type Zintl thermoelectrics for scalable mid-temperature waste heat recovery.

title: On the origin of superlattice stacking faults nucleation via climb of Frank partial in CoNi-based superalloys
abstract: High-temperature deformation in superalloys is governed by the cooperative glide-climb motion of dislocations. Superlattice stacking faults (SFs) in the γ′ phase are predominantly interpreted as nucleating via conservative Shockley partial glide. Here, we demonstrate that non-conservative climb of a / 3 〈 111 〉 Frank partials constitutes a kinetically viable pathway for both superlattice intrinsic (SISFs) and extrinsic stacking faults (SESFs) formation in the L1 2 structure of CoNi-based superalloys during compression at 850°C. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy reveals that Frank partials form at γ/γ′ interface can climb into the γ′ phase, generating SISFs via positive climb and SESFs via negative climb. Importantly, the negative climb-assisted nucleation of SESFs is experimentally confirmed for the first time, and the observed positive climb-assisted SISF configuration differs fundamentally from previously reported mechanisms. We show that these Frank partials originate from the reaction between a leading 30° Shockley partial and a 60° mixed dislocation on conjugate {111} planes, producing energetically stable configurations that promote subsequent climb. Energetic and kinetic analyses demonstrate that solute segregation induced reduction of SF energy provides a dominant contribution to Frank partial climb, enabling sustained climb and consequent SF expansion. Quantitative comparisons further indicate that, at elevated temperatures, solute drag-controlled Shockley glide can achieve mobilities comparable to vacancy diffusion-controlled Frank climb. These findings establish climb-assisted SF formation as an important deformation mechanism in γ′ phase, and that both SISF and SESF expansion can proceed through Frank partial climb, providing new insights into dislocation-controlled high-temperature deformation in CoNi-based superalloys.

title: Phase separation dynamics and the microstructure patterns of levitated immiscible alloy droplet
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation during solidification significantly influences the microstructure patterns and the properties of immiscible alloys. However, it remains a challenge to clarify the phase separation dynamics on ground due to the strong natural convection and Stokes motion of minority phase droplets. In this work, the solidification experiments are carried out with the containerless setup aboard the China Space Station and on ground. The results reveal that the TiCo-based Gd-Co-Ti alloy samples solidified in space show a shell/core structure with a surface Gd-rich layer and uniformly dispersed Gd-rich particles within the internal matrix, which is controlled by the nucleation behavior of the Gd-rich droplets on sample surface, the diffusion of solute Gd and the Marangoni motion of droplets. The Gd-based Gd-Co-Ti alloy samples solidified in space show a dispersed composite microstructure except for a thin surface layer of Gd-rich phase. In contrast, the samples solidified on ground show a macro-segregated microstructure due to the natural convection as well as the Stokes motions of precipitated phase. This work not only provides critical insights into the phase separation dynamics and microstructure evolution during the solidification of immiscible alloys, but also lays a theoretical foundation for designing immiscible alloys with core/shell structure or dispersed composite microstructure.

title: Synergistic improvements in efficiency and capability of abnormal grain growth of Fe-based shape memory alloys via regulating phase transformation behavior
abstract: Tailored abnormal grain growth (AGG) enables precise microstructure design. This work reveals a novel AGG mode, where phase transformation-induced subgrains not only provide an immense driving force but also govern the selection of abnormal grains through a specialized subgrain-evolution pathway. Co element is introduced to enhance the formation of γ precipitates with a high number density in the α matrix of a Fe-based shape memory alloy. The high number density of γ precipitates increases the number density of subgrains and broadens the subgrain misorientation distribution. A broad range of subgrain misorientations is beneficial to the abnormal subgrain growth, leading to a large difference in number density of subgrains within neighboring grains. Grains with a low subgrain number density grow preferentially by consuming those with higher number densities. The high number density of subgrains possesses a large amount of stored energy, providing a strong driving force for abnormal grain growth. As a result, grain boundary migration rates reach 1.6×10−5 m·s−1 and form large grains with sizes exceeding 1 cm in the Fe–34Mn–15Al–7.5Ni–7.5Co (at.%) alloy. This work provides new insights into the selective growth and driving force for AGG.

title: High-density inclined polar skyrmions with giant piezoelectricity
abstract: Abstract Topological polar textures offer a fertile ground for exploring fascinating physical behaviors and novel functionalities in modern electronics. Although many polar topological structures were discovered in the last decade, what new or enhanced properties could they endow remains poorly explored. Here we propose a design framework that integrates crystallographic orientation engineering and anisotropic strain modulation to construct high density inclined polar skyrmions with giant piezoelectricity (> 500 pC/N) in (111)-oriented PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices by the phase-field method. Crucially, the inclined skyrmions exhibit intrinsic field-induced strain amplification localized at their core polarization regions, effectively functioning as three-dimensional electromechanically active elements that drive the macroscopic piezoelectric enhancement in the superlattices, yielding nearly a 1000% increase compared to the PbTiO3 single-layer film under the same orientation and strain conditions. These findings uncover a topological route to amplified piezoelectric functionality, underscoring the promise of orientation-strain design strategies in reconfigurable ferroics and advanced topotronic platforms.

title: Mechanism of Ductile-to-Brittle Transition in Hexagonal Close-Packed Zinc
abstract: The ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT), a well-known phenomenon in body-centered cubic metals, has inconclusive evidence suggesting hexagonal close-packed (HCP) zinc (Zn) may also exhibit such a sharp transition. To confirm this behavior and uncover its mechanisms, we systematically studied DBT in Zn using small-punch test. We compared recrystallized Zn with hot-rolled Zn, which have different initial dislocation densities. Recrystallized Zn shows a sudden DBT with a DBT temperature (DBTT) of -20 °C, while hot-rolled Zn exhibits significantly higher toughness, with its DBTT lowered to -90 °C. Mechanistic analysis reveals that below DBTT, limited mobility of <c+a> edge dislocations restricts plastic deformation, suppresses twinning, and limits strain along the <c>-axis. Above DBTT, coordinated motion of <c+a> edge and screw dislocations and active {101¯2} twinning enable ductile deformation. The improved low-temperature toughness in hot-rolled Zn stems from its pre-existing mobile <c+a> screw dislocations. These results not only link the DBT of Zn to <c+a> dislocation characteristics and twinning propensity, but also propose a dislocation engineering method to enhance toughness in HCP metals.

title: Quantifying densification versus shear flow during glass nanoindentation via atomic-scale descriptors
abstract: Plastic deformation in glasses under sharp contact loading can occur through distinct mechanisms, ranging from volumetric densification to shear flow. While molecular dynamics simulations provide detailed atomic-scale information, a transferable framework to quantitatively compare these mechanisms across chemically distinct glasses is still lacking.In this work, we introduce a set of atomic-scale descriptors to quantify densification and shear flow during nanoindentation, derived from local irreversible deformation fields obtained from molecular dynamics simulations. The analysis combines volumetric and deviatoric strain components, atomic-scale densification, and the non-affine displacement measure D2min​, with particular emphasis on the residual deformation after unloading to isolate plastic effects.The proposed approach is applied to vitreous SiO2​, a sodium silicate, albite, anorthite glasses and the Cu64​Zr36 metallic glass, spanning densification-dominated, shear-dominated, and mixed deformation behaviours. We show that strain-based descriptors alone are insufficient to uniquely discriminate these mechanisms. To address this limitation, we introduce an end-member-based Densification–Shear Fraction (DSF), constructed from residual densification and non-affine rearrangement intensity. The DSF provides a continuous and physically grounded quantification of the relative contribution of densification and shear flow. This framework establishes a unified and transferable atomic-scale description of nanoindentation-induced plasticity, applicable to chemically diverse glassy systems.

title: Atomistic understanding of interdependence of crystal growth of two seeds embedded in glass
abstract: Recent results showed that during growth, a crystal seed embedded in glass experiences nonuniform forces from the host matrix. This result raised the possibility that during devitrification of glass, the growth of a crystal can be affected by the presence of neighboring crystals. To investigate the nature of any such interdependence of growth of neighboring crystals, atomic scale morphology of two seeds growing in a glass matrix was simulated as a function of their separation and relative misorientation. The results show a coupled rotation of seeds driven by (1) non-uniform forces from the surrounding glass, and (2) mutual interactions between the seeds. At small separations and low misorientation, each seed rotates toward perfect alignment, ultimately forming a single crystal. The onset and rate of alignment, as well as subsequent crystal growth, are strongly dependent on the growth temperature. In contrast, at larger separations and higher misorientation, the seeds can not achieve full alignment before coalescing, resulting in polycrystalline structures.

title: Hidden static length scale controls anomalous dynamical heterogeneity in sheared metallic glasses
abstract: Under external loads, disordered materials usually exhibit significant local (nanoscale) rearrangement before fracture, which plays a crucial role in controlling their mechanical properties. However, the underlying physics that governs their local plastic behavior remains largely unknown. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we show that the rearrangements in sheared glasses exhibit a non-trivial spatiotemporal heterogeneity. Unexpectedly, we observe that the shear-introduced dynamical heterogeneity decreases upon decreasing cooling rate. By adopting machine learning and activation-relaxation techniques, we unveil a direct linkage between the dynamical correlation length during the deformation process and the static correlation length from the undeformed structure. From the viewpoint of energy landscapes, we rationalize this linkage in terms of dynamic facilitation, which in turn is controlled by the spatial heterogeneity of the local energy barriers.

title: Decomposition of low-angle grain boundaries
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) merge and grains disappear during microstructure evolution. However, the Peach-Koehler model predicts that particular stress states may reverse such a process by exerting differential Peach-Koehler forces on different dislocations. This work considers this reversal as GB decomposition and illustrates it in a low-angle asymmetric tilt GB and a low-angle mixed tilt-twist GB via atomistic simulation. In both cases, the dislocations separate into two GBs separated by a new grain. This work describes the requirements for decomposition and the importance of dislocation separability. Additionally, we examine the dislocation behaviors and stress signatures associated with this process, along with the impact of strain rate and temperature on those aspects.

title: A full non-equilibrium partial solute drag model for rapid solidification of a binary alloy: modeling and verification
abstract: Rapid solidification technologies have driven imperative need for highly accurate kinetic models for migration of non-equilibrium solid/liquid (S/L) interface. Existing models, however, are unable to simultaneously address two critical issues, i.e., the non-equilibrium solute diffusion effect in the bulk phases and the solute drag effect influencing both interface migration and trans-interface diffusion at the interface. By employing the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) to self-consistently handle the dependent dissipation processes and their constraints, this study developed a full non-equilibrium partial solute drag (FNE-PSD) model for rapid solidification of a binary alloy, which integrates the above two issues into a unified description. To validate the current FNE-PSD model, molecular dynamics simulation was performed for the Ni-30 at.%Cu alloy and the key kinetic parameters in the composition and velocity response functions were derived directly without introducing any preset parameter. Results showed that the FNE-PSD model accurately captures the sharp transition to complete solute trapping (CST) as the interface velocity reaches the solute diffusion velocity in the liquid. Compared with the recent local non-equilibrium partial solute drag (LNE-PSD) model, the current FNE-PSD model could successfully predict the solute drag dependent solute trapping behavior from the case without solute drag to the case with full solute drag. The current work indicates the TEP might provide a robust framework that is critical to advancing modelling non-equilibrium kinetics and controlling non-equilibrium processing.

title: Mitigating hydride embrittlement in zirconium via twin-twin networks
abstract: Brittle hydride precipitation and fracture are primary causes of hydrogen embrittlement in zirconium (Zr). Mitigating hydride-induced cracking through microstructural design remains a challenge. Here, we demonstrate that twin boundaries (TBs) can be manipulated to effectively curb hydride precipitation and thwart hydride-induced ductility loss. Microscopic analysis reveals that TBs act as preferential nucleation sites for hydrides, with parallel long twins promoting continuous nucleation and growth of hydrides along TBs and in turn facilitating hydride-induced cracking. In contrast, a high density of intersecting narrow twins limits hydride growth and packing, yielding fine-sized hydrides that exhibit enhanced room-temperature deformability. These finer hydrides are likely to also serve as effective sources for pyramidal <c+a> dislocations, which helps to further suppress hydride-embrittlement and enhance ductility. The TB/hydride relationship discovered here introduces a potential pathway for designing hydride-embrittlement resistant microstructures.

title: Hardness and compression-induced cracking of lithium nickel oxide (LNO) secondary particles in a Li-ion battery
abstract: A macro-indentation technique is used to measure the hardness of polycrystalline lithium nickel oxide (LNO) particles in the composite cathode of a Li ion battery. The LNO particles are prepared at selected states of delithiation and are either uncoated or coated with amorphous alumina by particle atomic layer deposition (P-ALD): the P-ALD alumina coating enhances the electrochemical performance of the LNO cathode particles. A Vickers pyramidal indenter is used to indent the LNO cathode layer on a soft metallic substrate; the LNO layer thickness is much less than the indent depth, and consequently the indentation pressure is dictated by the hardness of the substrate. The average contact hardness of the LNO particles against the pyramidal indenter exceeds that of the substrate and is calculated from the true area of contact of the LNO particles, as measured by a scanning electron microscope (SEM). Additionally, high-throughput 3D profiling of the deformed cathode surfaces by an optical microscope is used to measure the true area of contact between LNO particles and indenter; the two techniques give excellent agreement. The average contact hardness of LNO particles is independent of both indent depth and hardness of the substrate. The contact hardness of the polycrystalline LNO particles is also independent of the presence of the P-ALD coating. A contact hardness of 345 +/- 22 MPa is measured for uncycled polycrystalline LNO particles in the initial, lithiated state; this hardness approximately halves when the LNO is delithiated.

title: Cyclic stability of nanolamellar titanium dictated by grain-boundary inclination and topology
abstract: The stability of microstructures during fatigue loading has emerged as a pervasive issue in both engineering practice and fundamental materials science. Addressing this challenge and elucidating the underlying mechanical mechanisms are essential prerequisites for ensuring the long-term reliable service of high-performance engineering materials and for advancing existing safety assessment frameworks. Here, a gradient nanolamellar structure was fabricated in commercially pure titanium via ultrasonic surface rolling processing, exhibiting superior fatigue performance compared with a gradient equiaxed ultrafine-grained counterpart. Post-fatigue microstructural characterization reveals that the nanolamellar layer undergoes limited coarsening during cyclic loading, indicative of excellent cyclic mechanical stability, whereas the equiaxed ultrafine-grained layer undergoes pronounced abnormal grain growth. The results of large-scale atomistic simulations attribute the enhanced cyclic stability of the nanolamellar architecture to a coupled grain-boundary configuration, in which vertical low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) accommodate cyclic deformation through highly reversible glide and absorption of grain-boundary dislocations, while horizontal high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) remain essentially immobile. Furthermore, extensive parametric investigations demonstrate that both the inclination of LAGBs and the grain-boundary topology strongly influence the cyclic stability of the lamellar structure. The results suggest that, although plastic deformation–induced microstructural evolution during fatigue is unavoidable, such evolution should not disrupt the key microstructural parameters governing strength in order to achieve a favorable balance between mechanical performance and fatigue stability. These findings further advance the mechanistic understanding of cyclic mechanical stability and may provide a new strategy for tailoring nanostructured metastable microstructures in metals for fatigue-critical applications.

title: Oxide nucleation via threshold-driven volume instability in Ni oxidation
abstract: Oxide nucleation dictates the onset of metal oxidation, yet the atomistic pathways bridging initial oxygen adsorption to bulk phase transformation remain elusive. Here, we utilize in-situ atomic-resolution imaging to directly capture the nucleation of nickel oxide, revealing a threshold-driven, cooperative transformation of Ni into NiO. Our observations identify a distinct incubation period during which oxygen progressively accumulates in subsurface layers. Once a critical concentration and penetration depth are reached, a collective lattice reconfiguration is triggered, abruptly converting multiple Ni layers into NiO. Atomistic simulations corroborate this mechanism, identifying a cooperative lattice instability induced by subsurface oxygen saturation. These results establish subsurface oxygen incorporation as the missing mechanistic link between surface adsorption and three-dimensional oxide formation, providing an atomistic framework to understand and control reactive phase transformations in materials synthesis, catalysis, and degradation.

title: High-throughput discovery of Ti-based low thermal expansion materials via machine-learning-accelerated ab-initio molecular dynamics
abstract: Low thermal expansion materials are essential for aerospace thermal-protection systems and electronic packaging, where strict requirements demand near-zero thermal expansion together with low density, non-magnetic behavior, low thermal-expansion anisotropy, and low thermal conductivity. In this work, the discovery of low thermal expansion compounds is accelerated using an on-the-fly machine-learning ab-initio molecular dynamics (ML-AIMD) framework. The accuracy and reliability of ML-AIMD are first validated against compounds with reported thermal-expansion coefficients. High-throughput screening of 672 binary Ti-based compounds yields 8 negative-expansion, 10 near-zero-expansion, and 5 zero-expansion candidates. The anisotropic thermal expansion and elastic properties of the shortlisted materials are systematically evaluated. Variable-temperature X-ray diffraction measurements confirm that the selected representative λ-Ti3O5 exhibits an ultralow volumetric thermal-expansion coefficient of −1.5 × 10−7 K−1 over 280–360 K. Anharmonic phonon calculations show that this behavior originates from negative Grüneisen parameters associated with low-frequency phonon modes. Compared with traditional low thermal expansion materials, λ-Ti3O5 uniquely combines near-zero thermal expansion with non-magnetic character, low density, ultralow thermal conductivity, and low thermal-expansion anisotropy. This work establishes a generalizable high-throughput paradigm integrating ML-AIMD simulations, experimental characterization, and anharmonic phonon analysis for the efficient discovery of advanced low thermal expansion materials.

title: Interfacial reactions, nanoscale precipitation and strengthening in a TiNiCuZrNbTa alloy deposited on copper by laser-directed energy deposition
abstract: Depositing refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) onto copper offers a promising route to enhance surface performance, but achieving interfacial compatibility and metallurgical integrity remains challenging because of the large differences in thermophysical properties and solidification behavior between the two materials. Here, a TiNiCuZrNbTa RHEA layer was fabricated on a copper substrate by laser-directed energy deposition (L-DED). By coupling thermodynamically informed alloy design with the non-equilibrium solidification conditions inherent to L-DED, a chemically and structurally graded interface was produced through elemental interdiffusion, nanoscale precipitation, and pronounced grain refinement. The interfacial region developed into a hierarchically organized nanocomposite architecture comprising TiCuNi, TiNb, and Zr14Cu51 phases with coherent or semi-coherent interphase boundaries, and dispersed Ta-rich nanoclusters in the adjacent Cu matrix. These features accommodate lattice mismatch and promote interfacial stability during solidification. As a consequence, the deposited layer exhibited a hardness exceeding 520 HV, accompanied by improved wear and corrosion resistance. The enhanced performance is attributed to the synergistic effects of hierarchical microstructural refinement, nanoscale phase strengthening and stable interfacial load transfer. These findings established a link between alloy design, interfacial nanostructure development, and interfacial integrity, providing mechanistic insights into interface engineering in additively manufactured surface modified systems.

title: Mechanisms of size effects in elastic architected solids
abstract: Architected solids, typically manufactured by additive manufacturing, contain a limited number of unit cells and therefore resemble discrete structures rather than continuum materials. The number of unit cells in a specimen of an architected solid is referred to here as the specimen size. Using extensive finite element simulations complemented by analytical analysis, we demonstrate counterintuitive specimen-size effects across several classes of architected solids subjected to different loading conditions. In contrast to conventional continuum materials, size effects are strongest under uniaxial loading, where the applied loading does not impose a macroscopic stress/strain gradient, and are comparatively weak under indentation loading, which imposes strong stress/strain gradients. Moreover, smaller could be either stiffer or more compliant dependent on the lattice topology and/or nature of loading. Two key mechanisms governing these size effects are identified: free-surface effects arising from differences in strut sharing between surface and bulk unit cells, and size-dependent changes in deformation mode from bending-dominated to stretching-dominated behavior. Consequently, no universal size-effect trend exists; instead, stiffness depends on both lattice topology and loading mode. These findings highlight the need for caution when extracting effective material properties from experiments on architected solids with a limited number of unit cells.

title: From phase state to pit pattern: A wetting-controlled mechanism for localized corrosion
abstract: The long-standing puzzle of why symmetric circular pits form on iron surfaces remains unresolved. Traditional acidity-based interpretations alone do not explain the symmetric pits and coffee-ring-like product bands observed under supercritical conditions. Here, using steel in a CO 2 –H 2 O environment as a model system and combining correlative microscopy and spectroscopy with molecular dynamics, ab initio molecular dynamics, and finite-element simulations, we show that phase state influences localized corrosion through its effect on interfacial wetting. As CO 2 changes from the gaseous to the supercritical state, the interfacial CO 2 layer becomes denser, more ordered, and less mobile, increasing the tendency for contact-line pinning of condensed droplets on the metal surface. The pinned geometry in turn promotes confined microenvironments, droplet-scale flow, and evaporation-driven solute redistribution, leading to FeCO 3 enrichment at the rim and oxide formation at the pit bottom. These coupled interfacial and transport effects provide a consistent explanation for both symmetric pit formation and the spatial separation of corrosion products. Similar morphology transitions observed across multiple steels suggest that this phase-to-pattern framework may be relevant beyond the present CO 2 –H 2 O system. Overall, the results identify interfacial wetting as an important factor in localized corrosion and suggest new opportunities for mitigating pitting through control of droplet attachment and mobility.

title: Promoting strain delocalization in refractory high-entropy alloys via local chemical fluctuations
abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) demonstrate significant potential due to their outstanding mechanical strength. However, the limited tensile ductility of most RHEAs hinders their widespread applications. Local chemical fluctuations (LCFs) have emerged as a research hotspot to overcome the dilemma between strength and ductility, yet their specific role during plastic deformation remains debated. To investigate the effect of LCFs on uniform plastic deformation, Ti50Nb20V30 (TNV) and Ti45Nb15V30Zr10 (TNVZ) RHEAs was designed by precisely controlling microstructures. Zr-V-enriched LCFs are present in TNVZ alloy. Here we show that LCFs change strain distribution by retaining edge dislocations during deformation. This edge dislocation retention transforms the dislocation system from screw-dominated to mixed. The strong interaction between screw and edge dislocations formed by the asymmetric stress field of edge dislocations enhanced latent hardening. The LCFs-induced high latent hardening activates {110} <111>, {112} <111>, and {123} <111> three slip systems. Meanwhile, the excellent deformation compatibility between grains enables slip transfer across grain boundaries, facilitating the propagation of plastic deformation into unhardened regions. This fundamentally alter the deformation localization characteristics of TNV alloy, achieving a fundamental transition toward macro-scale uniform plastic deformation along the entire gauge. This work provides systematic experimental evidence for understanding the role of LCFs in the plastic deformation, laying a scientific foundation for the future design of high-performance heterogeneous high-entropy alloy.

title: Systematic modeling of atomic matching in incoherent and heterointerfaces
abstract: Lattice defects commonly arise in crystalline materials, and interfacial atomic structures play a critical role in determining functional properties. This study develops a general theoretical framework for quantitatively describing atomic matching at incoherent grain boundaries and heterointerfaces. The approach extends the coincidence-site lattice (CSL) theory, originally formulated for commensurate grain boundaries, to systems with arbitrary lattice-parameter ratios and misorientations. By incorporating the displacement-shift complete lattice (DSCL), we introduce commensurability indices that characterize the degree of atomic matching even in heterointerfaces. The formulation shows that the commensurability index can be expressed using the ratio of unit-cell volumes between the CSL and the DSCL of two lattices. This relationship is further generalized to diverse lattice combinations, enabling systematic determination of relative rotation angles and matching periodicities. The dominant matching periodicity of an interface can be identified by determining a rational approximant to the lattice-parameter ratio between two crystals, allowing efficient construction of commensurate supercells for computational modeling, even in systems with large lattice mismatches. The proposed framework systematically relates higher-order matching relations to combinations of lower-order structural motifs through continued-fraction expansion and Farey sequences, providing a geometrical basis for interpreting interfacial matching. This work establishes a unified methodology for analyzing interfacial commensurability in crystalline materials and provides a mathematical framework for guiding the design of heterointerfaces and advanced functional materials, thereby contributing to the efficient exploration of novel materials.

title: TiC addition enhances thermal stability and mitigates intermediate-temperature embrittlement in Al–Ce–Ni additively manufactured via laser powder bed fusion
abstract: Al–Ce-based alloys processed using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are characterized by a high-volume fraction of eutectic networks. While exhibiting promising elevated temperature (250–400 °C) mechanical properties, they suffer from strength degradation after prolonged thermal exposure and a decrease in elongation-to-fracture (εf) with increasing temperature. Here, we show that adding 5 wt.% TiC particles to a near-eutectic Al–10Ce–4Ni (wt.%) (AlCeNi) alloy mitigates both issues, albeit at the expense of reduced room-temperature εf. TiC addition reduces solute supersaturation in the α-Al matrix, increases the volume fraction of intermetallics, and promotes a more homogeneous melt-pool-scale microstructure. It also enhances thermal stability, as evidenced by a higher hardness retention ratio after thermal exposure, due to the suppressed coarsening of intergranular Ni-rich phases and the formation of a stable Al20Ti2Ce phase. AlCeNi exhibits an εf dip over 250–350 °C, caused by aggravated void nucleation and growth in the relatively softer heat-affected zone (HAZ), even with an increased strain rate sensitivity (SRS). TiC addition induces melt-pool-scale homogeneity and a TiC–matrix heterogeneity, shifting strain localization from HAZ to TiC particles. The failure evolves from TiC particle cracking (RT–200 °C) to void nucleation (300–400 °C), enabling more progressive damage evolution. This weakens the heterogeneity-induced reduction in εf under the increased SRS at RT–350 °C, thereby eliminating the εf dip. These findings identify TiC-assisted composition control as an effective route to simultaneously enhance thermal stability and suppress εf dip in LPBF near-eutectic Al alloys for high temperature service.

title: Atomistic mechanisms of carbon-induced strengthening and oriented precipitation in TiAl-Nb-C alloys
abstract: Titanium aluminide (TiAl) alloys exhibit high specific strength and outstanding high-temperature performance, making them ideal for advanced aerospace applications. While alloying with Nb and C is known to enhance the high-temperature strength of TiAl alloys, the underlying atomistic mechanism remains unclear, due to challenges in reliably capturing dynamic processes. Here, we develop a high-precision neuro-evolution potential (NEP) that can describe the essential properties of TiAl-Nb-C alloys with near ab initio accuracy, including surface/interface energies, stacking fault energies, atomic diffusion barriers and even the pinning effect of C atoms on dislocations. Simulations with the NEP above 800 K suggest that C atoms suppress deformation twinning and dislocation gliding by raising the energy barriers for stacking faults formation, thereby improving the creep resistance of TiAl alloys. Moreover, the carbides/matrix interfaces further govern mechanical behavior: the Ti2AlC/γ-TiAl interface generates a triangular dislocation network that strengthens the alloy but compromises plastic compatibility, while the γ-TiAl/Ti3AlC interface activates multiple slip systems and provides more dislocation slip paths, synergistically enhancing both strength and uniform plastic deformation. We further demonstrate that thermodynamic preference and low TiAl antisite concentration promote the directed nucleation and growth of Ti3AlC along the [001] direction. Subsequent large-scale simulations reveal that this preference is strongly reinforced by a lower elastic misfit strain energy along [001] compared with other orientations, collectively leading to the experimentally observed needle-like morphology. These findings establish an atomistic foundation for the rational design of high-performance TiAl alloys through controlled carbide precipitation and interface engineering.

title: Cross-scale investigation of temperature-driven transition from intragranular slip to grain boundary sliding in Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloys
abstract: Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloys exhibit exceptional high-temperature thermal stability, presenting significant potential for lightweight, heat-resistant components in aerospace and transportation sectors. Understanding the temperature-dependent evolution of deformation mechanisms in Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloys is critical for evaluating service behavior in intermediate-temperature environments and optimizing high-temperature forming processes. However, quantitatively characterizing the thermal effects on strain localization and elucidating the cross-scale relationship between dislocation activity and strain partitioning remain significant challenges. Herein, we integrate in-situ high-resolution digital image correlation (HR-DIC), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to systematically investigate multiscale microstructural strain localization from room temperature (RT) to 450 °C. The study reveals a progressive evolution in strain partitioning: at RT, deformation is dominated by homogeneous intragranular slip driven by the synergistic activation of multiple slip systems. In the 250-350 °C range, grain boundary sliding (GBS) intensifies, while intragranular slip diminishes and slip bands become increasingly localized. At 450 °C, diffusion-assisted GBS dominates, suppressing intragranular slip and producing a quasi-superplastic response. Dislocation analysis further demonstrates that, with increasing temperature, the intragranular dislocation density decreases markedly, while dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries intensify, clearly delineating a transition from slip-controlled plasticity to grain-boundary-controlled diffusion creep. These results systematically and quantitatively reveal the deformation behavior of Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloys over a wide temperature range. In addition, the proposed cross-scale SEM-TEM analysis approach establishes a general framework for characterizing deformation mechanisms in metallic materials, which can be readily extended to the analysis of other metallic materials.

title: Giant electrostrain via field induced structural transformation in Sm doped BiFeO3-PbTiO3 ceramics revealed by in-situ synchronous X-ray diffraction
abstract: This study identifies the structural origin of giant electrostrain in samarium-doped bismuth ferrite lead titanate (0.55Bi1-xSmxFeO3-0.45PbTiO3) ceramics. A giant peak-to-peak electrostrain (~0.5 % at 60 kV cm-1) was obtained for compositions with x = 0.20 (20Sm), superior to Pb(Zr,Ti)O3 based ceramics with similar phase transition temperature of 275 oC, coupled with a piezoelectric coefficient of 276 pC/N comparable with hard PZT. While 20Sm is a macroscopically pseudo-cubic relaxor in its unpoled state, an irreversible, field-induced transformation gives a tetragonal (c/a~1.115) ferroelectric phase as revealed by in-situ poling synchrotron X-ray diffraction and confirmed by transmission electron microscopy. The field-induced domain structure of the tetragonal structure could be reversibly switched under AC field after transformation. Quantitative strain analysis confirmed that the structural transformation accounts for approximately half of the total electrostrain, with the remainder by domain switching. These results highlight the importance of field-induced structural transformations for the development of high-performance piezoelectrics.

title: Achieving superior strength-ductility synergy in additively manufactured austenitic steel through residual stress-driven nanotwin growth
abstract: To solve a field-wide problem of strength-ductility trade-off in metallic materials, decoupling strength and ductility is achieved in additively manufactured austenitic stainless steel (SS) by nanotwin (NT) engineering. Boosting growth of NTs is initiated in austenitic SS printed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) via surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) and low-temperature annealing. During annealing, the explosive growth of NTs in the SMATed sample is promoted from melt pool boundaries (MPBs), preset stacking faults and deformed NTs via sequences of γ→ε→NT and γ→9R→NT, while that in LPBFed sample is expressed by γ→ε→NT from MPBs. Crucially, this transition is driven by the high residual stress of -660 MPa induced by SMAT, which facilitates NT growth and suppresses martensitic transformation. Compared with the original LPBF sample, the strength-plasticity synergy is achieved in the SMATed sample annealed at 400 °C, representing by a yield strength from 400 MPa of the original to 829 MPa, and an elongation from 48% to 58%. The strengthening is primarily attributed to the cooperation of refined dislocation cells and NT proliferation, while the plasticity is gained by strain hardening of NTs. This approach provides an effective strategy to attain nanotwinned structure with exceptional mechanical properties in additively-manufactured high-strength alloys.

title: Strengthening and hydrogen-embrittlement resistance via in situ TiC reprecipitation in an additively manufactured high-entropy alloy
abstract: Additively manufactured alloys typically exhibit higher strength than their cast counterparts, owing to the formation of cellular substructures composed of high-density dislocations during the printing process. The high strength level increases the risk of hydrogen embrittlement (HE) of which the mechanisms and the mitigating strategies are unclear in additively manufactured materials. Here we show that an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy produced by additive manufacturing, in contrast to the cast and thermomechanically treated conditions, is rather susceptible to HE. This susceptibility arises from orientation-dependent, H-enhanced decohesion of specific high-angle grain boundary segments aligned relative to the loading direction. We further show that this decohesion process is mitigated by an in situ reprecipitation strategy enabled by rapid additive manufacturing of a carefully designed composite powder feedstock containing TiC nanoparticles. Beyond the intrinsic H trapping associated with TiC precipitates, this strategy also induces a set of correlated microstructural changes, including reduced Mn segregation at grain boundaries and modified deformation behavior and local stress states. These coupled effects collectively contribute to the suppression of H-induced decohesion. As a result, this in situ reprecipitation strategy yields a substantial increase in HE resistance compared to a microstructure devoid of such nanoprecipitates, together with a marked increase in strength (∼290 MPa). The successful reconciliation of these two competing properties provides valuable insights into the design of alloys with similar microstructure and deformation behavior, particularly for lightweight and safety-critical components used in H-rich environments.

title: Theory of coexisting dislocations, disclinations and inclusions in solid crystals: topological constraints and stress fields
abstract: Dislocations, disclinations, and inclusions (e.g., twins and second-phase particles) are three fundamental types of crystalline defects whose formation and interaction critically influence the microstructural evolution and mechanical as well as functional responses of metallic materials. Particularly during thermomechanical processing, their coexistence and interactions/reactions give rise to complex defect configurations and heterogeneous internal stress fields, significantly affecting strength, ductility, and fracture toughness. A quantitative understanding of the topological and energetic coupling among these defects is essential to elucidate their collective impact on microstructure and mechanical behavior, yet these aspects under consideration of their coupling effects remain underexplored. Here, we present a unified field theory framework for determining the stress fields induced by arbitrarily distributed dislocations, disclinations, and inclusions in anisotropic elastic media. By formulating generalized Green’s functions via a matrix pseudoinverse scheme in reciprocal space, the framework yields analytical expressions for stress fields and enables efficient numerical implementation through a Fast Fourier Transform-based solver. Validation against existing analytical solutions demonstrates that the calculated stress fields are in quantitative agreement with classical solutions across representative cases, such as dislocation/disclination dipoles and Eshelby inclusions. More importantly, the approach is particularly effective in analyzing complex defect configurations (e.g., low-angle grain boundaries, interface dislocations, and twin-twin intersections) within a general framework that captures the coupling of diverse coexisting defects. With the formulated topological and energetic coupling equations for multiple defect types, we show that the correlated configurations of coexisting defects determine structural and stress discontinuities at homo-/hetero-phase boundaries and at junctions. Our work suggests a new quantitative tool to characterize heterogeneous internal stress states in multi-phase polycrystalline microstructures, offering a theoretical foundation for understanding micromechanical behavior and the microstructure–property relationships in metals and alloys.

title: Dynamic coupling of TRIP effect and hetero-deformation-induced (HDI) hardening in a hierarchical eutectic high-entropy alloy
abstract: Overcoming the pervasive strength-ductility trade-off in metallic materials requires the synergistic activation of multiple deformation mechanisms. Heterostructural design offers an effective strategy to regulate strain partitioning and evoke extra deformation mechanisms. Here, we designed a hierarchical heterostructured eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring alternating equiaxed grain regions (EGR) and lamellar grain regions (LGR). This architected microstructure gives rise to a pronounced TRIP-assisted hardening behavior and delivers an outstanding strength-ductility synergy, achieving an ultimate tensile strength of ∼1.57 GPa together with a uniform elongation of ∼24% at room temperature. The exceptional tensile properties originate from the hierarchical heterostructure and the associated martensitic transformation activated in the EGR, which sustains a high work-hardening rate throughout tensile deformation. Hetero-deformation between EGR and LGR generates elevated internal stresses, thereby triggering martensitic transformation in the EGR, particularly near disrupted K-S interfaces. This transformation effectively redistributes strain and mitigates local stress concentrations. The occurrence of martensitic transformation is directly verified by in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction. Moreover, the formation of L10 martensite introduces additional phase boundaries and mechanical contrast, which promote dislocation storage and sustain hetero-deformation-induced (HDI) hardening, thereby delaying the onset of necking. This study demonstrates that hierarchical heterostructure design not only enables HDI hardening but also facilitates the activation and utilization of unconventional deformation mechanisms via increased internal stresses, providing a new paradigm for the development of high-performance eutectic high-entropy alloys.

title: Influence of sample size, strain rate and temperature on deformation of an Fe-2.4 wt.% Si Bi-crystal and its paired single crystals
abstract: Grain boundaries play an important role in determining mechanical properties of materials. To investigate the behavior of a single grain boundary, micropillar compression on bi-crystals has been widely applied, which however, mainly focuses on face-centered cubic metals. In this work, we investigate the influence of micropillar size, strain rate and temperature on deformation behavior of an Fe-2.4 wt.% Si bi-crystal with a high angle grain boundary and its paired single crystals. Tests were carried out at room temperature and -80°C, nominal micropillar sizes were 1 µm, 2 µm and 4 µm, while strain rates were 0.001 s-1, 0.01 s-1 and 0.1 s-1. Slip trace analysis reveals slip transmission across the grain boundary in bi-crystalline pillars. The transmitted slip systems can be different from those activated in single crystals depending on orientation. The identified transmission pair has a high transmission factor and is insensitive to strain rate and temperature, but dependent on pillar size. In contrast, the difference in yield strength between bi-crystals and single crystals is more closely related to testing parameters. For single crystals, smaller pillars can activate slip systems with a lower Schmid factor and slip traces become wavy due to cross-slip at a sub-ambient temperature.

title: Dual role of B in hydrogen embrittlement resistance of high-strength martensitic medium-Mn steel
abstract: The hydrogen embrittlement (HE) behavior of medium-Mn steel was investigated by varying the B content (0–280 wt ppm). All specimens exhibited fully martensitic structures with comparable prior austenite grain (PAG) sizes; however, B addition led to pronounced segregation at PAG boundaries and the formation of Fe2B precipitates, whose size and fraction increased with increasing B content. Under comparable diffusible H contents, HE resistance improved up to ∼30 wt ppm B and deteriorated at higher B contents. The enhanced HE resistance at 30 wt ppm B is attributed to B segregation at PAG boundaries, which suppresses H accumulation. Steels containing ≥60 wt ppm B exhibited reduced HE resistance due to crack initiation within or near coarse Fe2B particles. During tensile deformation, B-added steels showed an additional H desorption rate peak associated with H detrapping from misfit dislocations around Fe2B particles and H migration into borides, promoting embrittlement and crack initiation.

title: Morphological transition: From meanders to mound structures
abstract: Mound formation on flat and miscut crystal surfaces exhibits distinct growth behaviors. While mound structures are the predominant feature on flat surfaces, miscut surfaces display a smooth transition from meandered patterns to three-dimensional mounds, depending on both internal and external conditions. We investigate this morphological evolution-from meander-like surface patterns to faceted pyramidal structures-using a Vicinal Cellular Automaton modeling framework. The transition is shown to be governed by the competition between the Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier and adatom mobility on terraces. Under moderate barrier strengths and sufficiently high terrace diffusivity, the system demonstrates a reversible transition from mounded configurations to regular step meandered patterns. This reveals a complex interplay between kinetic barriers and mass transport. Our simulations cover a wide range of growth conditions, including variations in deposition flux, surface diffusion rates, temperature, and miscut angle. By applying the height-height correlation function, we calculate the correlation lengths along and across the steps and analyze their scaling behavior. These results offer insight into the continuum pathways that connect distinct classes of surface structures and provide a unified framework for describing pattern evolution across different crystal growth regimes.

title: Elastic moduli as quantitative surrogates of precipitation kinetics in age-hardenable aluminum alloys
abstract: Quantitative knowledge of precipitation kinetics is essential for designing heat treatments that tailor the properties of age-hardenable aluminum alloys. Conventional methods frequently show limitations for characterizing fast kinetics during quenching or slow kinetics during aging, and may be complex, giving rise to the need for reliable and effective approaches. This contribution presents a novel characterization approach for the determination of precipitation kinetics based on the evolution of the macroscopic elastic behavior. Precipitates and matrix exhibit different elastic properties, resulting in changes in macroscopic elastic moduli during dissolution and precipitation of intermetallic phases, which are measured by the impulse excitation technique (IET). This enables the assessment of quench sensitivity through time–temperature-property (TTP) analysis based on ex-situ measurements and the determination of precipitation kinetics during aging through in-situ measurements of elastic moduli. The proposed approach is applied to the aluminum alloy AA 2219 and is verified by complementary analyses, including eddy-current testing, scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy and tensile testing.

title: Quaternion-based quantification of disclinations and defect reactions from electron backscattered diffraction data in metals
abstract: Disclinations, alongside dislocations, are fundamental topological defects in crystals with rotational characteristics, whose formation and evolution significantly influence the deformation behavior of metallic materials. While advanced characterization techniques such as electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission Kikuchi diffraction provide local crystallographic orientation information, their connection to the rotational characteristics of disclinations remains unclear, partially due to the lack of a theoretical framework that relates the Frank vector with Euler angles while accounting for the non-commutativity of rotations. In this study, we propose a quaternion-based method to establish the mathematical relationship between Frank vectors and Euler angles, enabling a rigorous quantification of disclination density from EBSD data. Systematic quasi-in-situ EBSD characterizations on magnesium alloys demonstrate that disclinations critically accommodate local strain during defect reactions (e.g., twin-grain boundary, dislocation-grain boundary, and twin-twin reactions), governing three important strain compatibility mechanisms: disclination-mediated twin transmission, dislocation-disclination cooperative relaxation, and disclination-assisted twin boundary junction coordination. Experimentally determined dislocation/disclination density distributions have been quantitatively analyzed through dislocation-disclination coupling equations, integrating the diverse defect reactions within a unified field theory framework. By adopting a quaternion-based method for quantifying disclinations, this work reveals the critical role of disclination-mediated strain accommodation in defect reactions, providing new insights into the plastic deformation behavior of polycrystalline metals.

title: Twin–slip and slip–slip transfers and associated strengthening in a near-α Zr alloy with lamellar structures
abstract: Near-α zirconium alloys with lamellar structures offer a combination of both high strength and ductility, yet the roles of α/β interfaces and grain boundaries in the compatibility of coordinating slips, twinning, and strains are not fully understood. In this study, we unveil how these localized interfacial deformations, especially twin-slip and slip-slip transfers, govern the mechanical response in a near-α Zr–10Ti alloy with a fine lamellar colony structure. Such Zr alloy exhibits a superior strength–ductility synergy, with an average yield strength of ∼758 MPa and an average fracture elongation of ∼17.7%. Using synchrotron X-ray diffraction (SXRD), we show that α grains with favorable orientations yield first and preferentially accommodate plastic strain, and, subsequently, the β-{002} planes sustain the highest lattice stresses, indicating a pronounced load transfer from α phase to β phase. Distinct interface-mediated slip–slip and twin–slip transfer behaviors have been rarely reported in near-α Zr alloys. Distinct interface-mediated slip–slip and twin–slip transfer behaviors that have been rarely reported in near-α Zr alloys. The thin β lamellae and α/α boundaries act as barriers to dislocation glide, leading to dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentration. In contrast, tensile twins can readily propagate across α/β interfaces within a colony when the Burgers orientation relationship is satisfied, whereas α/β grain boundaries strongly hinder twin transmission and promote twin-induced slip in neighboring grains. Furthermore, the grain-boundary-associated geometrically necessary dislocations (GND) provide a local, upper-bound strengthening increment of ∼173 MPa. This study demonstrates that interface-controlled twin–slip interactions and GND accumulations play an essential role in achieving concurrent high strength, ductility, and strain compatibility in lamellar near-α Zr alloys.

title: Correlation between enhanced oxygen evolution and β→γ phase transition in Mn-doped NiOOH
abstract: NiOOH is a promising electrocatalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Here we systematically investigate the effect of Mn doping on the structure, oxidation state, bond length, phase transition, and OER activity of NiOOH using dispersion-corrected hybrid density functional theory (HSE06+D3) combined with experimental material characterization and electrochemical measurements for samples that were prepared through a synthesis route mimicking Ni recovery from wastewater with circular-material benefits. Our results reveal that Mn doping promotes not only the formation of surface oxygen vacancies but also the phase transition from β- to γ-NiOOH, a critical step overlooked by previous studies. This Mn-doping is found to largely reduce the calculated overpotential, especially with respect to undoped β system, in very good agreement with experimental observations.

title: Solid/liquid interface energy and its anisotropy of pure metals
abstract: Solid/liquid (S/L) interface energy ( γ sl ) and its anisotropy ( φ ) play a critical role in the understanding of nearly every single phenomenon that occurs during solidification of metals, such as nucleation, morphological instability and dendrite growth. However, due to difficulties associated with both experimental measurement and computer simulations, our current understanding of this topic is rather limited. In this work, a simple analytical model is developed to predict γ sl and φ for pure metals. This model suggests that S/L interface energy originates from atomic ordering in the S/L interface templated by the solid. γ sl can be expressed as the sum of contributions from both atomic layering ( γ z ) and the in-plane atomic ordering ( γ xy ). Further analysis shows that γ sl for pure metals is determined by both heat of fusion per atom ( Δ H f a ) and their crystal structures, while anisotropy depends only on crystal structure. The analytical model reveals that the physical origin of γ sl is atomic ordering in the S/L interface templated by the solid, while the physical origin of anisotropy is the difference in structural templating power between different crystal planes. It is demonstrated that the current analytical model is capable of predicting solid/liquid interface energy ( γ sl ) and its anisotropy ( φ ) for any metallic element using parameters readily available in the literature.
