title: Valence-electron-associated dislocation dissociation and glide mechanisms in transition-metal carbide and nitride alloys
abstract: Conventional and high-entropy alloying are widely employed to mitigate the intrinsic brittleness of transition-metal carbides (TMCs) and nitrides (TMNs), yet the underlying dislocation-controlled mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this work, we developed a new approach to determine the Peierls stress within the Peierls-Nabarro framework, and investigated the stacking fault energies and associated dislocation properties of pure TMCs, TMNs, and their alloys. For compounds with valence electron concentration (VEC) exceeding 8 electrons per formula unit (e - /f.u.), full a / 2 〈 110 〉 { 111 } dislocations dissociate into Shockley partials, enabling stepwise glide, substantially reducing the Peierls stress, and thereby facilitating activation of the 〈110〉{111} slip system, consistent with experimental observations. For compounds with VEC ≤8 e - /f.u., the absence of an intrinsic stacking fault suppresses dislocation dissociation, resulting in large Peierls stresses. Extending these insights to both conventional and high-entropy alloys, higher-VEC solutes promote dissociation and reduce the Peierls stress, whereas lower-VEC solutes exert the opposite effect, and same-group element doping has only a minor influence. These findings lay the groundwork for elucidating the dislocation-relevant mechanism underlying alloying-induced tailoring of mechanical performance in TMC and TMN alloys.

title: Anisotropic deformation and material removal mechanisms of p-type 4H-SiC
abstract: Mechanical anisotropy in 4H-SiC has been extensively investigated in n-type and semi-insulating crystals, whereas the corresponding behavior in p-type 4H-SiC remains largely unexplored. As an indispensable substrate for vertical power devices, p-type 4H-SiC enables high breakdown voltages and low on-state losses. However, its high hardness and brittleness, coupled with crystallographic anisotropy, present significant challenges for defect-free precision processing. Here, we systematically investigate the mechanical anisotropy and ductile-to-brittle transition behavior of p-type 4H-SiC by comparing the Si-terminated (0001) and the C-terminated (0001‾) surfaces along the principal in-plane directions, [112¯0] and [11¯00]. In-situ nano-scratching results show that the material removal rate is higher along [112¯0] than along [11¯00], accompanied by a lower coefficient of friction, with the Si-terminated surface exhibiting higher machinability. Micro-Raman spectroscopy analysis indicates anisotropic residual stress fields beneath the scratches, characterized by coexisting compressive and tensile stresses. Cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy shows that scratching along [11¯00] promotes high-density threading edge dislocations, whereas basal plane dislocations dominate along [112¯0]. First-principles calculations indicate a higher slip energy barrier along [11¯00], leading to limited dislocation-mediated plasticity and a more brittle response. Additionally, distinct bonding characteristics are observed between the two surface terminations, which are consistent with the experimentally observed polarity-dependent material removal behavior. Comparative experiments with semi-insulating and n-type 4H-SiC further indicate that dopant type influences the magnitude of deformation while preserving the underlying anisotropic framework. This work provides a mechanistic understanding of anisotropic deformation and material removal behavior of p-type 4H-SiC, with implications for precision machining and strain-engineered device fabrication.

title: Domain boundary induced crack deflection enhancing the toughness of lamellar TiAl alloys
abstract: Interfacial delamination is a critical failure mode in polysynthetic twinned (PST) TiAl single crystals. Understanding the failure mechanism and deflecting crack propagation are key for enhancing the toughness of TiAl alloys. In this work, we investigated the fracture mechanisms of γ/γ true-twin boundary (TTB), γ/γ pseudo-twin boundary (PTB), and γ/α2 phase boundary (PB) in PST TiAl single crystals via hydrostatic stress loading using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with the cohesive zone model (CZM). The results indicate that the fracture mechanism of these interfaces exhibits consistency, with brittle fracture failure dominated by the propagation of the right crack, while the left crack tip can emit dislocations, thereby suppressing interfacial decohesion. We proposed a domain boundary (DB) induced toughening strategy and validated it through simulations and experiments. This strategy deflected the crack propagation path, resulting in an increase of the volumetric strain at fracture from 0.044 in the PTB model (0.038 in the TTB model) to 0.056. Through long-term high-temperature heat treatment, DBs were introduced into the γ lamellae of PST TiAl single crystals. Compared to samples without crack deflection, those with introduced DBs and crack deflection exhibit a significantly higher fracture toughness, increasing from 16.4 MPa·m1/2 to 24.0 MPa·m1/2. These findings provide an effective pathway for designing higher toughness TiAl alloys.

title: Engineering diffusion pathways for simultaneous solid-solution formation and grain refinement in Mo-Nb alloys
abstract: Solid solution formation is an effective approach to enhance the performance of alloys. However, achieving complete solid-solution formation generally requires enhanced atomic diffusion, which typically promotes grain-boundary migration and leads to grain growth. The resulting grain coarsening reduces Hall-Petch strengthening and may offset the strengthening effect derived from solid-solution formation. Here we propose a seed-assisted strategy to engineer diffusion pathways and enable the simultaneous realization of complete solid-solution formation and grain refinement in Mo-Nb alloys. By introducing a small fraction (∼19 wt.%) of preformed Mo-Nb solid-solution seeds, rapid alloying is achieved during short-time sintering, accompanied by pronounced grain refinement. Transmission electron microscopy confirms the formation of a homogeneous solid solution together with retained nanoscale seeds. Density functional theory calculations further show that the presence of preformed seeds reduces the diffusion barriers along the Mo/Mo-Nb and Nb/Mo-Nb pathways by 62-81% compared with the Mo/Mo, Nb/Nb, and Mo/Nb diffusion pathways in the non-preformed-seed system, thereby establishing energetically favorable diffusion pathways that accelerate atomic interdiffusion. The retained nanoscale seeds and transient unalloyed phases also help suppress grain growth during sintering. As a result, dense Mo-Nb alloys with refined grains (∼0.87 μm) are obtained. The resulting alloy exhibits a yield strength of 968 ± 27.8 MPa and a hardness of 479 ± 10.35 HV, representing 20%/2% and 192%/69% improvements over conventional mechanical alloying and direct mixing, respectively. This study demonstrates that seed-assisted diffusion modifies the underlying diffusion pathways, enabling enhanced atomic diffusion while limiting grain-boundary migration, thereby achieving complete alloying without excessive grain growth in refractory alloys.

title: Explaining hydrogen-accelerated high temperature creep using the defactant theory
abstract: We propose a quantitative description of creep acceleration in gaseous hydrogen environment. The central hypothesis is that hydrogen enhances high temperature creep by reducing the vacancy formation energy, thereby facilitating faster dislocation climb. By employing the defactant theory, we derive the ratio of steady-state creep strain rate in gaseous hydrogen ε ˙ H to creep rate in the absence of hydrogen ε ˙ as ε ˙ H / ε ˙ = ( 1 − Γ / Γ max ) − Γ max , where Γ is the number of hydrogen atoms trapped at a vacancy and Γ max is the maximum number of hydrogen atoms that can be trapped by a vacancy. We demonstrate the predictive capability of the proposed model by comparing with experimental measurements of creep strain rates across a range of hydrogen pressures and temperatures. Notably, this defactant-theory based formulation of creep law introduces no additional fitting parameters and is defined entirely by physically well-established quantities.

title: A phase field model of the effects of dislocation microstructure on grain boundary motion during recrystallization
abstract: The internal energy associated with the defect microstructure of strongly deformed crystals provides an important driving force for grain boundary motion during recrystallization. Typical dislocation microstructures are strongly heterogeneous and this heterogeneity affects the motion of recrystallization boundaries. In this study, a phase field model for microstructure evolution encompassing the evolution of both dislocation densities and grain order parameters is formulated. The model is employed to generate typical dislocation microstructures exhibiting multiscale features such as incidental and geometrically necessary dislocation walls. It is then used to study the motion of recrystallization boundaries in the associated complex defect energy ‘landscape’. Results are compared to experimental observations.

title: Terahertz oscillation of 180° domain walls in ferroelectric membranes
abstract: A fundamentally intriguing yet not well understood topic in the field of ferroelectrics is the collective excitation of domain walls (DWs), with potential applications to DW-based nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices. Here we use dynamical phase-field simulations to identify the collective modes of an Ising-type 180° DW in a uniaxially strained BaTiO3 membrane. The membrane, which concurrently functions as a cavity for polarization and acoustic waves, permits cavity-enhanced resonant excitation of polarization waves. The simulation reveals an unconventional DW sliding mode that exhibits a bulk-polarization-charge-driven nonzero resonant frequency in the sub-terahertz (THz) regime with a dynamically changing internal structure during sliding. These features differ from the previously reported zero-frequency DW sliding mode or the surface-polarization-charge-driven DW sliding mode. The effect of strain on the frequency of this unconventional DW sliding mode and other previously known THz DW eigenmodes is investigated by dynamical phase-field simulations and interpreted by eigenmode analysis or analytical calculation in a simplified one-dimensional (1D) system. These results provide new insights into the high-frequency dynamics of ferroelectric DWs and suggest opportunities for realizing strain control of phonon-DW resonance, and more broadly, for discovering and controlling unconventional DW modes in conventional domain patterns with applications to reconfigurable THz and optical devices.

title: Amorphization-induced metallic-bonded heterointerface for ampere-level alkaline hydrogen evolution
abstract: Alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) often incorporates hydroxide to activate and dissociate water, but conventional hydroxide-based heterostructures with strong intermediate adsorption and interfacial polarization substantially hinder hydrogen transfer across interfaces. Here, we develop a crystalline Ni/amorphous Ni(OH)2 (c-Ni/a-Ni(OH)2) heterostructure featuring metallic Ni-Ni interfacial bonds via a liquid-phase pulse discharge (LPD) strategy. The amorphous Ni(OH)2 provides diverse coordination environments that broaden the adsorption-energy distribution and weaken hydrogen adsorption, while the Ni-Ni bridges serve as highly conductive bridges for rapid hydrogen spillover. Additionally, the amorphous/crystalline (a/c) interface optimizes H2 desorption kinetics of interfacial metallic Ni atoms. Resultantly, the c-Ni/a-Ni(OH)2 delivers a low overpotential (0.26 V vs. RHE) for 300 h and cell voltage (1.97 V) for 150 h at 1 A cm-2 in the electrolytic cell and alkaline water electrolyzer (AWE), respectively. This work demonstrates an amorphization-driven interface engineering to establish a scalable pathway toward industrial-grade alkaline HER catalysts.

title: Competing adsorption of H and CO on Pd-alloy surfaces:Mechanistic insight into the mitigating effect of Cu on CO poisoning
abstract: Multi-component alloys offer broad tunability for materials science applications, but are highly sensitive to operating conditions through adsorption and segregation phenomena. Here, we study Pd–Au–Cu alloy surfaces in H 2 and CO environments motivated by their use in H technologies, where alloying can mitigate limitations intrinsic to Pd such as CO poisoning. To this end, we establish a framework combining machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on density-functional theory data with cluster expansions, with effectively no limitations on training set size. By constructing continuous surface phase diagrams for H–CO coadsorption, we find that adsorption under operating conditions is governed by the H coverage during the preceding annealing. Au-rich surfaces, formed under H-poor conditions, suppress both CO and H adsorption, while H-rich conditions yield Pd-rich surfaces that promote CO and H adsorption. Furthermore, Pd-rich alloy surfaces maintain higher H coverages compared to pure Pd at relevant CO partial pressures, indicating improved CO poisoning resistance. The coadsorption behavior of PdAuCu alloys is indistinguishable from that of PdAu alloys, despite experimental observations of Cu, specifically, mitigating CO poisoning. However, kinetic barriers of H sorption in dilute alloys indicate that H pathways near Au are highly unfavorable, while Cu leaves the energetics unchanged compared to pure Pd. Based on these findings and the experimental evidence, we hypothesize that alloying promotes H adsorption while Cu, specifically, preserves viable H absorption pathways in the presence of CO.

title: Cr-mediated modulation of κ-phase shearability and stacking fault energy enabling hetero-deformation strengthening in CoNiV-based multi-principal element alloys
abstract: Chromium (Cr) alloying is demonstrated to serve as a key compositional lever to engineer the microstructure and deformation mechanisms of CoNiV-based multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs). Increasing the Cr content from 5 to 15 atomic percent (at.%) modulates both κ-phase formation and stacking fault energy (SFE) in CoNiV-based MPEAs, thereby enabling controlled cooperative deformation between the κ phase and face-centered cubic (FCC) matrix. Thermodynamic simulations and first-principles calculations reveal that Cr addition suppresses κ-phase precipitation while significantly lowering the SFE, which enhances κ-phase shearability and promotes planar slip within the FCC matrix. Transmission electron microscopy indicates that the 10Cr alloy possesses deformable κ precipitates and abundant stacking faults, leading to enhanced hetero-deformation-induced (HDI) strengthening. The resulting heterogeneous κ/FCC architecture achieves an exceptional combination of yield strength (∼0.93 GPa) and elongation (∼41%), surpassing most reported Co-based MPEAs. Quantitative analysis of back stress and effective stress further suggests that HDI strengthening contributes significantly to the strain-hardening response. This work proposes a compositional–mechanical coupling pathway, i.e., Cr-mediated modulation of κ-phase shearability and SFE, that provides a mechanistic foundation and design implication for overcoming the intrinsic strength–ductility trade-off in advanced MPEAs.

title: Evolution of radiation-induced grain boundary segregation in an ion irradiated Fe-Ni-Cr alloy undergoing spinodal decomposition
abstract: Radiation-induced segregation (RIS) is a non-equilibrium phenomenon that is observed in irradiated alloys and results from the interactions of solute atoms and point defects at defect sinks such as grain boundaries. RIS is often considered to reach a steady state behavior at relatively low doses. However, using two model Fe-Ni-Cr alloys that were ion irradiated at 400 °C, we show that the evolution of RIS at grain boundaries correlates with phase evolution in grain interiors. In the alloy undergoing irradiation-accelerated spinodal decomposition, grain boundary chemistry was dominated by RIS at low doses with the expected Ni enrichment and Fe and Cr depletion. RIS, however, evolved significantly at higher doses as phase separation evolved in the grain interior from mid (15 dpa) to high doses (70 dpa). In the second alloy, the extent of the phase separation did not evolve from low (5 dpa) to high dose (70 dpa), correlating with no notable changes in the RIS response at grain boundaries. The findings highlight the synergy between grain interior and grain boundaries during irradiation.

title: Mesoscopic connectivity of second phases regulates long-term oxidation stability in Mg–RE alloys: A topological isolation strategy
abstract: The long-term high-temperature oxidation resistance of multi-phase alloys critically depends on the structural integrity of the oxide scale; however, the influence of second-phase topological configuration on oxidation stability remains insufficiently understood. In this work, the oxidation behavior of Mg–8Gd–3Y–0.6Al alloys was investigated at 500 °C for up to 3000 h to elucidate the role of mesoscopic connectivity in oxide-scale integrity. The solution-treated alloy, characterized by high mesoscopic connectivity of clustered second phases, exhibits a pronounced kinetic transition after ∼500 h, shifting from weight gain to rapid weight loss due to extensive scale spallation. In contrast, the rotary-swaged alloy exhibits a topological isolation state, maintaining stable, near-parabolic growth throughout the 3000 h exposure. Multi-scale characterization reveals that oxidation instability in the solution-treated alloy is closely associated with coarse second-phase particles, where geometric discontinuities promote localized stress concentration and microcrack initiation. Owing to the high mesoscopic connectivity of these second phases, the resulting defects evolve into percolating crack networks, thereby facilitating accelerated oxygen transport and progressive oxide-scale degradation. By comparison, rotary swaging induces fragmentation and spatial redistribution of second phases, effectively disrupting their connectivity and establishing topological isolation. This configuration suppresses the development of continuous crack pathways and, when combined with grain-refinement-induced rare-earth redistribution, promotes the formation of a continuous rare-earth-enriched layer. These results indicate that regulating mesoscopic second-phase connectivity through topological isolation, together with grain-refinement-induced rare-earth redistribution, provides an effective structural strategy for enhancing the long-term oxidation stability of Mg–RE alloys and related multi-phase systems.

title: Variable-charge model of GaN within the Streitz–Mintmire formalism
abstract: An ionic–covalent interatomic potential for GaN is developed by combining the Tersoff potential and electrostatic energy with point charges determined self-consistently with atomic positions using the charge equilibration method of Streitz and Mintmire (1994). The electrostatic parameters of both elements are derived from their experimental ionization energies and electron affinities, whereas the rates of decay of electron densities are represented by Slater’s 1s orbitals and optimized to reproduce net atomic charges obtained from DFT data using the DDEC6 charge partitioning scheme. The incorporation of variable charges resolves a long-standing error in degenerate ground state between the wurtzite and zincblende structures and correctly predicts wurtzite as the ground state. As a consequence, the model predicts finite stacking fault energy, which is shown to be in excellent agreement with DFT calculations. Under high pressure, the model predicts a phase transition from wurtzite to rocksalt at 48 GPa, consistent with measurements based on X-ray diffraction.

title: Fatigue crack growth of tungsten in the semi-ductile temperature regime
abstract: Tungsten will play an indispensable role for novel fusion reactors due to its exceptional physical properties, however, its low damage tolerance involves risks. Therefore, fracture toughness has been extensively investigated over decades, but the understanding on the resistance against fatigue crack growth remains scarce. In this study, fatigue crack growth and fracture toughness experiments were performed on pure tungsten (ITER-grade) in the semi-ductile temperature regime at 773 K in high vacuum. To account for microstructural anisotropy, different crack plane orientations were investigated, and the impact of shielding effects was examined by varying the load ratio R between 0.1 and 0.7. A central outcome is the unexpected behavior in the threshold regime compared to common metals. Doubling the stress intensity factor barely affected the propagation rate, while in the Paris regime, the rate increased by two orders of magnitude. This behavior is attributed to the changing slip reversibility of dislocations and the rewelding of the crack wake in vacuum. Further findings are the insensitiveness of the crack growth rate against changes of mean stress up to R = 0.5 and the early onset of delamination in the case of fatigue loading, caused by the reversible loading in the cyclic plastic zone. This study constitutes an important step towards elucidating the intrinsic and extrinsic fatigue crack growth mechanisms in tungsten and represents a key milestone in developing safe, damage-tolerant structural tungsten-based components.

title: Geometric effects of inclusions on hydrogen embrittlement in high-strength steel
abstract: The effect of non-metallic inclusion (NMI) geometry on hydrogen embrittlement (HE) in high-strength steel remains unresolved because the size, shape, and composition are inseparably correlated. The present work isolates the geometric contribution using artificial Al2O3 particles with prescribed sizes and shapes embedded in the steel matrix. Slow strain rate tensile (SSRT) testing under hydrogen charging showed that the presence of artificial Al2O3 particles reduced the fracture stress, with the reduction becoming more pronounced with increasing particle size, and at an equivalent size, cubic particles exhibited lower fracture stress than spherical ones. Fracture surface topography analysis (FRASTA) confirmed particle–matrix interfacial debonding for both spherical and cubic particles. Finite element (FE) simulations, performed with the fracture stress measured in the SSRT experiments as the applied stress, reproduced geometry-dependent fields and indicated that the particle–matrix interface attained comparable levels of local stress and hydrogen concentration at the fracture initiation sites identified by FRASTA in both shapes. These results support the interpretation that interfacial debonding occurs when critical levels of local stress and hydrogen concentration are satisfied, suggesting that HE susceptibility is governed not only by NMI size but also by NMI shape.

title: Duality of wave modulation and nanotwinning in Ni–Mn–Ga martensite via long-period commensurate states
abstract: Structural modulation is a key ingredient behind the extraordinary (magneto)elastic response of Ni–Mn–Ga martensite, yet its link to fine microstructural features and twin-boundary supermobility remains unresolved. Here we analyse martensitic single crystals of Ni 50.0 Mn 27.7 Ga 22.3 and Ni 50.0 Mn 28.1 Ga 21.9 . Neutron and X-ray diffraction reveal an anharmonic five-layer structural modulation—evidenced by high-order satellite reflections—that evolves from commensurate ( q = 2/5) to incommensurate (2/5 < q < 5/12) upon cooling. Interpreting the refined modulation displacements as a basal-plane stacking sequence links the wave description to the microstructural evolution on cooling. In this view, evolving incommensurability produces periodic nanodomains interpreted as emerging a/b -nanotwins with a characteristic size of ≈20 nm at ≈290 K. With further cooling, the modulation can lock into long-period commensurate (LP-C) states, such as 34O ( q = 7/17), 24O ( q = 5/12), and 14O ( q = 3/7), whose orthorhombic unit cells can be viewed as a/b -nanotwins. Ab initio calculations show that LP-C structures are energetically competitive with the initial commensurate state, supporting a shallow martensitic energy landscape. We propose a physical picture in which the martensitic transformation selects a commensurate state with q = 2/5 in the Mn-rich compositions studied here, while subsequent cooling drives relaxation within the martensitic landscape toward LP-C states, particularly 24O in the present alloys. The resulting structure is neither purely wave-like nor purely nanotwinned; rather, it reflects coupling between a coherent modulation wave and local accommodation via NM-like tetragonal distortions, nanotwinning, and LP-C lock-ins, providing a structural basis for the wave–nanotwin duality in Ni–Mn–Ga martensite.

title: Beyond linear elastic fracture mechanics: Atomistic modeling of fracture toughness in silicate glasses via energy landscape sampling
abstract: Fracture in oxide glasses is traditionally interpreted through linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM), which assumes homogeneous materials and ideal crack geometries. However, these assumptions break down at the atomic scale, where local structure and energetics govern crack propagation. In disordered materials, this breakdown becomes especially difficult to account for, due to local stochasticity. We present an open-source, graph-based algorithm that estimates the elastic contribution to the critical energy release rate (Gc) using atomistic structures generated with classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The method evaluates fracture trajectories as stochastic traversals of a local energy landscape, optionally incorporating structural relaxation after each propagation step to capture iterative changes in material response. We apply this approach to a series of sodium silicate glasses and compare the results with classical theoretical estimates and flat-surface cleavage-based calculations. Our findings demonstrate that the energy landscape near a propagating crack tip evolves significantly, influencing both the energy cost and direction of fracture. Normalizing fracture energies using projected (flat) surface area or assuming theoretical bulk averages systematically overestimates Gc. Statistical analysis reveals a bimodal distribution of fracture pathways: while the majority of sampled trajectories traverse structurally varied bulk regions, a distinct, highly consistent low-energy regime emerges associated with nanoscale void networks. This highlights glass fracture as a localized, weakest-link phenomenon. Consequently, treating fracture toughness strictly as a deterministic macroscopic property overestimates the true failure threshold, as macroscopic cracks could systematically exploit these rare weak pathways. Theoretical limits must therefore be redefined to account for crack path tortuosity and the probabilistic occurrence of critical low-energy limits within finite simulation volumes. Our algorithm offers a fast, generalizable framework for compositional screening and provides new insight into the atomistic origins of fracture in glasses.

title: Effects of short-range order on void growth in single-crystalline CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys
abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit superior resistance to ductile damage and failure compared to conventional metals and alloys. In this work, we focus on the dislocation-plasticity-dominated regime of void growth (athermal, relatively high stress), and examine how chemical short-range order (SRO) that develops upon annealing plays a critical role in suppressing void growth and thereby enhancing the ductile damage and failure tolerance of single-crystalline CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Combining large-scale atomistic simulations with crystal plasticity finite element modeling, we demonstrate that Cr-rich SRO nanodomains significantly homogenize plastic deformation in the matrix, effectively reducing the strain localization that occurs around the void in the absence of SRO. The CoCrFeMnNi HEA with SRO exhibits a lower void growth rate than a typical pure fcc metal, in which strain localization around the void is severe and microcracks nucleate at the void surface (leading to rapid ductile failure). These findings highlight the governing role of atomic-scale SRO in void evolution and provide direct evidence of the origin of the superior resistance to ductile damage and failure of fcc HEAs over pure metals. This work establishes a scientific foundation for the rational design of next-generation damage-tolerant structural materials through SRO engineering.

title: Time-resolved evolution of micro-, crystal structure, and temperature field during resonant laser sintering of SnO2 nanoparticles
abstract: The structural evolution of tin dioxide (SnO₂) nanoparticle films during resonant laser sintering is investigated using simultaneous, time-resolved small-angle (SAXS) and wide-angle (WAXS) X-ray scattering combined with high-speed near-infrared (NIR) thermography. A focused synchrotron X-ray beam enables spatially and temporally resolved probing of structural changes at both the microstructural and crystal structure scale. The evolution of the temperature field is monitored to correlate the structural dynamics with the temperature–time profile and to analyze the grain growth kinetics. The structural changes observed in situ are complemented by ex situ scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the evolved microstructure. In addition, the lattice expansion by laser induced heating is determined, and the corresponding thermal expansion coefficients are derived. These space- and time-resolved measurements provide detailed insights into the mechanisms governing resonant laser sintering of SnO₂ nanoparticles.

title: An experimental-based multiscale method for calculating radiation-enhanced mobility in solids: Application to radiation-induced microstructure in FeCr
abstract: By combining MD simulations with a Phase Field approach, this work enables the modeling of radiationinduced microstructures based on the minimization of a quasi-potential  within the framework of macroscopic fluctuation theory. The methodology we propose is an alternative way to bypass the difficulty of calculating the radiation-enhanced mobilities. The model we propose is validated by a direct comparison between simulated and experimental microstructures extracted from APT measurements performed on an ultra-pure alloy concentrated in Fe 0.81 Cr 0.19 irradiated with 2 MeV Fe ions at different temperatures and fluxes. This work is able to explain flux effects observed in this materials and can be easily extended for modeling microstructures induced by neutron flux paving the way for the simulation of radiation-induced microstructures in nuclear reactors.

title: Mechanism of early crack growth in carbide-free bainitic steel during impact fatigue
abstract: Carbide-free bainitic (CFB) steels are widely used in structural components subjected to repetitive impact loading, where high strain rates accelerate damage evolution and promote catastrophic impact fatigue (IF) failure. Since crack propagation dominates fatigue life for structural components, early crack growth (ECG) is a critical stage in IF failure. However, the ECG behavior of CFB steel under IF and its microstructural dependence remain unclear. In this work, the low-cycle IF behavior of a CFB steel was systematically investigated with emphasis on ECG. Fractographic and microstructural analyses show that IF failure involves four stages, with ECG accounting for the majority of the crack propagation life. During ECG, the crack-tip plastic zone undergoes different degrees of microstructural evolution, leading to distinct crack–microstructure interactions. Without obvious microstructural evolution, ECG is governed by the Schmid factors of the {110} <111> and {112} <111> slip systems during intragranular propagation, whereas high-angle grain boundaries impede transgranular propagation by restricting slip transfer and promoting crack deflection. In specific regions, high local strain rates trigger continuous dynamic recrystallization, producing dislocation cells and fine equiaxed grains. The heterogeneity of this evolution is controlled by the relative orientation between bainite blocks and the crack plane, together with the Schmid factor. These evolved microstructures suppress slip transmission, promote crack-tip blunting, and homogenize local stress concentration, thereby enhancing crack growth resistance. This work clarifies the IF failure mechanism of CFB steel and provides guidance for microstructural design for improved IF resistance.

title: Sub-monolayer interface complexion to achieve significantly strength-ductility enhancement in aluminum matrix composite
abstract: Metal matrix composites (MMCs) are stronger and stiffer than matrix metal, but they often suffer from reduced ductility due to weak-bonding interfaces. Despite advances in interface engineering, achieving a completely-coherent interface (CCI) at the atomic scale remains a major challenge, perpetuating this strength–ductility trade-off. In this study, we overcome this limitation by introducing a sub-monolayer interface complexion (SMIC) strategy to establish atomic-scale CCI between the reinforcement particles and the matrix in a case of TiB2/Al composite. Such SMIC can be obtained by doping with alloying elements, which can be screened and evaluated through first-principles calculations. The resulting SMIC-particles facilitate greater dislocation multiplication without inducing interface failure, thereby promoting increased strain hardening and progressive plastic deformation. As a result, the SMIC reinforced TiB2/Al composite demonstrates remarkable simultaneous improvements in yield strength (∼44%) and ductility (∼53%) compared to the matrix alloy—far exceeding the typical performance gains observed in conventional MMCs. Notably, the exceptional ductility of our aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) rivals that of pure aluminum and surpasses nearly all reported aluminum alloys and AMCs. These findings highlight the potential of atomic-scale CCI design as a transformative strategy for developing next-generation high-performance MMCs with balanced mechanical properties.

title: Ergodicity controlled excellent transverse and shear mode piezoresponse in samarium doped PMN-xPT ceramics
abstract: Many actuation and sensing devices require piezoelectric materials with high shear and transverse mode strain coefficients. Owing to their superior performance as compared to the other state-of-the-art alternatives, this application space is largely dominated by soft PZT. In this investigation, we report excellent transverse, shear, and planar mode piezoelectric responses in samarium-doped PMN-xPT polycrystalline ceramics. In the transverse mode, the highest d31 and k31 coefficients were obtained for 2.75% Sm-doped PMN-0.28PT, with values of – 497 pC/N and 0.44, respectively. This composition also exhibited exceptional shear mode piezoelectric strain and coupling coefficients of 1020 pC/N and 0.66, respectively. The optimum planner mode coupling coefficient was 0.76 for 2.25% Sm-doped PMN-0.29PT. All these parameters exceed those of soft PZT, positioning Sm-doped PMN-xPT as an alternative for room-temperature device applications. The optimum longitudinal mode [[EQUATION]] parameter of 3.0 X 10-11 m2/N highlights the potential of 2.75% Sm-doped PMN-0.28PT as an excellent choice for energy harvesting devices. To explore the underlying mechanism for high functional response in Sm-doped PMN-xPT, the roles of contributing factors such as dielectric constant, spontaneous polarization and electrostriction were analyzed. We show that in addition to dielectric constant, the degree of ergodicity makes a subtle yet profound contribution to the piezoresponse in different modes of operation.

title: Ordered oxygen vacancies in tetragonal BiFeO3
abstract: Bismuth ferrite (BiFeO 3 , BFO) is a prototypical multiferroic material, whose crystal structures and physical properties are sensitively dependent on the strain state, forming an exotic super tetragonal phase with compressive strain. Although the compressive strain is associated with dramatically reduced oxygen vacancy formation energy, it is intuitively considered that the crystal structures of BFO are all stoichiometric. However, through multislice electron ptychography with adaptive propagator, we found that the tetragonal phase of bismuth ferrite has approximately 1/4 oxygen vacancies at the apical oxygen positions, challenging the conventional wisdom of stoichiometric BFO. Since oxygen vacancies significantly influence the physical properties of transition metal oxides, this finding offers new insights into the physicochemical behavior of bismuth ferrite and opens opportunities for the development of novel functionalities.

title: Grain-size-dependent dynamic mechanical response and plastic deformation of the FeCoCrMnNi high-entropy alloy during high-strain-rate impact
abstract: The dynamic mechanical response of FeCoCrMnNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is strongly governed by microstructural characteristics, whereas most existing understanding has been established under quasi-static or low to intermediate strain-rate conditions. Experimental insight into how microstructural features govern the dynamic mechanical behavior and plastic deformation mechanisms under high-strain-rate loading conditions remains limited. In this study, a laser-driven high-strain-rate impact indentation technique was employed to impose controllable localized loading at strain rates up to 105 s−1 while effectively avoiding macroscopic failure. The dynamic mechanical behavior and plastic deformation mechanisms of FeCoCrMnNi HEAs with different grain sizes were systematically investigated. The results show that, during high-strain-rate impact, both the dynamic mechanical response and plastic deformation behaviors of FeCoCrMnNi HEAs exhibit evident grain-size sensitivity. Microstructural analyses demonstrate that the plastic deformation of the coarse-grained HEA is dominated by long-range stacking-fault networks and high-density dislocation accumulation within large grains. In contrast, with decreasing grain size, the fine-grained HEA develops a more complex deformation microstructure, including short-range stacking faults, deformation twins, nanoscale grains with dense boundary networks, and local lattice disorder. Molecular dynamics simulations further confirm the difference in deformation mechanism through quantitative analyses of cluster size of hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) atoms, the fraction of newly generated HCP atoms near grain boundaries, and dislocation evolution. This study clarifies how grain size regulates dynamic mechanical characteristics of FeCoCrMnNi HEAs, providing insights into their scale dependent deformation under extreme impact loading.

title: Solute-defect interaction and oxidation govern high-temperature low-cycle fatigue in Mo-added CoCrNi-based multi-principal element alloy
abstract: Understanding high-temperature fatigue of novel alloys is crucial for their use in high-temperature applications. This study systematically investigates the monotonic tensile and low-cycle fatigue (LCF) behavior of a Co35.4Cr22.9Ni35.5Mo6.2 alloy at room temperature (RT) and 550 °C. At RT, the alloy exhibits a favourable combination of strength and ductility, while LCF at ± 0.5% strain amplitude shows initial cyclic hardening followed by stress stabilization. At 550 °C, the alloy displays strain-rate-dependent serrated flow, continuous cyclic hardening, reduced ductility and a shorter fatigue life. Cyclic hardening at both temperatures stems from increased dislocation density, though this is more pronounced at 550 °C. RT deformation is dominated by planar glide of extended dislocations and the formation of sessile Lomer–Cottrell locks and extended nodes, resulting in a homogeneous dislocation distribution without significant rearrangement. Deformation twinning is confined to localized regions ahead of fatigue crack tips. At 550 °C, atomic-scale analysis reveals Suzuki-type segregation (Mo/Co enrichment and Cr/Ni depletion) at stacking faults (SFs). A first-order analytical assessment suggests that this local solute redistribution contributes to dynamic strain ageing (DSA), while also lowering the local stacking-fault energy, promoting extensive SF formation, sustained planar slip, bulk deformation twinning, and their interactions. Simultaneously, solute-defect-interaction-driven DSA reduces dislocation mobility and increases defect density and their interactions, contributing to continuous cyclic hardening. Concurrently, grain boundaries exhibit Mo–Cr enrichment and Ni–Co depletion driven by elastic strain relaxation, chemical interactions, and deformation-enhanced diffusion. The combined effects of grain-boundary segregation, DSA-enhanced planar slip, elastic–plastic strain incompatibility, and oxidation promote a transition in crack initiation behaviour from annealing twin-boundary-dominated at RT to grain-boundary-dominated at 550 °C. Propagation follows a mixed intergranular–transgranular path filled with layered oxide scales (a Cr–Mo-rich inner and a Co–Ni-rich outer layer), consistent with thermodynamic stability. A continuous cycle of oxygen ingress, oxide-layer formation, and subsequent oxide fracture and spallation accelerates crack propagation through localized metal loss, thereby reducing fatigue life at 550 °C. These findings underscore the synergy between solute–defect interactions and environmental degradation in governing the high-temperature fatigue of low-SFE Co–Cr–Ni–Mo alloys.

title: Crystallinity-dependent lithium storage behavior of molybdenum dioxide for lithium rechargeable batteries
abstract: Molybdenum dioxide (MoO2) is a promising anode material owing to its electronic conductivity and a theoretical capacity of 838 mAh g−1. However, MoO2 shows suppressed conversion at room temperature because strong Mo–O bonding hinders bond cleavage. This study shows that lowering crystallinity activates conversion. Low-crystalline MoO2 (lc-MoO2) delivers 937.4 mAh g−1 at 100 mA g−1 in the 100th cycle (91.6% retention vs the 10th) and 404.5 mAh g−1 at 5000 mA g−1, outperforming crystalline MoO2. The defect-rich framework lowers the barrier for Mo–O cleavage and provides flexibility, while short diffusion paths and a larger surface area increase the surface-capacitive contribution and accelerate Li storage. Synchrotron-based X-ray absorption spectroscopy and electron microscopy reveal an evolution toward MoO3 that correlates with increased capacity. Lithium insertion, partial conversion, and gel-like film formation account for the high reversible capacity. These findings highlight crystallinity control as a design parameter for oxide anodes in lithium-ion batteries.

title: Phase-field simulations of polar topologies in K0.5Na0.5NbO3 ferroelectric thin films
abstract: Polar topologies in ferroelectric materials have attracted significant attention in condensed matter physics and materials science due to their novel physical properties and immense potential for advanced ferroelectric devices. Current polar topologies are predominantly found in tetragonal or rhombohedral ferroelectrics. However, the polar topologies in orthorhombic ferroelectrics remain inadequately understood. Here, taking K0.5Na0.5NbO3 thin film as a model system, we systematically explore the possible polar topologies through manipulating misfit strain, film thickness, electric field, and electrical screening effect via phase-field simulations. We further establish phase diagrams of polar topologies, including vortices, spirals, periodic polarization waves, and skyrmions. Our results reveal that misfit strains can modulate the orientations of vortices, spirals, and periodic polarization waves, as well as the amplitudes of periodic polarization waves. Notably, a periodic in-plane electric field can reversibly switch the chirality of spirals. Moreover, tunable skyrmion density is attained via the coupling of the electrical screening effect with an external electric field. Our simulations also demonstrate the universality of Kittel's law in polar topologies. These results provide systematic theoretical guidance for discovering and manipulating polar topologies in orthorhombic ferroelectric materials, paving the way for rational design of topology-engineered ferroelectric microelectronic devices.

title: Hydrogen (deuterium) dynamics and thermal stability in ion-irradiated platinum-hydride thin films synthesized at low temperature
abstract: Hydrogen (H) and deuterium (D) interactions with transition metals are important in heterogeneous catalysis and related technologies. While H–Pt surface interactions are studied, investigations of hydrogen incorporation and transport in Pt remain limited due to its low solubility. Here, we study H(D) incorporation and desorption in metastable PtH(D) x thin films prepared by low-energy ion irradiation, enabling loading above equilibrium concentrations. Nuclear reaction analysis (NRA) reveals a nonuniform hydrogen depth profile with two accumulation regions: the subsurface and the film-substrate interface. Thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) exhibits two peaks near 190 and 230 K, consistent with hydrogen release from these regions. Resistance relaxation measurements, analyzed within a two-parallel-channel conduction model, indicate distinct kinetics for subsurface and near-interface hydrogen. For PtH x with an average hydrogen concentration of x = 0.15, Arrhenius analysis reveals two thermally activated processes, with activation energies of 130 ± 18 meV (subsurface) and 164 ± 26 meV (near interface). Above 140 K, D exhibits slower relaxation rates with activation energies of 117 ± 8 and 121 ± 7 meV for PtD x prepared under the same implantation dose. Within experimental uncertainty, the activation barriers for H and D are comparable or slightly lower for D, while the prefactors are significantly reduced for D, indicating isotope-dependent attempt frequencies and zero-point energy effects. TDS simulations based on the Polanyi-Wigner formalism reproduce the desorption spectra by resolving subsurface and near-interface contributions, consistent with the NRA profile. These findings elucidate hydrogen kinetics in PtH x relevant to Pt-based catalysis, sensing, and hydrogen–metal interactions.

title: Indium dual role in tuning ionic transport, vacancy ordering, and phase stability in SrFe1–xInxO3–δ: A concentration-dependent effect
abstract: Effectively managing the intrinsic compromise between ionic conductivity and vacancy ordering is crucial for the mixed ionic-electronic conductor SrFeO3–δ. This study demonstrates that In3+ doping serves as a potent tool for this purpose, the efficacy of which depends critically on its concentration. An investigation of SrFe1–xInxO3–δ (x = 0–0.30) combining a suite of experimental techniques with DFT calculations reveals a dual role of In3+. At low concentrations (x = 0.05, 0.10), In3+ suppresses vacancy ordering, stabilizing the cubic structure and maximizing oxygen-ion conductivity (≈ 0.47 S·cm−1 at 950 °C for x = 0.05). First-principles calculations show that at low In levels, covalent Fe–O–In bonds are formed. Beyond x > 0.20, high In content favors the formation of strong covalent In–O–In bonds and associated defect complexes that block migration pathways, degrading ionic transport. For x ≥ 0.20, the high-temperature-metastable cubic phase readily orders upon cooling under reducing conditions, potentially leading to phase decomposition. Consequently, In3+ serves as a structural disordering agent at low concentrations but evolves into a defect-trapping and destabilizing cation at high concentrations.

title: Pressure-induced topological Lifshitz transition driven by band shift leading to enhanced superconductivity in MgSH5
abstract: Understanding the interplay between electronic topology and superconductivity is crucial for advancing superconducting critical temperature (Tc) materials. Through crystal structure search and first-principles calculations, we establish an intrinsic connection between pressure-induced Fermi surface (FS) topological Lifshitz transitions and Fermi-surface nesting, with the goal of revealing the underlying mechanism that governs the pressure-dependent superconducting performance of ternary hydrides in the Mg-S-H system. At 200 GPa, we identify two novel stable phases: Pmmm MgSH5 and P2/m MgSH7, both characterized by the presence of covalently bonded quasi-H2 molecular units within an ionic Mg-H/S framework. While both are superconducting at 200 GPa, with predicted Tc values of 63.12 K and 86.68 K respectively, MgSH5 demonstrates a pronounced sensitivity to pressure. Our results indicate that as pressure increases, and while the crystal symmetry remains unchanged, the band shift toward the Fermi level, inducing a topological Lifshitz transition of the FS. This electronic transition markedly enhances the electron-phonon coupling (EPC), ultimately achieving a maximum Tc as high as 103.66 K. Our findings demonstrate that, by establishing the correlation between pressure-induced topological Lifshitz transitions and FS nesting properties, this work yields significant insights into the regulation of EPC and superconducting properties by Fermi-surface evolution. Moreover, it provides a new perspective on understanding pressure-regulated EPC and highlights the key design concept for high-performance superconducting hydrides governed by pressure-induced FS evolution.

title: Defect-mediated elemental segregation and local chemical ordering in TiZrNbTaV multi-principal element alloys
abstract: Elemental segregation and local chemical order (LCO) are critical microstructural features in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs). The driving force for element segregation in MPEAs often exhibits an antagonistic or synergistic relationship with the formation of LCO. Nevertheless, the precise nature of their interaction at crystal defects has not yet been fully elucidated. Here we systematically investigate body-centered cubic (BCC) TiZr(90-x)/2Nb5Ta5Vx (x=5, 10, 15, 20) MPEAs using hybrid Monte Carlo (MC)/Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, thermodynamic analysis, and complementary experiments. We reveal that Zr segregates universally to all studied defects including grain boundaries (GBs), dislocations, vacancies and interstitials. Ta and V do not segregate to defect cores; instead, their strong mutual attraction drives the formation of Ta-V ordered clusters in grain interiors. Segregated Zr strongly repels these clusters, forcing them to maintain a characteristic distance from defect cores. Substitution energy analysis shows that a negative net energy difference drives enrichment at defects, as observed for Zr at all defects and for Nb at interstitials, whereas a positive value drives depletion, as observed for Ta and V at GBs. Importantly, elemental enrichment does not necessarily translate into enhanced local chemical ordering. Zr self-clustering is enhanced near GBs but suppressed near dislocations and point defects. Low-Σ GBs promote Ta-V clustering near GBs, while dislocations mainly modulate the spatial arrangement of Ta-V clusters without increasing their overall population. These defect-specific responses demonstrate that defect-mediated segregation and LCO are coupled in a nontrivial and defect-type-dependent manner.

title: Structure and soft-mode induced phase transformation of rhombohedral phase in zirconia
abstract: ABSTRACT This work solves a long-standing ambiguity about the metastable rhombohedral (R) phase in zirconia and identifies its atomic structure and transformation pathways. Guided by X-ray diffraction (XRD)-constrained ab-initio random structure searching (AIRSS), we obtain a structural model whose Raman mode at 690 cm⁻¹ reproduces a new experimental fingerprint. In spark plasma sintered 4 mol% Y 2 O 3 -doped ZrO 2 , transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) reveal a self-accommodating lamellar microstructure (150 ± 15 nm) of alternating R and tetragonal (T) domains with a fixed orientation relationship (100) R ∥(001) T ; [01-1] R ∥[100] T . Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) O-K edges provide phase-specific spectral signatures distinguishing R from T phases. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations place R between cubic (C) and T phases in energy and show a doubly degenerate Γ-E soft mode that drives R→T phase transformation on relaxation, consistent with annealing experiments. A minimal Landau model (Γ-E order parameter coupled to in-plane shear) rationalizes stress stabilization of R and its relaxation to T or C depending on material parameters. These results newly establish the structure, spectroscopic fingerprints, and soft-mode mechanism of the R phase, informing processing-microstructure control in zirconia.

title: How glass breaks—Damage explains the difference between surface and fracture energies in amorphous silica
abstract: The relationship between free surface energy and fracture energy in amorphous silica is investigated using multiscale simulations. We combine the homogenization of an atomic scale fracture model with a phase-field approach to track and quantify the different energy contributions. Free surface energy, localized as potential energy at the surface, is clearly separated from damage diffusion extending over a 16-23 Å range around the crack path while the plastic contribution is found negligible. Analysis of the local structure reveals that diffuse damage is primarily associated with changes in the ring structure, whereas variations in free surface energy correlate with changes in the coordination number of silicon atoms. These findings provide new insight into brittle fracture mechanisms in amorphous silicates and are consistent with experimental measurements of silica toughness.

title: Shear-coupled grain growth statistics
abstract: Grain growth (GG), mediated by grain boundary (GB) migration, is a fundamental mechanism of microstructure evolution in polycrystalline materials. GB migration is frequently accompanied by a relative shear displacement of grains meeting at GBs, a phenomenon known as shear-coupling. This coupling induces internal stresses within the microstructure, which recent studies have shown to play a decisive role in dictating microstructure evolution and GG pathways. This work provides a detailed characterization of the statistical features of two-dimensional GG in the presence of GB shear-coupling through continuum modeling of GB migration that incorporates fundamental microscopic mechanisms and diffuse-interface simulations. We demonstrate that incorporating shear-coupling produces a more heterogeneous, less equiaxed microstructure than conventional curvature-driven GG, while yielding topological and geometric properties consistent with experimental and atomistic observations. We further demonstrate that as grain grows in this regime, internal stress relaxes. Highly stressed grains shrink faster, and lightly stressed grains grow faster than other grains. These findings demonstrate that internal stress, an intrinsic feature of GG, profoundly changes essential features of GG microstructure and kinetics, consistent with experiments and atomic-scale simulations. Moreover, we discuss their implications for GG regimes and scaling behavior.

title: The contribution of grain boundary complexions to the Taylor-Quinney coefficient in Cu-Zr polycrystals
abstract: During high-strain-rate plastic deformation, only part of the plastic work is dissipated as heat, quantified by the Taylor-Quinney coefficient (TQC). Although introduced nearly a century ago, the microstructural origins of TQC at high rates remain debated, with recent studies suggesting that grain boundaries (GBs) play a key role in energy storage. In this work, we quantify TQC using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Cu-Zr polycrystals, a model system that enables controlled tuning of GB composition, Zr concentration, and thickness. Cu-Zr polycrystals containing 0-3 at.% Zr were constructed and equilibrated using hybrid Monte Carlo/MD simulations to promote Zr segregation at GBs. The equilibrated cells were then sheared under adiabatic conditions, allowing simultaneous calculation of plastic work and heat generation, from which both differential and integral TQC values were extracted. The differential TQC initially ranged between 0.75 and 0.85, depending on Zr content, and increased with strain, occasionally exceeding unity. To identify the origin of the non-thermal energy fraction, we evaluated the stored dislocation energy from dislocation densities and found it insufficient to account for the discrepancy. The remaining energy was attributed to GB storage. By reconstructing GB surfaces and monitoring GB thickness during deformation, we established that GB energy density correlates with volumetric GB changes. Early-stage GB thickening accommodates a measurable portion of the non-thermal energy, while later amorphous GB transformations lead to partial energy relaxation. These results establish a direct quantitative link between GB evolution and the Taylor-Quinney coefficient in nanocrystalline Cu-Zr alloys.

title: Formation of interstitial–vacancy pairs within solute clusters of Al–Zn–Mg alloys
abstract: Vacancy-type defects introduced in water- and furnace-cooled Al–Zn–Mg alloy samples were investigated using positron annihilation spectroscopy combined with first-principles calculations. While the thermal equilibrium vacancies decreased in the sample cooled in the furnace to 373 K, vacancy-type defects were reintroduced in the sample cooled in the furnace to 303 K. This behavior is attributed to the formation of interstitial–vacancy pairs in solute clusters known as the truncated cube octahedron (TCO) shell structures. These results indicate that excess quenched-in vacancies of 10 -6 or more are not required for precipitation hardening at temperatures between 373 and 303 K. The formation of an interstitial-vacancy pair in the TCO shell structure was confirmed by first-principles-based Monte Carlo simulations starting from the solid-solution state of the Al–Zn–Mg alloy. The increase in positron lifetime observed in the furnace-cooled samples is explained by the corresponding increase in the theoretically calculated positron lifetimes associated with the formation of an interstitial Zn–vacancy pair in the TCO shell structure. Structural relaxation induced by the interstitial–vacancy pair was found to play an important role in the evolution of TCO shells into GP(I) zones.

title: Clarifying the effects of tensile stress on the intergranular oxidation of Ni-15Cr alloy in high-temperature hydrogenated water
abstract: In this work, the effect of tensile stress within the elastic range on the intergranular oxidation behavior of Ni-15Cr model alloy in high-temperature hydrogenated water was investigated through a combination of high throughput constant load test and atomic-scale simulation. The statistical results show that tensile stress significantly accelerates intergranular oxidation rate, with the average intergranular oxidation depth increasing from 2.7 μm under an applied stress at 85.2 MPa to 6.5 μm at 158.4 MPa. Microstructural analysis reveals that under high tensile stress, the intergranular oxide becomes locally fragmented, accompanied by the formation of filament-like oxide and a pronounced diffusion-induced grain boundary migration (DIGM) zone, indicating that tensile stress accelerates the diffusion of both O and Cr. A new Ni-Cr-O reactive force field (ReaxFF) was developed and employed in hybrid MD/GCMC simulations. The simulation results demonstrate that tensile stress lowers the energy barrier of oxygen diffusion along grain boundary (GB). Moreover, the combination of tensile stress and oxygen ingress promotes Cr migration to the GB by decreasing its diffusion energy barrier and lowering the energy state at GB. Analysis of oxidation kinetics demonstrates that tensile stress accelerates intergranular oxidation mainly by enhancing the oxygen diffusivity along GB. These findings greatly advance the mechanistic understanding of stress corrosion cracking of nuclear materials.

title: Microstructural evolution of heterogeneous grains in dual-main-phase (Nd, Ce)-Fe-B sintered magnets: Mechanisms of solution-reprecipitation and diffusion
abstract: Chemically heterogeneous microstructures, manifested by non-uniform distributions of rare-earth (RE) elements among and within grains, critically influence the magnetic performance of dual-main-phase (DMP) sintered (Nd, Ce)-Fe-B magnets. Despite intense research activity, the mechanisms governing their formation and evolution during liquid-phase sintering remain insufficiently understood. Here, the microstructural evolution and RE elemental distribution of heterogeneous grains in DMP sintered magnets containing 60 wt.% Ce of the total RE content (Ce-60) are systematically investigated at different sintering stages. A unified mechanism involving solution-reprecipitation and diffusion is proposed to elucidate the development of the heterogeneous microstructure. During liquid-phase sintering, fine grains and surface protrusions preferentially dissolve into the liquid phase and reprecipitate epitaxially onto larger grains, generating outer regions with distinct RE compositions while preserving crystallographic continuity. RE interdiffusion between inner and outer regions promotes the formation of compositional transition zones. Meanwhile, the progressive dissolution of fine grains reduces the fraction of grains smaller than 4 μm to below 45%, accompanied by an increase in outer-region thickness of >1 μm. Nd-rich grains exhibit more pronounced growth than Ce-rich grains, with their average grain size and outer-region thickness exceeding those of Ce-rich grains by up to ∼1.3 μm and ∼0.7 μm, respectively. Despite the pronounced chemical heterogeneity, dense DMP Ce-60 magnets maintain high demagnetization curve squareness (>0.90). These results provide mechanistic insights into the origin and evolution of heterogeneous grains and offer guidance for the microstructural design of high-performance DMP sintered (Nd, Ce)-Fe-B magnets.

title: Locally concentrated protons control the proton diffusivity in heavily Sc-doped perovskites
abstract: Proton-conducting perovskites with heavy acceptor doping exhibit promising proton conductivity at intermediate-to-low temperatures. However, the understanding of how the high concentration of protons interacts with the local structure of dopants and the consequent effects on proton diffusivity remains insufficient. In this study, we combine in situ and isotope exchange Raman spectroscopy with neutron total scattering to investigate the effects of local structure and high proton concentration on proton diffusivity in BaSc1–xMoxO2.5+3x/2 (BSM). BSM exhibits high bulk proton conductivity of above 0.01 S cm–1 at 350 °C. However, in BSM with higher Sc and proton concentrations, the proton diffusivity is reduced. Neutron pair distribution analysis reveals that the energetically preferred proton sites are located around ScO6 octahedra. The locally concentrated protons lead to the carrier blocking effect, which predominantly restricts proton diffusion by decreasing the pre-exponential factor. Furthermore, the localized protons induce greater local lattice asymmetry, further impeding proton transport. The results indicate a critical trade-off between localized proton concentration and proton diffusivity in metal oxides. This study highlights the importance of considering local structure, in addition to long-range crystal structure, to understand proton transport properties in heavily doped perovskites. Our findings suggest optimization strategies for heavily acceptor-doped proton-conducting ceramics by using lower-valence B-site elements.

title: Configuration of Schottky defects in transition metal carbides
abstract: Vacancy defects in Group 4 and 5 transition metal carbides are studied employing ab initio calculations to obtain the energies of formation of Schottky defects as well as the interaction energies for the pair of unlike vacancies in various spatial arrangements. The present calculations take into account the recently established fact that metal vacancies in these compounds may undergo a reconstruction where the octahedron of carbons surrounding the metal vacancy transforms into a lower-symmetry structure stabilized by formed C–C bonds. This reconstruction significantly lowers the formation energy of Schottky defects in cubic carbides of transition metals and also qualitatively changes the interactions between a metal vacancy and a carbon vacancy, from strong attraction to strong repulsion in the nearest-neighbor shell. The latter result shows the need to rethink the models considering clusters of unreconstructed metal vacancies with carbon vacancies in transition metal carbides. The mutual repulsion between metal and non-metal vacancies at short distances restores the usual view of a Schottky defect as a pair of dissociated vacancies in the studied equiatomic compounds.

title: Temperature dependent DC-bias effects in polycrystalline CaTiSiO5
abstract: As power devices become increasingly crucial to advanced technologies, the development of passive components, such as capacitors, has gained significant research attention. Among various candidate materials, CaTiSiO 5 stands out as a particularly promising lead-free dielectric due to its positive-bias dependence of dielectric permittivity, which originates from its antipolar structure. Although considerable efforts have been devoted to studying the effects of chemical substitutions on the crystal structure and temperature-dependent dielectric properties of CaTiSiO 5 , research on its electrical response under large electric fields remains limited, particularly regarding its behavior across wide temperature ranges relevant to practical applications. Remarkably, CaTiSiO 5 exhibits a positive DC-bias effect at room temperature, where the permittivity increases with applied electric field. This behavior is significantly different from conventional ferroelectric capacitors, arising from the coupled effects of electric field and temperature on phase structure modulation. In this work, the temperature-dependent DC-bias effect was characterized from -30°C to 150°C, where both positive and negative DC-bias effects were observed as temperature changes, providing important insight into the role of the high temperature antiferroelectric-paraelectric phase transition observed at approximately 170°C using temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy as well as small signal dielectric and elastic measurements. These data are contrasted to large-field polarization – electric field and electric-field-dependent relative permittivity measurements to more fully understand its antiferroelectric behavior and dielectric response under large electric fields, providing valuable guidance for the design of next-generation power electronic devices.

title: Strain and dopant-induced band-gap formation in metastable ZrO: resolving the experiment-simulation discrepancy
abstract: Commercial zirconium alloys form a metastable ZrO suboxide layer at the metal–oxide interface during reactor operation, yet its electronic properties remain poorly understood. Conventional PBE-DFT predicts ZrO to be metallic, in contrast to Dual-EELS measurements on corroded Zircaloy-4 that indicate a finite band gap. Here we resolve this discrepancy using a multiscale mechanical–electronic simulation approach. Bond-based peridynamics at experimentally relevant length scales was used to sample residual interface strains, which were then applied directly to atomic scale DFT models. Using higher accuracy electronic-structure methods, including the HSE06 hybrid functional and the GW approximation, we show that compressive basal-plane strain together with Sn substitutional dopants can stabilise an electronic band gap in ZrO. These results provide a mechanism consistent with experimental observations and demonstrate that strain and dopants can control gap formation in metastable transition-metal suboxides. The findings clarify the electronic nature of ZrO under reactor conditions and offer new insight into its role in the corrosion resistance of zirconium alloys.

title: Unlocking high-rate and ultra-stable sodium storage in bismuth via a catalytic-buffering intermetallic strategy
abstract: Alloying represents an effective approach to ameliorate the sodium storage performance of bismuth (Bi)-based anodes, primarily through static improvement in conductivity and buffering capability. However, the dynamic regulation of kinetics in the intermediate process remains largely unexplored. Guided by theoretical calculations, this work proposes a synergistic catalytic-buffering strategy that integrates intermetallic NiBi3 with a nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) matrix to actively modulate the Bi alloying reaction. The NC matrix provides a fundamental conductive and protective scaffold, while NiBi3 accounts for additional kinetic and structural improvements. As a pseudo-catalyst component, Ni not only restructures the Bi lattice to promote electron/ion transport and accelerate the initial Na-Bi alloying stage, but also enhances Na+ adsorption and reduces the alloying barrier in subsequent Na-NaBi reaction. Meanwhile, the dynamically generated Ni framework, together with the NC scaffold, effectively accommodates volume variation throughout the alloying process. Thanks to this cooperative material design, the NC-encapsulated NiBi3 composite (NiBi3@NC) achieves exceptional rate performance up to 50 A g⁻1, a record-long lifespan over 36,000 cycles, as well as excellent cyclability and fast-charging capability even at -30 °C. In-situ X-ray diffraction and electrochemical impedance analyses unravel the underlying Na+ storage mechanisms and provide critical insights for the development of advanced alloy-based anode materials.

title: Sintering of core-shell particles: Chemical interdiffusion initially resists then assists densification
abstract: Chemical interdiffusion has been reported to accelerate densification during sintering, particularly in cases where separate phases homogenize into a single solid solution during the sintering cycle. Here we explicitly study the role of chemical interdiffusion in sintering, by designing a fully miscible alloy prepared in a core-shell powder structure. Specifically, Ni-Au core-shell particles were prepared by electroless deposition of Au on Ni powder. Sintering dilatometry revealed an initial expansion of the Ni–Au samples prior to densification, which is attributed to void formation arising from an imbalance in diffusion fluxes during interdiffusion. Thus, interdiffusion initially hinders densification through the Kirkendall effect. Later, it promotes faster densification through most of the densification cycle. This synergistic effect ultimately enables full densification and lowers the required sintering temperature. These results suggest “powder engineering” strategies to optimize accelerated sintering involving interdiffusion.

title: Simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility of multicomponent alloys via a synergistic study of machine learning, DFT modelling and experimental validation
abstract: In this research, we have designed, tested and optimized the compositions and properties of the Sn-Ag-Cu based multiple-component solder alloys by applying the active learning machine learning strategy and density functional theory. The active learning of adaptive iterations optimization strategy allows us to use a relatively small set of samples and much less number of experiments to achieve the alloy design goal with simultaneously increased shear strength and ductility. We discovered that Bi, In and Ni are the dominant alloying elements in controlling the trade-off between strength and ductility. Among these, Bi and In simultaneously dissolve into the Sn matrix and intermetallic compounds (IMCs) phases, synergistically improving solder joint strength through solution strengthening. Ni also plays important role in inhibiting the η → η' phase transition, producing low misfit and high-strength interfacial structures that facilitate load transfer and extrinsic toughening mechanisms via crack deflection and bridging, thereby enhancing ductility and deformation compatibility. Overall, by optimizing the alloy compositions, the newly designed alloy and the solder joints have both strength and ductility increased simultaneously with 59% higher in shear strength and 61% higher in elongation. This research has demonstrated a multi-objective optimization strategy for designing and developing multiple-component alloys, which is applicable to many other materials systems.

title: Growth twinning of the β(In) during lamellar growth of β(In) – In2Bi – γ(Sn) eutectic in rotating directional solidification: Cases with anisotropic phase boundary energy
abstract: In this work, we report on the growth twinning of the β(In) phase in the ternary β(In) – In2Bi – γ(Sn) eutectic alloy observed during rotating directional solidification (RDS) experiments. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) measurements were performed on the RDS samples in order to identify the crystal orientations of the phases and the crystal orientation relationships (ORs) between the phases. In two samples showing clear locking of the In2Bi/β(In) boundary, the OR between In2Bi and β(In) phases was the same and identified as {1‾100}In2Bi∥{131}β(In) and 〈0001〉In2Bi∥〈101〉β(In). This OR indicates that the energy plot of the In2Bi/β(In) phase boundary is two-fold symmetric with two minima being potential locations for locking of the phase boundary during rotational growth in RDS. Indeed, locking occurred in the angular range corresponding to the energy minimum, near the common plane of the OR. Surprisingly, we identified a second angular range with clear locking and were able to show that it is achieved due to twinning of the β(In) phase. To our knowledge, this is the first report of growth twinning in a nonfaceted crystal associated with forcing the energetically anisotropic phase boundary to change its orientation with respect to the imposed temperature gradient. We open a discussion on the origin of the twinning in the locked grains, in which the strongly anisotropic boundary energy with forbidden orientations is present.

title: Fingerprints of Efimov quasi-bound-state and topological phase transition in Cu2HgSnSe4 under pressure
abstract: The Efimov quasi-bound-state, a two-body version of the original Efimov state of a trimer bound state proposed in heavy atomic nucleus physics, has recently been observed in topological materials. However, the formation condition of the Efimov quasi-bound-state still remains to be determined. Here, we report pressure-driven electronic transport and electronic-structure evolutions in Cu2HgSnSe4 crystals. The results suggest a pressure-induced electronic phase transition, from narrow-bandgap-semiconductor to Dirac-semimetal. Remarkably, the logarithmical magnetic-field dependent quantum oscillation, a fingerprint of Efimov quasi-bound-state, is observed at the intermediate pressures of 0.1–1.5 GPa. The first-principles calculations, combined with dielectric-screening analysis, suggest that the dielectric constant of semiconductors/semimetals locates in a specific regime to give rise to the Efimov quasi-bound-state, and demonstrate that the system undergoes from subcritical to supercritical regime. Accordingly, the pressure-dependent electronic topological phase diagram of Cu2HgSnSe4 is proposed. Our work elucidates the formation condition of Efimov quasi-bound-state under the effect of dielectric screening in solids and demonstrates that rich quantum states can be manipulated by hydrostatic pressure.

title: Conventional solid-state synthesis achieves advanced P'2-type Mn-rich cathodes for sodium-ion batteries with 35 mA·h·g−1 capacity increase and 28.7% stability improvement
abstract: P'2-type manganese-rich layered oxides are promising cathodes for sodium-ion batteries. However, their synthesis requires unconventional rapid quenching to prevent O₂ absorption and P'2-P2 phase transformation during cooling, which compromises scalability and safety. Moreover, Jahn-Teller active ion enrichment and irreversible phase transitions during cycling impair structural stability. These synthesis challenges and inadequate electrochemical performance hinder practical applications. Herein, we report for the first time a simple solid-state synthesis of P'2-Na0.55Mg0.05Mn0.90O2 (Na□MM□) cathode with a 3.78% lattice distortion through a dual-vacancy strategy. The Na□MM□ cathode delivers an ultrahigh energy density of 786 Wh·kg−1. Na vacancies stabilize P'2 structure and enable a reversible P'2-OP4 transition, delivering 35 mA·h·g⁻¹ extra capacity. TM vacancies further synergize with Na vacancies to stabilize the TM-O framework, suppressing lattice oxygen loss and Mn³⁺ enrichment, which improves 100 cycles capacity retention by 28.7%. This work advances the synthesis and electrochemistry of P'2-type materials, offering a practical path toward application.

title: Crystallography- and microstructure-driven design of lightweight titanium-based shape memory alloys
abstract: To facilitate the diverse functionalities of lightweight shape-memory alloys (SMAs) in various applications, it is crucial to address the research gaps in understanding and optimizing their shape-memory effects. This study presents a systematic investigation into the crystallography–microstructure–property correlations conducted on a series of lightweight TiV-based alloys. The crystallographic effect was quantitatively analyzed by tuning the lattice parameters as a function of V content. The intrinsic transformation strain was found to increase with the decreasing V concentration, reaching 7.4% along the [011] β direction while preserving a predominantly β-phase structure. However, compositional variations also influenced the phase stability and deformation mechanisms, producing distinct functional responses. Notably, the V12.5 alloy, located near the compositional threshold for the α'' martensitic transformation, exhibited a synergistic deformation mode combining the stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) and additional reorientation, achieving a recoverable strain of ∼ 9%. In contrast, alloys with higher or lower V contents primarily deformed via SIMT or reorientation alone, resulting in reduced shape recovery response. Overall, these findings provide a quantitative framework linking the variation of lattice parameters, phase stability, and deformation behaviors.

title: Recipients of the 2026 Acta Materialia, Inc. student awards
