Manipulating coercivity via magnetic domains and free energy by B2-type nano-range order fluctuations in Fe45Co45Ni5Cr3Al2 alloy
abstract: Although the reduction of magnetic anisotropy has been demonstrated as an effective means of lowering the coercivity (Hc) of soft magnetic materials, its efficacy appears limited when applied to FeCo-based alloys. Consequently, the present study introduces an innovative approach aimed at regulating Hc through the manipulation of magnetic domains and nanostructure. We demonstrate that a B2 phase structured Fe45Co45Ni5Cr3Al2 (wt.%) alloy can generate nano-range order fluctuations, measuring between 1.34 and 5.98 nm. Remarkably, this results in a reduction of Hc from 476.39A/m to 103.31A/m. This outcome is attributed to increased demagnetisation energy within these B2 nano-order fluctuations, arising from their ability to reduce exchange energy rather than magnetic crystalline anisotropy energy. This, in turn, facilitates the expansion of magnetic domains, thereby reducing the work required for magnetisation under external fields. In contrast to conventional soft magnetic alloys, which lower Hc primarily by reducing magnetic anisotropy, this study—supported by first-principles calculations—demonstrates that the key factor for lowering Hc in the Fe45Co45Ni5Cr3Al2 alloy is the reduction of exchange energy. The material also exhibits a superior saturation magnetic induction (Bs, 2.26T) compared with traditional FeCo-based counterparts, offering distinct performance advantages. This study elucidates the interplay between magnetic domains and nanostructure and proposes a novel pathway for reducing Hc in soft magnetic alloys.

title: Constructing localized zn vacancies for enhanced thermoelectric efficiency of zintl phase EuZn2Sb2
abstract: Thermoelectric materials, which enable direct conversion between heat and electricity, hold great promise for sustainable energy applications. However, their performance is limited by the close coupling between electron and phonon transport. In this work, localized Zn vacancies have been introduced into EuZn2Sb2, effectively scattering phonons while preserving high carrier mobility. Meanwhile, the lattice softening effect induced by localized Zn vacancies further reduces the lattice thermal conductivity from ∼2.6 W m-1 K-1 in EuZn2Sb2 to ∼1.7 W m-1 K-1 in Eu1.05Zn1.95Sb2 at 300 K. By simultaneously maintaining a high carrier mobility of ∼150 cm2 V-1 s-1, a peak zT as high as ∼0.96 at 773 K was achieved in Eu1.05Zn1.95Sb2. Furthermore, Ca alloying introduces extensive dislocations, nanoprecipitates, and point defects, enabling full-spectrum phonon scattering and yielding a decent zT of ∼1.1 at 773 K, which outperforms the previously reported EuZn2Sb2-based materials. Remarkably, a high energy conversion efficiency of ∼11.1 % has been realized under a temperature difference of 480 K for the EuZn2Sb2/Mg3Sb2 device. This work demonstrates that localized vacancy engineering is an effective strategy for decoupling electron and phonon transport, providing new insights into the design of high-performance thermoelectric materials.

title: Structural stability and superconductivity of tetragonal TiB4 with an open boron framework
abstract: Polyborides incorporating metal, characterized by the abundant geometries, inherent outstanding mechanical properties, and intrinsic exceptional superconductivity, have recently generated growing interest. However, the high-pressure phase diagram of high-boron-concentration titanium-boron system and their highly promising superconductivity remain poorly understood. Herein, we conducted a comprehensive exploration of dense boron-rich Ti-B compounds through first-principles structure search approach and discovered two previously unraised phases stabilized by robust covalent B-B and ionic Ti-B bonds: TiB3 and TiB4. In particular, TiB4 has a tetragonal geometric motif with symmetry I4/mmm and exhibits a unique host-guest architecture, featuring a three-dimensional boron covalent network with open channels that encapsulate the guest titanium atoms. Electron-phonon coupling calculations reveal that the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) of TiB4 at 140 GPa is 33 K, exceeding that of existing binary bulk metal-bearing tetraboride superconductors. In-depth analysis indicates that the superconductivity of TiB4 is primarily derived from the coupling of the Ti 3d and B 2p electron states at the Fermi level with the softened phonon modes resulting from the cooperative vibration of Ti and B atoms in the low-frequency region. Furthermore, by substituting titanium atoms with bimetallic elements, we identified that LiLaB8 is a potential ambient-pressure hard superconductor with a Tc of 24.3 K, whereas LiNaB8 is a promising superconductive superhard material with a Vickers hardness (Hv) of 39.4 GPa. These findings highlight the profound insights into the titanium borides and lay the groundwork for research into emerging functional metal borides.

title: Editorial Board
Grain boundary structure mediated heterogeneity in solute segregation and dislocation nucleation of aluminum alloys
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) are usually in a metastable state and contain various types of ledges in polycrystalline materials. The presence of these structural features may lead to heterogeneous solute segregation at nearly flat GBs in Al alloys and affect the mechanical properties of materials. In this study, the effects of GB structural features on solute segregation and dislocation nucleation are investigated by hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that local GB structural transitions and GB ledges result in the heterogeneous segregation of solutes Cu and Mg. The solute density at the GB is determined by the average segregation energy in different regions. Local structural transitions and ledges at GBs intensify strain localization, and result in a lower nucleation stress for dislocations compared to the ground-state GBs. A low concentration of the solute Cu tends to promote dislocation nucleation when it segregates at ground-state GBs, but inhibits it in other types of GBs. Conversely, the segregation of solute Mg promotes dislocation nucleation at all GBs. This difference is attributed to the effect of solute segregation on GB disorder. Increased GB disorder generates a stress gradient that provides an additional driving force for the atomic shuffling and free volume migration required for dislocation nucleation. Therefore, a negative correlation has been identified between GB disorder and dislocation nucleation stress.

title: Ni diffusion in the equiatomic CoFeMnNiV high-entropy alloy: Unexpected impact of second-phase precipitation on bulk diffusion rates
abstract: Ni diffusion in the equiatomic CoFeMnNiV high-entropy alloy is measured over an extended temperature range that covers both single-phase (face-centered cubic, FCC, solid solution) as well as two-phase (FCC solid solution + σ-phase) states. In addition, Ni diffusion experiments were performed on a single-phase σ-alloy. The σ-phase precipitation is found to affect significantly the self-diffusion kinetics in the FCC solid solution. The measured tracer diffusion coefficients follow an Arrhenius-type relationship when estimated in the single-phase solid solution, and a characteristic enhancement of the Ni diffusivity is observed at lower temperatures when the σ-phase precipitates during the diffusion annealing treatments. The enhancement is significantly suppressed when the alloy is pre-aged to approach a nearly equilibrium σ-phase volume fraction at a given temperature. Since Ni volume diffusion in the σ-phase was found to be similar to that in the FCC equiatomic counterpart, the observed diffusion enhancement is attributed to an excess vacancy concentration, generated during the growth of σ-precipitates. This excess gets eliminated when approaching thermodynamic equilibrium, i.e., when precipitation ends. A simple model of the diffusion enhancement during precipitation is proposed.

title: The origin of dislocation structures and chemical segregation in additively manufactured δ-ferritic steel microstructures
abstract: Dislocation structures generated during thermal cycling play a critical role in governing the mechanical and corrosion performance of additively manufactured (AM) alloys. While extensive studies have addressed dislocation cell formation and associated chemical segregation in face-centered cubic alloys, less attention has been paid to body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructures. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)-processed BCC alloys, dislocation densities are typically lower, solidification cell-related chemical heterogeneities minimal, and dislocation cells often absent, leaving the dislocation-related chemistries largely unexplored. Consequently, the origin of chemical segregation and the solute-dislocation interactions in LPBF-processed BCC alloys remain poorly understood. Here, a multiscale correlative microscopy approach combining plasma focused ion beam, transmission Kikuchi diffraction, scanning transmission electron microscopy, and ultrawide field-of-view atom probe tomography is employed to characterize the chemistry and crystallography of individual dislocations in LPBF-fabricated duplex stainless steels containing >98% δ-ferrite. The results reveal pronounced enrichment of N and Cr at dislocations. N segregation is attributed to elastic strain relaxation around dislocations. Density functional theory demonstrates weak and short-range Cr-N attractions, and strong and long-range Mn-N attractions, meaning Mn is stabilized in the matrix while Cr can move towards dislocations. Cr segregation levels depend on dislocation crystallography, deviating from the classical Cottrell theory. The interplay between solute drag and the thermally activated motion of BCC screw dislocations during LPBF thermal cycling influences the dislocation arrangements. These findings provide new insights into dislocation-mediated chemical heterogeneity in LPBF-processed BCC alloys and offer guidance for AM alloy design by linking LPBF parameters, dislocation evolution, and phase transformations.

title: The effect of high magnetic field on Al/Cr0.5MnFe0.5NiCu1.4 liquid-solid diffusion kinetics
abstract: The liquid-solid diffusion processes in the Al/Cr0.5MnFe0.5NiCu1.4, Al/Cu and Al/Ni were quantitatively analyzed using a liquid-solid diffusion couple under weak convective conditions. The microstructure of the diffusion couples and the influence of high magnetic fields on the diffusion behavior were systematically investigated. In the Al/Cr0.5MnFe0.5NiCu1.4 system, the diffusion behaviors of different components exhibit significant differences with the variation of the magnetic field. The diffusion rates of Mn and Cr show a non-monotonic variation within the same magnetic field range, with the maximum values achieved at 3 T; in contrast, those of Fe, Ni and Cu increase monotonically with the enhancement of the magnetic field. The analysis demonstrates that the partition coefficients k at the Al/Cr0.5MnFe0.5NiCu1.4 solid-liquid interface under varied magnetic fields directly induce the change in the total solute diffusion capacity. This also applies to Al/Cu and Al/Ni. Furthermore, the phase transformations occurring in the diffusion couple during both diffusion and solidification processes were analyzed, providing theoretical and experimental insights for designing multicomponent alloy systems with superior performance. By introducing the magnetic dipole interaction mechanism, this study elucidates the differences in magnetic forces exerted on different components under a high magnetic field, as well as the corresponding effects of these forces on the diffusion rate.

title: Controlling the dealloying morphology of Fe-36Ni alloy exposed to liquid Pb using temperature and in situ proton irradiation
abstract: Liquid metal dealloying is a unique processing technique to generate nano- and micro-scale porous materials through the selective dissolution of miscible elements in a liquid solvent. The kinetics of this process are governed by the interplay of diffusion in the liquid, solid, and at the solid/liquid interface. However, previous studies have primarily focused on the role of liquid phase and interfacial diffusion, under the assumption that solid-state diffusion is too sluggish to impact morphological evolution. Here, we examine the role of solid-state diffusion by dealloying Invar (Fe-36Ni) in liquid Pb under the influence of both temperature and simultaneous 3 MeV proton irradiation. Our results show that both temperature and simultaneous irradiation significantly affect the resulting morphology. Increasing temperature shifts the dealloyed morphology from fine bicontinuous ligaments at 500 °C to elongated structures at 600 °C and coarser features at 675 °C. In situ irradiation affects the dealloyed morphology via radiation-enhanced diffusion at 500 °C and 600 °C, but has a minimal role at 675 °C because thermal diffusion is sufficiently high to dominate mass transport. These findings establish that solid-state diffusion has a non-negligible impact on the pattern formation mechanism during dealloying, and demonstrate that in situ irradiation is a powerful lever for deconvoluting its effect.

title: Accelerating oxygen evolution reaction reconstruction by d-π orbital engineering to mediate disruption of electron localization in pentlandite
abstract: The electrochemical reconstruction of precursors into active (oxy)hydroxide phases is a critical step toward achieving high-performance oxygen evolution reaction catalysis. However, for materials with intrinsic electron localization such as pentlandite, strong electron correlation effects hinder the oxidation kinetics required for deep reconstruction, fundamentally limiting their catalytic potential. Herein, we create d-π orbital engineering at the interface by supporting nickel pyrite on a carbon substrate, and leverage this electronic coupling to disrupt its intrinsic electron localization. The resulting electron delocalization significantly accelerates electron extraction from the nickel pyrite lattice and lowers the formation energy barrier of high-valence metal ions, thereby driving a rapid reconstruction phase transformation. The lifting of localization is not confined to interfacial atomic layers, rather, it establishes three-dimensional charge transport pathways through the delocalized π-system. At a current density of 100 mA cm-2, the catalyst achieves an extremely low overpotential of 220 mV and exhibits outstanding stability. When applied in an AEMWE, the FNS-C-1 delivers a high current density of 1 A cm-2 at 1.75 V with stable operation exceeding 200 h. This work demonstrates that interfacial electron delocalization represents a general and effective strategy to transform intrinsically inert precursors into dynamically evolving, highly active OER electrocatalysts.

title: Atomic mechanism of topologically close-packed phases twinning transformation in Ni-based single crystal superalloys during creep
abstract: This study systematically investigated the twinning transformation mechanism of topologically close-packed phases (μ phases) in a Ni-based single crystal superalloy during creep deformation. Two distinct types of twins were identified in the μ phase: misaligned (TB1-type) and symmetric (TB2-type) twins. The formation of the TB1-type twin occurred when shear stress acted along the [1¯101]μ direction within the (011¯2)μ crystal plane of the μ phase, initially generating stacking faults, which subsequently evolve into a TB1-type twin structure through atomic rearrangement. Interestingly, the transformation of TB2-type twins followed two separate pathways: (1) further shear deformation of TB1-type twins along the [1¯101]μ direction within the (011¯2)μ plane under external stress; (2) structural retention of P phase configurations resembling TB2-type twin boundaries during the P→μ phase transformation. These findings provide fundamental insights into the relationship between TCP phase transitions and creep behavior, offering valuable theoretical guidance for the design of advanced superalloys.

title: Microstructural strain distribution and plastic localization from grain boundary sliding activation in an FCC material
abstract: The activation of grain boundary sliding (GBS) and its effect on strain distribution and plastic localization are investigated in a polycrystalline FCC Fe–Ni alloy deformed at elevated temperature using high-resolution, discontinuity-tolerant digital image correlation combined with electron backscatter diffraction. A statistical analysis is performed at the microstructural scale and compared with deformation behavior at room temperature. At both temperatures, plastic deformation is predominantly accommodated by slip, even when GBS is activated at elevated temperature. However, GBS leads to pronounced plastic localization, revealing a clear distinction between deformation accommodation and localized deformation. The intensification of plastic localization associated with GBS and slip is investigated as a function of the applied macroscopic deformation. The competition between slip and GBS is found to play a limited role in controlling localization, while microstructural features strongly influence the activation and localization behavior of GBS.

title: Understanding creep behaviour in high performance alloys through use of the Wilshire equations
abstract: This study explores the creep behaviour of three polycrystalline alloys—stainless steel 316, Haynes 282, and Inconel 713C—chosen for their varying precipitate volume fractions. The primary aim is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms that control creep behaviour in these alloys, with a particular focus on determining the creep activation energies (Qc*) involved.SS316 displays a gradual transition in Qc* values, attributed to dislocation movement at low temperatures and twinning above yield stress at elevated conditions. Haynes 282 shows a wider range (276–427 kJ/mol), with γ′ precipitate resistance at low stress and forest hardening above yield strength. In contrast, Inconel 713C with highest volume fraction of precipitates, exhibits a constant Qc*, indicating creep governed by confined dislocation motion within γ channels, with no clear transition.The findings reinforce the application of the Wilshire equations in rationalising Qc* values and linking them to microstructural mechanisms. This provides a robust framework for predicting creep behaviour, aiding alloy development and high-temperature material optimisation.

title: Relative contributions of solutes and forest dislocations to thermally activated plasticity in hydrogen-alloyed Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic steels: analyzing stress-dependence of Haasen plot
abstract: A competitive relationship between solute atoms and forest dislocations in determining the kinetics of thermally activated plasticity was studied for a Type310S (Fe-24Cr-19Ni) austenitic steel containing ∼8500 at ppm hydrogen (H), where solute H promotes solid solution-hardening through an increase in the effective stress. The investigation was performed by constructing Haasen plot ( i.e ., strain rate sensitivity (SRS) vs. flow stress) based on stress relaxation tests, and by analyzing its evolution in relation to the decay of effective stress. In the regime of high effective stress, alloying solute elements—whose overcoming by dislocations is retarded by the presence of H—acted as primary rate-controlling obstacles to dislocations, giving rise to a relatively large and strain-independent SRS. In terms of Haasen plot , these manifested as an increase in the intercept and a decrease in the slope. Beyond the phenomenological findings of these H-induced characteristic changes, the present study elaborates their physical origin and transient nature. As the effective stress decreased and dislocation density increased, such predominance of solutes was progressively taken over by forest dislocations, leading the Haasen plot for H-charged specimens to approach that for non-charged specimen. These new insights further establish how H, alloying elements, and forest dislocations sequentially compete as rate-controlling obstacles depending on mechanical loading condition and internal state of the material.

title: Evolution of dislocation cells overlaid on solidification cells resulting from Hf/O segregation in additively processed Nb-Hf-Ti alloys
abstract: While there are many observations of dislocation cell formation overlaid on solidification cells in fusion based additively processed alloys, including stainless steels, nickel base alloys, aluminum alloys, and refractory alloys, there is limited understanding of the underlying mechanisms. This study delves into a detailed investigation of such dislocation cell formation, associated with the underlying solidification sub-structure, in the case of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processed Nb base C103 (Nb-10Hf-1Ti, wt. %) alloy, which is highly relevant for aerospace applications. Using multi-scale characterization, the progressive and concomitant evolution of both the dislocation cell structure and the solidification sub-structure has been systematically probed from a single laser track to three layers, to twenty layers, and finally the full build consisting of nearly 150 layers. The results revealed a more random distribution of dislocations at the early stages, not associated with the solidification cells, evolving into a regular patterned arrangement, aligned along the inter-cellular channels. The underlying mechanism appears to be thermal cycle driven recovery process during LPBF, where the dislocations generated from the cycling are pinned at the Hf-O rich inter-cellular channels during their rearrangement into lower energy configurations. This coupled dislocation / solidification cell structure offers a strong barrier to subsequent dislocation motion during tensile testing, as manifested in the high yield stress (∼500 MPa) of the as-built C103 alloy compared to the corresponding stress-relieved condition (∼300 MPa) that does not demonstrate a similar substructure.

title: Enhancing the strength and ductility of an additive-manufactured body-centered-cubic multi-principal-element alloy by chemical medium-range order
abstract: Achieving high strength and ductility simultaneously in additive-manufactured body-centered-cubic (BCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) remains a significant challenge, while utilizing the local chemical order is considered a possible pathway. Here, we report a novel Al2Ti7Zr2Nb5 MPEA fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), which exhibits chemical medium-range order (CMRO) clusters embedded within a BCC matrix. Mechanical testing demonstrates that the CMRO enables a high strength-ductility synergy in the alloy (yield strength ∼ 1023 MPa, tensile ductility ∼ 32%, and fracture toughness ∼ 158 MPa·m1/2). Phase-field simulations indicate that CMRO formation is thermodynamically driven by strong interaction among Al, Ti, and Zr elements. Further analysis reveals that dislocations shear through CMRO, which decreases the glide resistance for the subsequent dislocations and facilitates the following dislocations to slip through the CMRO and form dislocation channels. The associated disruption of chemical ordering introduces lattice distortions that facilitate elastic strain accumulation and dislocation debris, thereby activating dynamic hardening and secondary planar slip and promoting the plastic deformation zone into the bulk specimen. Furthermore, the frequent intersection of dislocation channels sustains a sufficient strain-hardening rate to large strains. This work demonstrates CMRO as a promising pathway for developing high-performance MPEAs.

title: Toughening Sm2Co17-type permanent magnets via cu-segregation-mediated nanoscale cellular structures
abstract: The inherent brittleness of Sm2Co17-type magnets critically limits their reliability in advanced magnetic power systems. Conventional toughening via second-phase particles or grain boundary engineering inevitably compromises magnetic performance, leaving the simultaneous enhancement of mechanical and magnetic properties a fundamental challenge. This study reveals for the first time that the mechanical deformability of the nanoscale cellular structure is governed by an interplay between basal slip at the lamellar/intracellular phase interfaces and pyramidal amorphization shear at the cell boundaries—a process regulated by nanoscale copper partitioning. Reducing Cu segregation at lamellar/intracellular phase interfaces substantially elevates the energy barrier to basal slip. Concurrently, optimizing Cu concentration within the cell boundary phase increases its elastic modulus and confines shear-induced amorphization to specific nanodomains. This localized deformation strategy effectively accommodates strain while suppressing microcrack initiation. Through optimized Cu distribution, we achieve a superior balance between flexural strength (209 ± 15 MPa) and magnetic energy product (261.6 kJ/m3). This Cu-segregation-mediated toughening mechanism not only establishes a new paradigm for strengthening Sm-Co magnets but also provides fresh insights into optimizing the structural integrity of other advanced permanent magnets.

title: Cryogenic ultrahigh strength-ductility synergy in complex concentrated alloys enabled by stacking-fault-assisted nanoprecipitation-induced hierarchical microstructures
abstract: Achieving ultrahigh yield strength (>2 GPa) while retaining uniform ductility in metallic alloys remains a central challenge, particularly at cryogenic temperatures. Here, we demonstrate that deformation-inherited planar defects can be exploited not only as strengthening units but also as chemical and crystallographic selectors for subsequent nanoprecipitation in a (CoNi)85Mo10Al3Ti2 complex concentrated alloy. By tailoring thermomechanical processing to regulate the competition between grain-boundary σ phase formation and intragranular Co3Mo-type D019 precipitation, deformation-induced stacking faults (SFs) are engineered to retain Mo-rich segregation and transform into coherent D019 nanoplates via a coupled displacive-diffusional mechanism during recrystallization annealing. These D019 nanoplates traverse recrystallized ultrafine grains, suppress grain growth, and subsequently promote the precipitation of L12Ni3(Al, Ti) nanoparticles both along coherent D019/matrix interfaces and within the matrix during tempering. The resulting hierarchical heterogeneous microstructure, comprising ultrafine grains, Mo-segregated SFs, a high density of D019 nanoplates, and L12 nanoprecipitates, delivers a cryogenic yield strength of ∼2.4 GPa together with ∼10% uniform ductility at 77 K. Moreover, the coherent D019/matrix interfaces simultaneously enhance strength and mitigate local strain incompatibility by emitting partial dislocations, thereby generating additional SFs and nanotwins during deformation. These findings establish planar-defect-assisted nanoprecipitation and coherent-interface-mediated hardening as a general strategy for designing 2-GPa-class, damage-tolerant alloys for extreme environments.

title: An E(3)-equivariant interatomic potential uncovers the atomistic origin of solute and LPSO strengthening in Mg–Y–Zn alloy
abstract: The absence of a reliable interatomic potential for the Mg–Y–Zn ternary system has long hindered atomistic understanding of its strengthening mechanisms, where solid-solution hardening, dislocation–interface interactions, and LPSO kink deformation operate concurrently across multiple length scales. Here, we develop an E(3)-equivariant Allegro machine-learning interatomic potential that combines computational efficiency with near-DFT accuracy, validated against an extensive set of benchmarks, particularly the properties most critical to dislocation-mediated plasticity, including generalized stacking-fault energies, dislocation core structures, and Peierls stresses. This potential enables a large-scale framework that treats, within a single description, dislocation glide in the α-Mg matrix, basal-dislocation transmission across the α-Mg/LPSO interface, prismatic slip and its role as a dislocation source for kink boundaries in the LPSO structure. The simulations reveal that short-range ordered Y–Zn clusters impede basal ⟨a⟩ dislocation glide more effectively than isolated solutes. Meanwhile, both Y solute atoms and short-range ordered Y–Zn clusters are observed to promote cross-slip of pyramidal I ⟨c+a⟩ screw dislocations possessing a non-planar core structure. The semi-coherent α-Mg/LPSO interface impedes basal dislocations effectively, with a barrier governed by the dislocation orientation, the polytype (14H vs 18R), and the hard-layer spacing, largely suppressing their transmission into the LPSO. We further trace the origin of the basal dislocations that populate the LPSO kink boundaries to prismatic ⟨a⟩ slip. Prismatic dislocation shear simulations distinguish kink-pair formation from propagation and identify the LPSO hard layer as a character-selective filter that promotes the conversion of prismatic screw segments into basal ⟨a⟩ dislocations.

title: From heat capacity to Gibbs energy: An experimental thermodynamic route for single-phase high-entropy alloys
abstract: A comprehensive experimental methodology was developed to determine the thermodynamic functions of single-phase AlxCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The approach integrates calorimetric measurements, thermophysical characterization, and physically based entropy models. Low-temperature heat capacities, Cp(T), were measured between 4 and 473 K, while high-temperature Cp(T) values were determined near the solidus temperature. Controlled interpolation across decomposition regions enabled the construction of metastable Cp(T) functions over the entire temperature range. The enthalpy of formation at 298 K, Hf,elem0(298K), was determined by high-temperature oxide melt solution calorimetry and combined with the measured Cp(T) data to derive temperature-dependent enthalpy functions, ΔHT(T). The configurational entropy, Sconf, was calculated using the ideal solid-solution model for the FCC alloys, whereas for the B2 alloys it was estimated from CALPHAD-predicted sublattice occupancies (TCHEA8 database) due to the absence of experimental methods capable of directly determining site-specific compositions. The thermal entropy contribution, ΔSthermal(T), was obtained by integrating Cp(T)/T, and combined with Sconf to generate Gibbs energy functions, ΔGT(T), for each single-phase alloy. For the FCC alloy, the experimentally derived ΔGT(T) values are in good agreement with the TCHEA8 predictions. In contrast, the B2 alloys exhibit significant deviations from the CALPHAD description, reflecting discrepancies in both Cp(T) and entropy. Nevertheless, the overall temperature dependence and magnitude of ΔGT(T) are reproduced reasonably well. This work establishes an experimentally grounded framework for determining Gibbs energy functions in complex alloys and provides valuable benchmarks for the development and validation of CALPHAD databases.

title: Insights into Ni migration in long-term tested Ni-yttria stabilized zirconia electrodes by three-dimensional reconstruction aided phase-field simulations
abstract: Nickel (Ni) migration is a crucial factor in the degradation of Ni-yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) electrodes during operation. However, current hypotheses to explain the Ni migration of Ni-YSZ electrodes remain inconsistent. In this paper, three-dimensional (3D) phase-field simulations based on 3D reconstructed microstructures were utilized to understand Ni migration in long-term tested solid oxide fuel and electrolysis cells (SOFCs and SOECs). Phase-field simulations on two representative sub-volumes under open-circuit voltage (OCV) conditions revealed the impact of microstructural heterogeneity on Ni migration. Further simulations under SOEC and SOFC modes demonstrated the combined effect of this heterogeneity and contact angle gradients on Ni migration. A comparative analysis of the evolution of the microstructure, phase volume fraction, and volumetric center for two sub-volumes in OCV, SOEC, and SOFC modes revealed distinct migration behaviors depending on sub-volume size and operating mode. Ni migration was more pronounced in the small sub-volume under SOEC mode, but more significant in the large sub-volume under SOFC mode. These differences stem from the alignment or opposition of driving forces from microstructural heterogeneity and contact angle gradients. With further experimental validation, the microstructure of Ni-YSZ electrodes may be quantitatively described, even enabling lifetime predictions by integrating machine learning.

title: Machine learning-driven creep law discovery across alloy compositional space
abstract: High-temperature creep characterization of structural alloys traditionally relies on serial uniaxial tests, which are highly inefficient for exploring the large search space of alloy compositions and for material discovery. Here, we introduce a machine-learning-assisted, high-throughput framework for creep law identification based on a dimple array bulge instrument (DABI) configuration, which enables parallel creep testing of 25 dimples, each fabricated from a different alloy, in a single experiment. Full-field surface displacements of dimples undergoing time-dependent creep-induced bulging under inert gas pressure are measured by 3D digital image correlation. We train a recurrent neural network as a surrogate model, mapping creep parameters and loading conditions to the time-dependent deformation response of DABI. Coupling this surrogate with a particle swarm optimization scheme enables rapid and global inverse identification with sparsity regularization of creep parameters from experimental displacement–time histories. In addition, we propose a phenomenological creep law with a time-dependent stress exponent that captures the sigmoidal primary creep observed in wrought INCONEL 625 and extracts its temperature dependence from DABI tests at multiple temperatures. Furthermore, we employ a general creep law combining several conventional forms with regularized inversion to identify the creep laws for 47 additional Fe-, Ni-, and Co-rich alloys and to automatically select the dominant functional form for each alloy. This workflow, combined with the DABI experiment, provides a quantitative, high-throughput creep characterization platform that is compatible with data mining, composition–property modeling, and nonlinear structural optimization with creep behavior across a large alloy design space.

title: Frustrating dislocation resistance inhomogeneity at multiscale levels to enable strength-ductility synergy in multi-principal element alloys
abstract: Designing metallic alloys of high strength-ductility synergy has remained an unremitting pursuit for many engineers and scientists. Recent advance in designing multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) offers an ample and unprecedented space for advanced microstructure design to address this need. In this work, we investigated a strategy to push the strength-ductility trade-off envelop by utilizing multiscale local chemical inhomogeneity created on the principle of negative mixing enthalpy alloying. This is achieved in an FCC CoCrNi MPEA added with Al, Ti and V as negative mixing enthalpy elements to the host elements. This promoted the alloy to form complex structural variations at multiple scales, including short-, medium- and long-range chemical orders; at the nanoscale, L12 nanodomains with varying morphologies and planar fault energies within the FCC matrix; and at the microscale, a bimodal grain size distribution. Such microstructure frustrates and disunifies dislocation resistance, promoting cascading activation of various lattice deformation and hardening mechanisms, such as stacking faults, deformation twins, and L12 nanodomain shearing, during the deformation process. This design yields an exceptional combination of mechanical properties, with a yield strength of ∼1.3 GPa, an ultimate tensile strength of ∼1.92 GPa, and a uniform elongation of ∼28% at ambient temperature. Our findings may provide potential reference for designing various degrees of local chemical ordering in alloys to manipulate the movement of dislocations for achieving high strength and ductility synergy.

title: Kinetic phase selection enables wide-temperature strength-ductility synergy in additively manufactured Al0.3CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy
abstract: Conventional annealing of additively manufactured (AM) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) often induces brittle σ-phase precipitation, leading to severe embrittlement and limiting their applicability over a wide temperature range. In this work, a kinetically guided short-time annealing (STA) strategy is developed in a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) Al0.3CoCrFeNiMn HEA by identifying a 700 °C time window that limits σ-phase formation. The optimized 700 °C/15 min treatment generates a multiphase nanoscale architecture comprising coherent Al/Ni-rich FCC zones, a Cr-rich FCC phase, and B2 precipitates. As a result, the alloy exhibits a sustained strength–ductility synergy from −196 °C to 600 °C, with a yield strength of ∼1.16 GPa at -196 °C and ∼730 MPa at 600 °C, while maintaining a nearly constant total elongation of ∼11%. Notably, microstructural observations at -196 °C reveal that stacking faults readily cut through the Al/Ni-rich FCC zones, whereas the B2 phase strongly resists shearing. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal that the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) disparity drives a mechanistic transition from penetrable obstacle shearing to Orowan bypassing, ultimately prolonging work-hardening capability and uniform ductility. These findings demonstrate an effective kinetic phase-selection strategy for designing precipitation-strengthened LPBF HEAs with excellent mechanical performance across a wide temperature range.

title: Multiscale generative inverse design for porous media via property-conditioned unit-cell assemblies: Application to VRFB electrodes
abstract: Porous materials are the reactive backbone of many technologies, especially electrochemical systems, making their inverse design a central challenge. Because microstructural features (e.g., porosity, permeability, etc.) govern fluid flow, transport, and reaction kinetics, they ultimately control component‐level and system performance from the inverse design perspective. As the utilization of additive manufacturing (AM) for porous materials continues to mature, there is a growing need for computational frameworks that co-evolve with experimental efforts and actively inform them. AI-enabled inverse design offers such a pathway: by learning meaningful latent representations that capture complex structure–property relationships, it broadens the reachable property space, helps avoid suboptimal designs, and fully exploits AM’s design freedom to manufacture high-performance materials. Building on our prior work in property-conditioned microstructure generation, we extend these tools to larger material systems by treating the material layout as an assembly of potentially 3D-printable microscale unit cells with targeted effective properties. As a case study, we leverage this proposed approach to design more energy-efficient porous electrodes to help tackle the challenges in developing vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB). More specifically, we optimize a VRFB half-cell to minimize power loss, illustrating how microstructures generated through data-driven algorithms can translate into improved porous electrode efficiency and, ultimately, lower commercialization costs for VRFBs. Although focused on VRFBs, the proposed framework is broadly applicable to other materials and engineering design problems.

title: A closed-loop multiscale computational framework for predicting barocaloric effects: Entropy decomposition and transformation mechanisms
abstract: The predictive design of metallic barocaloric materials requires a unified framework linking thermodynamics, atomistic mechanisms, and transformation kinetics. Here, we develop a closed-loop multiscale Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) framework combining quasi-harmonic thermodynamic modeling, density functional theory, and molecular dynamics simulations to enable self-consistent prediction and mechanistic understanding of barocaloric effects. Using magnesium as a representative model system, the framework quantitatively captures pressure-induced phase transitions and associated barocaloric responses with cross-scale consistency. The phase-transitional entropy change across the hcp-to-bcc transformation is dominated by vibrational contributions (~89.5%), with a secondary electronic contribution (~9.6%) associated with enhanced density of states near the Fermi energy level, while configurational effects are negligible. Atomistic simulations further reveal a shear-coupled Burgers transformation pathway linking lattice dynamics to macroscopic entropy changes. The giant barocaloric response identified near the phase boundary reflects intrinsic thermodynamic sensitivity of first-order transitions rather than practical operating conditions, highlighting the need to tune transition pressures via alloying. Based on these insights, we extract transferable design principles for metallic barocaloric materials including high lattice compressibility, dominant vibrational entropy, and favorable electronic structure features. These results establish a direct link between atomistic mechanisms and macroscopic barocaloric performance, enabling physically guided design of metallic barocaloric materials. This work provides a generalizable computational strategy for bridging multiscale modeling and materials design, offering a pathway toward the discovery of barocaloric materials with experimentally accessible operating conditions.

title: Formation of the cellular structure in the Sm2Co17-type permanent magnets: a phase-field study
abstract: The cellular structure consisting of ordered rhombohedral (2:17R) phase in the cells and disordered hexagonal (1:5H) phase in the cell boundary is key to the high coercivity and large magnetic energy product of the Sm2Co17-type permanent magnets. However, a theoretical understanding on the formation of this cellular structure is still lacking. Here in this work, we developed a phase field model to simulate the microstructure evolution of Sm2Co17-type permanent magnets during isothermal aging. The model takes into account the lattice misfit strain energy between the parent 1:7H phase and product phases (2:17R and 1:5H), as well as the six distinct 2:17R antiphase domains (APDs) generated during 2:17R phase ordering. The model well reproduces the cellular structure observed in experiments. Analysis shows that the cell morphology on different crystallographic planes is governed by the minimization of the misfit strain energy. More importantly, the six types of 2:17R APDs are proven indispensable for the formation of the unique cellular structure, where the 1:5H phase with a volume fraction as low as 20% interconnects to form a continuous cell boundary matrix. Specifically, reducing the number of 2:17R APDs, or lowering the 2:17R antiphase domain boundary energy relative to the 2:17R/1:5H interfacial energy, will destabilize the cellular structure. This work elucidates the formation mechanism of the cellular structure in the Sm2Co17-type permanent magnets. It could shed light on the design of high-performance permanent magnets.

title: Impact of oxygen and sulfur on dislocation glide in zirconium – I. Dislocation dynamics from in situ tensile tests
abstract: Sulfur addition to zirconium alloys is known to have a tremendous strengthening effect, with only a few ppm leading to a strong hardening and a noticeable decrease of the creep rate above 300 °C. Although previous works have shown an interdependent effect of oxygen and sulfur, with sulfur amplifying the strengthening of oxygen in the domain of dynamic strain aging, the physical mechanism behind this impact of sulfur addition on zirconium mechanical properties is still unknown. Using in situ straining experiments in a transmission electron microscope, we study how sulfur and oxygen modify the glide motion of dislocations for temperatures between 200 °C and 550 °C in zirconium samples with an oxygen concentration between 80 and 1300 weight ppm and a sulfur concentration up to 25 wppm. These experiments show that the velocity of gliding dislocations is reduced by the dragging of their enriched oxygen atmosphere, when the temperature is high enough for oxygen to diffuse and segregate on dislocations. Once the motion of dislocations is slowed down, segregation of sulfur on dislocations becomes also possible despite the low sulfur content, leading to a further reduction of dislocation velocity. This synergistic effect of sulfur and oxygen segregation on dislocation explains the enhancement by sulfur of oxygen strengthening in zirconium alloys.

title: A unified predictive framework for α′ precipitation in Fe–Cr–Al alloys based on effective diffusion length: From dense-cascade irradiation to thermal aging
abstract: Quantitative prediction of α′ precipitation in Fe–Cr–Al alloys across the several-orders-of-magnitude dose-rate gap between ion and neutron irradiation is essential for accident-tolerant fuel (ATF) cladding design, yet no unified framework exists. Twelve Fe–(10–22)Cr–(0–14)Al (at.%) model alloys were self-ion irradiated at 350 °C over three dose rates (8×10−6–8×10−4 dpa/s) and three doses (0.24–1.44 dpa) to construct an 84-condition atom probe tomography (APT) database. At the highest dose rate, a nucleation→growth→ballistic-dissolution-dominated transition was directly observed. Published irradiation and thermal-aging APT data were integrated, and a unified framework was developed using the effective diffusion length Leff, derived from Sizmann’s point-defect theory, as a physical compression variable. Leff compresses dose rate, dose, temperature, and time into a single scalar with no irradiation-type-specific fitting parameters. Machine learning models employing only three variables — Cr, Al, and log10(Leff) — yielded cross-validated R2=0.56–0.82 for the four target α′ metrics (number density Nd, mean radius R̄, volume fraction Vf, and Cr concentration CCrin). Leave-Neutron-Out validation, in which all neutron data were withheld from training, demonstrated that Vf (R2=0.69) and log10(Nd) (R2=0.58) can be extrapolated from ion-irradiation and thermal-aging data alone. In contrast, R̄ and CCrin could not be extrapolated, cleanly separating the diffusion-controlled aspects of α′ precipitation that Leff captures from the irradiation-type-dependent ballistic-mixing contribution that it does not encode. Partial dependence analysis revealed a non-monotonic effect whereby ∼5 at.% Al addition promotes rather than suppresses α′ formation across the entire Leff range, identifying an Al composition window to be avoided in ATF cladding alloys.

title: Trimesic-acid etching assisted adsorption-shielded Zn(101) retention promoting interfacial reaction kinetics for long-life Zn metal batteries
abstract: The cycling stability of aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) is limited due to the uncontrollable deposition behavior of the zinc (Zn) anode and severe interfacial side reactions. In this study, kinetically favorable Zn(101) planes are directly introduced via selective Trimesic acid (TMA) etching, producing a Zn(101) dominated anode (TMA@Zn). The exposed Zn(101) planes lower the nucleation energy barrier and reduces the nucleation overpotential, enabling faster and more uniform Zn nucleation. Meanwhile, an increased Zn2+ surface diffusion coefficient accelerates interfacial nucleation and growth kinetics, which decreases local Zn2+ concentration at the electrode surface and suppresses concentration polarization, thereby preventing dendritic formation. In light of theoretical calculations, all these advantages are contributed from the strongest affinity and electronic interaction of Zn(101) with TMA, thereby shielding the attack of H+ in the solution and selectively retaining the Zn(101) crystal planes. Thanks to these, the TMA@Zn symmetrical battery has a cycle life of over 6200 h at 0.5 mA cm–2, and the TMA@Zn//Cu half-cell maintains a CE of 99.7% for 1100 cycles. Strikingly, the TMA@Zn//MnO2 full-cell can stably cycle for over 11,000 cycles at a current density of 5 A g–1. Meanwhile, the pouch battery with TMA@Zn also shows significantly improved durability and stability.

title: In situ observation of faceted and branched eutectic growth patterns during directional solidification of thin Al–Si samples
abstract: A fundamental challenge in eutectic solidification is the morphological selection of faceted/nonfaceted systems like Al–Si, where the faceted phase (Si) exhibits strong kinetic anisotropy. The role of crystallographic defects, especially twinning, in enabling coupling between the eutectic solids remains unresolved, largely due to the lack of real-time observations. Here, we present in situ directional solidification experiments on thin Al–Si samples of near-eutectic concentration, leveraging visible-light optics for real-time observation. Multiscale crystallographic analysis is performed ex situ using EBSD and TEM. We explore the evolution of growth patterns as a function of the imposed velocity V (0.1–5 μm s−1), at a fixed temperature gradient G (11 K mm−1). We identify three regimes: At low velocity, growth is dominated by intermittent coupling and decoupling between faceted Si crystals and the Al matrix, with most Si crystals presenting Σ3 twins. At intermediate velocity, disordered branched patterns emerge with increasing twin density. At higher velocity, a divorced/branched dynamics is observed, with new Si crystals nucleating and growing ahead of the interface, reaching sizes of a few 10 μm before being incorporated into the front. The microstructures are then highly disordered, with no prevailing crystal orientation. From measurements of interface recoil across the explored velocity range, we estimate an effective interfacial mobility in the 1 μms−1 K−1 range, indicating that growth is strongly limited by interface attachment, without evidence of a transition to rough (flake-to-fiber) growth. Based on these observations, we initiate a discussion on twin-mediated growth, trijunction dynamics, and wall effects.

title: Structural and electronic origins of enhanced thermoelectric performance in metastable p-type TiNiSn–HfNiSn solid solutions
abstract: The development of high-performance p-type half-Heusler alloys is crucial for thermoelectric power generation. Although a miscibility gap exists in the TiNiSn–HfNiSn system, recent studies report excellent thermoelectric performance. To clarify the microscopic origin of this enhancement, we investigated the crystal and electronic structures of p-type Ti1-xHfxNi0.8Co0.2Sn solid solutions using synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES), and density functional theory (DFT). XRD revealed a homogeneous single-phase C1b structure across the entire composition range. This metastable stabilization originates kinetically from rapid densification via pulsed electric current sintering and thermodynamically from the spontaneous formation of short-range order (SRO), which minimizes internal elastic strain. Additionally, lattice strain—dominated by alloy disorder—strongly correlated with electrical resistivity. Furthermore, HAXPES measurements showed a systematic shift of the valence band edge and core levels toward lower binding energies with increasing Hf content. Direct comparison with DFT-simulated spectra demonstrates that this shift is not caused by intrinsic band modulation. Instead, it is governed by a defect-mediated downward shift of the macroscopic Fermi level. Specifically, Hf substitution suppresses electron-donating Ni interstitials, removing carrier compensation and allowing Co-induced holes to pull the Fermi level onto the steep valence-band slope. This study provides comprehensive evidence that the enhanced p-type thermoelectric performance in metastable solid solutions arises from a synergy of SRO-driven phonon scattering and defect-mediated Fermi-level tuning.

title: Material-level characterization of the intrinsic mechanical quality factor of Al1-xScxN
abstract: Aluminum scandium nitride (Al1-xScxN) is a promising piezoelectric material for radio frequency (RF) filters due to its enhanced electromechanical coupling coefficient relative to AlN. However, its relatively low mechanical quality factor remains a critical challenge for improving the device performance. In this study, the intrinsic dissipation of the longitudinal acoustic vibrations in AlN and Al0.8Sc0.2N diaphragms was characterized from 40 GHz to 150 GHz using a laser-based pump-probe method. The decay of the longitudinal vibration amplitude was analyzed to extract the intrinsic mechanical quality factor. The analysis accounts for boundary scattering, phonon scattering, and the Akhiezer effect. Density functional theory calculations were performed to obtain mode-resolved anharmonic phonon scattering rates and the Grüneisen parameters, which were used to evaluate the acoustic lifetime associated with the Akhiezer effect from first principles. The results show that the Akhiezer effect governs the mechanical quality factor in this frequency range. The product of mechanical quality factor and frequency was determined to be 11.7 THz and 9.6 THz for AlN and Al0.8Sc0.2N, respectively. The lower mechanical quality factor of Al0.8Sc0.2N is attributed to the increased energy dissipation associated with its reduced mechanical stiffness. This work demonstrates a material-level method for extracting the intrinsic mechanical quality factor of Al1-xScxN films, providing guidelines for the optimization of RF filter design at the device-level.

title: Electrostatic levitation processing and deep learning investigation of liquid W-Zr refractory alloys
abstract: The competitive nucleation mechanism, crystal growth kinetics and solute diffusion dynamics in undercooled liquid W-Zr refractory alloys were investigated by comparing hyperperitectic W-50Zr, hypoeutectic W-64Zr, and eutectic W-80Zr alloys through electrostatic levitation experiments and deep learning computations. In hyperperitectic W-50Zr alloy, the peritectic transition was suppressed at moderate undercoolings, resulting in the partial retention of the primary (W) phase. When further undercooled beyond a critical threshold of about 280 K, the nucleation rate of W2Zr surpassed that of (W) phase, enabling its direct formation from the undercooled alloy. A discontinuity in the crystal growth velocity with respect to undercooling was observed at this threshold, corresponding to the transformation of the primary phase from (W) to W2Zr phase. In both hyperperitectic W-50Zr and hypoeutectic W-64Zr alloys, a gradient of solute W content formed in the residual liquid after the growth of primary or peritectic W2Zr phase. This gradient is attributed to the low transport mobility of W atoms, with a diffusion coefficient of 5.15×10−9 m2·s−1 determined through non-equilibrium molecular dynamics employing a deep neural network interatomic potential. In these three alloys, the significantly higher nucleation rate of (βZr) phase compared to W2Zr during eutectic transition promoted its preferential formation and increased its volume fraction at high undercoolings.

title: Impact of oxygen and sulfur on dislocation glide in zirconium — II. Insights from atomistic simulations
abstract: Experimental observations during in situ tensile tests experiments have shown that a tiny amount of sulfur as low as 5 weight ppm induces a strong reduction of dislocation velocity when they interact with diffusing oxygen, amplifying the dynamic strain aging associated with oxygen in zirconium alloys above 300 °C. Using ab initio calculations, we study the interaction of sulfur and oxygen solute atoms with 〈 a 〉 dislocations in hexagonal close-packed zirconium. We show that the impact of sulfur on dislocation mobility can be rationalized by a strong short-range attraction of sulfur to the dislocation core, with attractive insertion sites existing in the stacking faults created through dissociation of 〈 a 〉 dislocations in two partials lying either in prismatic or pyramidal planes. Ab initio calculations further show that the energy barriers, which need to be overcome by sulfur atoms to reach these attractive sites, is lower than the activation energies for sulfur bulk diffusion. With sulfur diffusing faster than oxygen in zirconium, kinetics allow for sulfur segregation at temperatures where oxygen form enriched atmospheres around dislocations. This sulfur segregation in the dislocation core, which comes on top of the elastic attraction of sulfur atoms in the dislocation strain field, explains the enhancement by sulfur of the dynamic strain aging caused by oxygen in zirconium.

title: Competition and coordination of disconnection modes in shear-coupled migration of asymmetric tilt grain boundaries
abstract: Grain boundaries play a critical role in determining the mechanical properties of polycrystalline materials, and their shear‑coupling behavior is essential for stress‑driven boundary migration and plastic deformation. Asymmetric tilt grain boundaries (ATGBs) are ubiquitous in polycrystals, yet their shear‑coupling mechanisms remain much less understood than those of symmetric tilt grain boundaries (STGBs). Here, we combine molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and theoretical modeling to systematically compare the shear‑coupling behavior of Σ5 and Σ25 〈001〉 ATGBs, revealing how different combinations of 〈100〉 and 〈110〉 migration modes govern their migration dynamics. Based on the disconnection‑mediated migration model, a three-dimensional geometric superposition model is developed to describe the shear‑coupling factor of ATGBs. Phenomenological parameters are further introduced to account for finite-temperature effects and deviations from ideal faceted migration. MD simulations reveal that Σ5 ATGBs exhibit a divergent coupling factor, corresponding to a sliding‑dominated transition, whereas Σ25 ATGBs show a smooth variation of the coupling factor with values lower than those of their constituent STGBs, indicating that the coexistence of 〈100〉 and 〈110〉 modes accelerates migration of the grain boundary. These findings suggest that intersecting disconnection modes do not necessarily lead to kinetic blocking. The disconnection‑superposition model and the dislocation‑coordination mechanism uncovered here provide a theoretical tool for grain boundary engineering to tailor shear‑coupling behavior by tailoring misorientation and inclination angles.

title: Multi-scale investigation of the anisotropy of lath martensite plasticity in dual-phase steel
abstract: In Dual-Phase (DP) steel, lath martensite is generally regarded as the hard and brittle phase that determines strength and limits ductility. However, recent studies have shown that lath martensite in DP steels can also deform in a markedly ductile manner. These observations have been linked to fully lath martensitic steels, in which plasticity preferentially develops along the habit plane through several competing micromechanical mechanisms. It has remained unclear, however, to what extent these insights extend to DP steel microstructures. This paper therefore correlates the plastic anisotropy of lath martensite in DP steel to the orientation of the martensite habit plane. To this end, advanced micromechanical measurement and identification methods are applied on the same material across multiple scales, to reveal the governing deformation mechanisms and quantify statistically the influence of habit-plane orientation. Well-defined ‘1D’ and ‘2D’ tests, analyzed by microstructure-correlated strain mapping and local slip-system identification, reveal that early martensite plasticity occurs predominantly as habit-plane-aligned intra-lath slip, i.e. plasticity percolates mainly between lath boundaries. These insights are complemented by a statistical study on coarse martensite islands under realistic ‘3D’ large-strain loading, showing that strong plasticity occurs most frequently along the habit plane, even at relatively unfavorable orientations. At later deformation stages, local substructure boundary sliding is also observed. A packet-level competition analysis further indicates that IHP plasticity is approximately twice as easy to activate as out-of-habit-plane slip. Together, these results show that habit-plane-induced anisotropy is a key factor controlling the heterogeneous plasticity of martensite in DP steels.

title: Achieving cryogenic wear resistance in multi-principal element alloy via coherent precipitation and gradient nanostructuring
abstract: Developing cryogenic structural alloys with simultaneous high strength, damage tolerance, and wear resistance remains challenging because conventional incoherent second phases, although beneficial for hardening, often intensify interfacial strain localization and premature damage under low-temperature deformation. Here, a CoCrNi-based multi-principal element alloy strengthened by a high density of coherent L1₂ nanoprecipitates is developed to establish a microstructure design strategy for cryogenic load-bearing applications. The alloy exhibits pronounced cryogenic strengthening, with the yield strength and ultimate tensile strength increasing from 721 to 1057 MPa at 233 K to 856 and 1162 MPa at 113 K, respectively, while retaining an elongation of about 8.0 %. Under sliding conditions, the friction coefficient decreases from 0.48 to 0.35 and the wear rate declines from 17.3 × 10–5 to 6.5 × 10–5 mm3/Nm as the temperature decreases from 233 to 113 K, corresponding to a 2.7-fold improvement in wear resistance and clearly surpassing the single-phase CoCrNi counterpart. Multiscale characterization reveals a transition in subsurface deformation from localized plasticity at 233 K to a deeper gradient nanostructure at 113 K, accompanied by distributed dislocation activity, dynamic nanotwinning, and suppressed delamination. Molecular dynamics simulations further confirm deeper dislocation penetration and stronger local atomic rearrangements under cryogenic sliding, consistent with more spatially distributed plastic deformation. The present work demonstrates that coherent precipitation engineering, together with deformation-induced gradient nanostructuring, provides an effective route to simultaneously enhance cryogenic strength and wear resistance in advanced structural alloys.

title: Enabling programmable crystal morphologies by exploiting external magnetic fields to tune interfacial energies
abstract: Interfacial energy anisotropy plays a central role in nucleation, crystal growth, and microstructure evolution in materials. It is generally considered to be governed primarily by crystallographic symmetry and thermodynamic state variables such as composition and temperature. Whether external fields can modify solid/liquid interfacial energy anisotropy under near-equilibrium conditions remains an open question. Here, equilibrium droplet shape measurements and three-dimensional X-ray tomography are combined with a magnetically coupled phase-field crystal (MPFC) model to investigate the influence of static magnetic fields on solid/liquid interfacial anisotropy in Al-Cu alloys. The experimental results show that both equilibrium droplet shapes and dendritic growth patterns evolve systematically under applied magnetic fields, accompanied by pronounced changes in anisotropic interface contours. In both weakly and strongly anisotropic Al-Cu interfaces, the interfacial shape exhibits enhanced twofold symmetry characteristics under applied magnetic fields, together with significant changes in equilibrium interface shape. The MPFC model further suggests that the magnetic fields may introduce orientation-dependent modifications to the interfacial stiffness, which are qualitatively consistent with the experimentally observed morphology evolution. These results provide evidence that static magnetic fields can influence the interfacial energy anisotropy and correlate with morphology selection during non-directional solidification. The present work provides a framework for exploring how externally applied magnetic fields may influence crystal growth behavior through modifications of effective interfacial energy anisotropy.

title: Chemical gradient interfaces enable strength-ductility synergy via multi-stage back stress and cross-interface dislocation transfer in LPBF Ti-Al-Fe alloys
abstract: Heterostructured materials derive their strength–ductility synergy from back-stress strengthening via geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs), yet the requisite GND accumulation simultaneously induces strain localization and premature damage—a long-standing paradox that fundamentally limits further performance advancement. Here, we report that continuously graded chemical interfaces can break this strengthening–damage coupling. By leveraging incomplete elemental diffusion during laser powder bed fusion of pre-mixed Ti, Al, and Fe elemental powders, we construct Ti-6Al-xFe alloys featuring such continuously graded chemical interfaces. These interfaces enable multi-stage back-stress strengthening by promoting GND multiplication and cross-interface motion, while continuously distributing these dislocations across extended gradient zones to avert the pile-up-induced strain localization characteristic of sharp heterogeneous boundaries. The optimal Ti-6Al-1Fe alloy attains an ultimate tensile strength of 1378 MPa and a total elongation of 11%, outperforming reported Ti-6Al-4V alloys. Mechanistic analysis reveals that the work-hardened soft domain undergoes a strength reversal relative to the hard domain before necking, enabling cooperative deformation without interfacial damage. This study establishes continuously graded interfaces as a general route to circumvent the back-stress-versus-damage dilemma in heterostructured alloys, offering a new paradigm for designing high-performance metallic materials via compositionally graded interfaces.

title: Jahn–Teller distortion of Mn³⁺ ions as a decisive factor for the electrochemical performance of Mn substituted Na2.5-x(Fe1-yMny)1.75(SO4)3 alluaudites
abstract: Partially manganese-substituted alluaudite-type Na 2.5-x (Fe 1-y Mn y ) 1.75 (SO 4 ) 3 materials represent an attractive group of cathode materials for Na-ion batteries, offering a balance between high voltage (4 V vs. Na/Na⁺) and operational stability; however, in the case of high Mn content, it leads to a significantly reduced capacity, indicating a lack of electrochemical activity of manganese. In this study, we address the problem of explaining the lack of electrochemical activity of manganese in Na 2.5-x (Fe 1-y Mn y ) 1.75 (SO 4 ) 3 (y=1/3 and 1/2) as determined from the electronic structure calculations using the Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker with the coherent potential approximation (KKR-CPA) to account for chemical disorder. The results of both non-spin-polarized and spin-polarized KKR-CPA calculations will be discussed. Although the investigated as-synthetized Na 2.5 (Fe 1-y Mn y ) 1.75 (SO 4 ) 3 materials do not exhibit magnetic order at room temperature, information on local magnetic moments provides additional insight into the evolution of valence states during changes in chemical composition, which is essential for a better understanding of electrochemical properties. These theoretical studies will be supported by comprehensive in-situ X-ray diffraction studies, Mössbauer and X-ray absorption spectroscopies, and studies of the magnetic and electrochemical properties of the manganese-substituted iron sulfate cathode material.

title: Anisotropic fracture of metal-halide perovskites
abstract: We combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations and single-crystal cleavage fracture experiments to systematically evaluate fracture energetics and crack-propagation behavior of two prototypical metal-halide perovskites (MHPs): formamidinium lead triiodide (FAPbI3) and methylammonium lead tribromide (MAPbBr3). For the respective MHPs it is found that: fracture of (100) planes leads to FAI/PbI2 or MABr/PbBr2 terminated surfaces; fracture of (110) leads to symmetric stoichiometric terminations; and fracture of (111) planes leads to FAI3/Pb or MABr3/Pb terminated surfaces. In both MHPs the (100) fracture energy is the lowest, followed by (110) and then (111). It is also found that the unrelaxed fracture energy of (100) orientation is 72% and 52% of that along (110) orientations for FAPbI3 and MAPbBr3, respectively. This suggests that if cracks are forced to propagate along (110) orientation, they would deflect by 45° and propagate along (100) planes. Results from experimental single-crystal cleavage fracture tests are consistent with these computational predictions, i.e. when force is applied along the (100) plane, both MHPs fracture along that plane. However, when the force is applied along the (110) plane, the crack path deflects by ∼45° and propagates along the lower-energy (100) plane in both MHPs. These findings establish a direct correspondence between DFT-predicted fracture-energy anisotropy and experimentally observed crack paths, providing fundamental insight into the mechanical anisotropy and intrinsic fracture mechanisms of MHPs. Additionally, the average {100} fracture energy of MAPbBr3 is experimentally measured to be ∼0.3 J·m−2, which compares with the DFT-computed 0.31 J·m−2 (relaxed) and 0.47 J·m−2 (unrelaxed) values.

title: Kinetics of monolayer and bilayer graphene nano-ribbon formation on 3C-SiC: Influence of substrate geometry and growth conditions
abstract: For the first time, epitaxial graphene (EG) growth kinetics on {110} facets of 3C-SiC is investigated using molecular dynamics simulations. Graphene nanoribbon (GNR) formation is simulated using a machine learned force field for the Si-C system and is quantified via a new graph-based carbon-ring type and layer analysis method. We examine the effects of substrate facet height and separation, and thermodynamic growth conditions (temperature and sublimation fraction) on structural and kinetic aspects of EG growth. An energetic explanation for Si sublimation and subsequent graphene growth behavior is provided, relating previously reported observations to the local bonding environment of Si atoms. Analysis of facet height and separation distance reveals two distinct growth regimes: (i) at smaller dimensions, GNR formation is dominated by the growth of initial nuclei; and (ii) at larger dimensions, GNR formation is dominated by multiple nucleation events over the increased surface area. The EG formation sequence involves graphene island nucleation, growth, and coalescence, leading to grain boundary formation. This investigation also analyzes bilayer graphene growth (T = 1750 K), where bottom-layer nucleation begins once the top layer approaches full coverage. The bottom layer initiates beneath the top-layer grain boundaries which are composed of pentagon-heptagon carbon ring pairs. This structure facilitates bottom-layer growth, while simultaneously accelerating the reduction of top-layer grain boundary content and promoting top-layer decoupling from the substrate. These findings provide atomistic level insights into graphene growth kinetics on 3C-SiC, crucial for effective design and fabrication of GNRs.

title: Stress corrosion cracking mechanisms in additively manufactured alloy 718 revealed through oxidation and deformation decoupling
abstract: The nonequilibrium microstructures inherent to additive manufacturing fundamentally alter environmental degradation behavior, raising significant concerns for deploying additively manufactured (AM) alloys in nuclear environments. Here, we initially elucidate the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) mechanisms of laser powder bed fusion fabricated precipitation-hardened alloy 718 in simulated pressurized water reactor primary water, compared with its conventional counterpart. Annealing converted dislocation cells into subgrain boundaries, serving as preferential nucleation sites for precipitates during aging in the AM alloy. The resulting superior SCC resistance against grain boundary (GB) and slip-band cracking arises from an interplay between localized oxidation and deformation localization. Although γ′/γ″- decorated subgrain boundaries act as preferential pathways for deep localized oxidation, they simultaneously suppress SCC initiation by redistributing plastic strain. Dense nanoscale precipitates at subgrains repeatedly impede dislocation glide and disrupt long-range planar slip, markedly reducing strain localization at GBs. A pronounced SCC anisotropy was identified. Loading perpendicular to the building direction promotes cracking due to poorer slip transfer compatibility across columnar GBs, and a higher fraction of GBs under tensile normal stress, accelerating intergranular oxidation. Furthermore, intragranular short cracks exhibit a strong crystallographic dependence. They initiate from fractured oxidized γ″ precipitates or matrix-precipitate interfacial decohesion driven by local strain incompatibility, and subsequently propagate preferentially along the <001> direction of γ″ variants. In some cases, this mechanism drives the crack to transition from intergranular to intragranular propagation. By decoupling localized oxidation and deformation, this work reveals that the hierarchical microstructures inherent to AM alloys can be strategically exploited to mitigate SCC degradation.

title: Corrigendum to “Strain-induced dynamic evolution of the T1 phase and its influence on recrystallization behavior” [Acta Materialia 308 (2026) 122032]
Unraveling doping effects in LaCoO3 via machine learning-accelerated atomic simulations and active learning
abstract: Lanthanum cobaltite (LaCoO 3 ) perovskites hold promise for energy conversion, catalysis, and sensing applications, yet their performance is often limited by structural instability and moderate ionic conductivity. Strategic doping can mitigate these issues, but rational dopant design remains challenging due to the vast configurational space. In this work, we present a machine learning-accelerated framework to unravel doping effects in LaCoO 3 . Utilizing the Matlantis platform powered by universal neural network potentials, we enable efficient, near-DFT-accurate atomic simulations. The two-stage approach begins with active learning via a Bayesian neural network to distill composition–structure–energy relationships, predicting formation energy, lattice distortion, and atomic distortion across diverse A- and B-site dopants and concentrations. An artificial neural network then forward-models ionic conductivity from these properties under varying temperatures and oxygen vacancy levels. Key findings indicate that B-site doping generally stabilize the structure, while A-site doping enhances ionic conductivity by promoting structural distortions. Elevated temperatures and vacancy concentrations amplify diffusion coefficients, aligning with established transport mechanisms. To support practical applications, we developed an interactive web application, LCO-DOPER, enabling rapid dopant screening and property optimization. This framework establishes a robust foundation for data-driven design of doped perovskite materials.

title: Role of defects in the thermodynamic stability of grain boundary phases at asymmetric tilt boundaries in copper
abstract: Grain boundaries can exist as different grain boundary phases (also called complexions) with individual atomic structures. The thermodynamics of these defect phases in high-angle grain boundaries were studied mostly with atomistic and phase field computer simulations, but almost exclusively for special, symmetric boundaries. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations combined with structure search methods, as well as scanning transmission electron microscopy experiments to take a step towards understanding more general grain boundaries. Using the example of Σ 37c [ 11 1 ¯ ] tilt boundaries in Cu, we show how the grain boundary phase transition on a symmetric boundary plane is changed by the geometrically necessary defects introduced in inclined, asymmetric boundaries. We analyze the disconnections—which are dislocation-like line defects of grain boundaries—both in the simulations, as well as in experimental Cu and Al samples. A main finding is that defect energies can have a major influence on the stability of grain boundary phases, even at small inclinations. Furthermore, some defects are not able to effect large inclinations. At that point, defective asymmetric GB phases compete with grain boundaries faceting into the adjacent symmetric GB phases.

title: Entropy-regulated morphotropic phase boundary-like region in BiFeO3-based ceramics with giant electrostrain
abstract: The entropy-stabilization strategy through multielement substitution is rapidly developing in ferroelectrics owing to their potentially vast compositional space and striking functional properties. Here, other than focusing on the high-entropy ferroelectrics, we describe a novel low-entropy framework that enables markedly enhanced electromechanical response in lead-free ferroelectric bismuth ferrite (BiFeO3). We reveal the formation of a morphotropic phase boundary (MPB)-like region upon doping multiple elements at a low concentration corresponding to a low-entropy regime, which may rationalize enhanced strain response. As a result, the low-entropy BiFeO3 ceramics exhibit an ultrahigh electrostrain of 1.5%, far exceeding that of pristine BiFeO3. This finding not only widens the entropy regulation method but also may inspire the discovery of new phenomena to develop entropy-regulated ferroelectrics with greatly enhanced functionalities.

title: Ferroelectricity, valley polarization, and anomalous valley Hall effect in antiferromagnetic bilayer VN2(AlO)2
abstract: The combination of layer, spin, and valley degrees of freedom makes antiferromagnetic bilayer valley materials as a unique platform to revolutionize the spintronic materials. Here, bilayer VN2(AlO)2 is proposed as an A-type antiferromagnetic van der Waals material, and its AA, AB and BA stacking configurations are systematically investigated. The AA stacking bilayer VN2(AlO)2 exhibits neither ferroelectric nor valley polarizations because of M^zT^ symmetry, hosting intrinsic spin-valley-layer coupling (SVLC). Comparatively, the AB and BA configurations break M^zT^ symmetry accompanied by spin-layer coupling (SLC), giving rise to out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization and valley splitting. Interestingly, a phase transition from SVLC to SLC could be also obtained through applying an external electric field, which originates from the competition of band splitting from the electric field and the spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, a valley polarization phase diagram governed by interlayer sliding and external electric field is constructed.
