Based on these findings, a spin field-effect transistor is designed, which not only enables on/off switching of the anomalous valley Hall effect under different stacking configurations and electric fields, but also simultaneously tuning the polarity of the Hall voltage and spin polarization. The present study offers a general scheme to design multifunctional materials for antiferromagnetic valleytronics and spintronics.

title: PolyMicros: A foundation model for polycrystalline material structure
abstract: Foundation Models for Materials Science promise the state-of-the-art performance achieved by deep learning techniques on tasks such as microstructure reconstruction and inverse material design, while claiming to avoid large data requirements and time consuming preparation for these specialized tasks. This respite is significant when, for example, studying polycrystalline microstructures where challenging tasks are plentiful but “large” microstructural datasets comprise of single digit examples. However, in practice, current frameworks still require (1) large, multi-million sample pre-training datasets and (2) further fine-tuning to specialize the model to solve down stream tasks of interest. We introduce a novel foundation model approach designed specifically for data sparse, structural materials science applications. For (1), we introduce a physics-driven data augmentation scheme that coordinates an ensemble of local diffusion models to generate a large-scale, physically diverse synthetic dataset. For (2), we demonstrate that a foundation model built using an unconditional diffusion model backbone can be specialized to downstream tasks without fine-tuning. We utilize this framework to construct PolyMicros, the first Foundation model for polycrystalline materials from an initial dataset of just five experimentally gathered 3D polycrystalline microstructures. We demonstrate the utility of PolyMicros by zero-shot solving several long standing challenges related to accelerating 3D experimental microscopy including reconstruction from partial observations for accelerated serial sections and reconstruction from partial statistics for 2D to 3D dimensionality expansion. Finally, we make both our models and datasets openly available to the community.

title: Cavity evolution in irradiated alloy 800H studied with in-situ ion irradiation
abstract: In order to elucidate the role of displacement cascades during high dose ion irradiation of alloy 800H, samples that were previously bulk irradiated to 32 dpa at 480 °C with dual ions, Fe and He, were irradiated to an additional dpa in situ with 1 MeV Kr ions at the Intermediate Voltage Electron Microscope at Argonne National Laboratory. The in-situ irradiations were conducted at room temperature and 480 °C over a wide range of dose rates. The evolution of the size of individual pre-existing cavities in the material was monitored during in-situ irradiation. It was found that, when irradiated at room temperature, the irradiation-induced displacement cascades caused cavities to shrink at similar rates, independent of the varying dose rates. In contrast, when irradiated at 480 °C, cavities shrank when irradiated at high dose rates but remained largely unchanged when irradiated at low dose rates. The results can be rationalized by considering that at low dose rates and high temperatures, the vacancies dissolved from the cavities by the displacement cascades have enough mobility and time to return to the cavities before the next cascade hits, while at high dose rates, this recovery is incomplete, leading to gradual cavity dissolution. A simple rate theory model is presented that can rationalize the results observed. Our findings provide important guidance for emulating neutron-induced swelling using irradiation.

title: Direct prediction of experimental irradiation defect structures in tungsten at room temperature using stochastic cluster dynamics
abstract: The foundations of irradiation damage theory were laid in the 1950s and 60s within the framework of chemical reaction kinetics. While helpful to analyze qualitative aspects of irradiation damage, the theory contained gaps that delayed its implementation and applicability as a predictive tool. The advent of computer simulations with atomistic resolution in the 80s and 90s revealed a series of mechanisms that have proved essential to understand key aspects of irradiation damage in crystalline solids. However, we still lack a comprehensive model that can connect atomic-level defect physics with experimental measurements of quantitative features of the irradiated microstructure. In this work, we present a mesoscale model that draws from our improved understanding of irradiation damage processes collected over the last few decades, bridging knowledge gained from our most sophisticated atomistic simulations with defect kinetics taking place over time scales many orders of magnitude larger than atomic interaction times. Importantly, the model avoids any direct a posteriori fitting, and combines several essential pieces of irradiation damage physics: each playing an irreplaceable role in the context of the full model but of limited utility if considered in isolation. Crucially, we validate the model against a set of irradiation experiments specifically designed to isolate the key damage variables. Using tungsten as a model material, we find exceptionally good agreement between our numerical predictions and detailed experimental measurements of defect densities and defect cluster sizes.

title: Cellular automaton framework for non-equilibrium solidification in metal additive manufacturing
abstract: A physics-based cellular automaton (CA) model is developed to describe microstructure evolution during non-equilibrium solidification under laser additive manufacturing (AM) conditions. Unlike conventional CA approaches that assume equilibrium partitioning and lattice-dependent interface propagation, the present framework combines implicit solid–liquid interface reconstruction with a velocity-dependent partition coefficient based on the continuous growth model (CGM). The solid–liquid interface is reconstructed from a continuous solid-fraction field, while interface normals, curvature, and anisotropic growth kinetics are evaluated from spatial derivatives of the evolving solid-fraction field, reducing grid-induced growth bias commonly associated with classical CA approaches. The framework consistently couples interface kinetics, solute diffusion, curvature effects, and interfacial mass conservation within a computationally efficient CA formulation and enables quantitative prediction of dendrite tip dynamics, solute redistribution, and primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS). The model is applied to binary and ternary alloys to investigate the combined influence of growth velocity, thermal gradient, and kinetic partitioning on morphology selection and the columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET). By unifying thermodynamic consistency and kinetic effects within a CA framework, this study provides a physically grounded tool for exploring rapid solidification phenomena and microstructural selection across rapid-solidification regimes relevant to metal AM.

title: Cooling-rate effects on structural heterogeneity and the mechanical properties of aluminosilicate glasses observed over seven orders of magnitude
abstract: ABSTRACT Thermal history strongly affects structure and the mechanical properties of glasses. However, consistent experimental studies on the connection between fictive temperature, structural heterogeneity and fracture of real-world glasses remain elusive. Here, we report on a chemically homogeneous sodium aluminosilicate glass produced under cooling rates varying over seven orders of magnitude. This variation leads to a spread in fictive temperature over a range of ∼200 K; it causes distinct changes in structural heterogeneity as observed through low-frequency vibrational spectroscopy and low-temperature heat capacity studies. Independent evaluation is reported on the basis of the soft potential model (SPM), and heterogeneous elasticity theory implementing a coherent potential approximation, both providing quantifiers of structural disorder and non-affinity. Parallel analysis of mass density, elasticity, and indentation-induced plasticity and fracture allow for a direct correlation of disorder-induced changes in macroscopic material characteristics. These significantly exceed approximations obtained when considering a continuous medium transformation, underlining the foundational role of disorder and SPM percolation in macroscopic glass behavior. Our findings provide new avenues for using structural disorder as an ex ante design parameter in the conception of oxide glass materials.

title: Slip- and shuffling-based cross-slip mechanisms of c+a screw dislocations in magnesium
abstract: Cross-slip of c+a screw dislocations is a key process governing non-basal dislocation multiplication and ductility in magnesium, yet its atomistic mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, using nudged elastic band calculations with a neural network potential (NNP), we identify two distinct constriction-free cross-slip mechanisms between pyramidal II (Pyr. II) and pyramidal I (Pyr. I) core states: a slip-based mechanism dominated by collective atomic glide and a shuffling-based mechanism enabled by localized atomic rearrangements intrinsic to the Pyr. II stacking fault structure. The energetic origin of these mechanisms is first clarified through Pyr. II stacking fault migration, where the slip-based mechanism involves severe interlayer atomic overlap and has an NNP-predicted barrier of 127 mJ/m2, whereas the shuffling-based mechanism avoids such overlap and is nearly barrierless. The NNP-predicted MEPs show that the same distinction governs both two- and three-dimensional c+a cross-slip, with the shuffling-based mechanism markedly reducing the zero-stress barrier. In the three-dimensional analysis, a 2D cross-sectional energy descriptor reveals cross-slip as a wave-like propagation of local two-dimensional core transformations and refines the interpretation of jog-pair nucleation. These results establish an atomistically resolved framework for modeling c+a cross-slip in magnesium and suggest analogous mechanisms in a broad range of hexagonal close-packed metals.

title: From bulk to surface: Structure and dynamics of amorphous alumina from deep potential molecular dynamics
abstract: Understanding the atomic-scale structure and dynamics of amorphous oxide surfaces is essential for interpreting their chemical reactivity, mechanical stability, and interfacial behavior, yet direct experimental characterization remains challenging. We employ Deep Potential (DP) molecular dynamics to generate large-scale, ab initio -quality models of amorphous Al 2 O 3 bulk glasses and melt-quenched free surfaces, enabling a quantitative analysis of both structure and relaxation dynamics with statistical confidence inaccessible to direct ab initio simulation. The trained DP model reproduces experimental liquid and glass structure, captures the cooling-rate dependence of the bulk glass transition, and corrects systematic biases in the polyhedral populations predicted by widely used classical force fields. At the free surface, mass density recovers to bulk values over ∼ 10 Å, while local coordination requires a slightly wider subsurface region to fully converge. The outermost layer is oxygen-enriched, exhibits altered polyhedral connectivity with contracted Al–O bonds, and hosts a broad population of under-coordinated motifs (notably AlO 3 and OAl 2 ) whose abundances are governed by glass stability. These under-coordinated surface motifs exhibit distinct vibrational signatures and occur as locally paired Lewis acid and Brønsted base sites consistent with bond-valence compensation, yet remain spatially dispersed rather than aggregating into extended clusters. Despite this pronounced structural heterogeneity, surface relaxation and the glass-transition temperature remain comparable to their bulk counterparts, suggesting that the disordered surface is kinetically stable once formed. Together, these results establish a molecular-level picture of amorphous alumina surfaces and demonstrate the capability of machine-learned potentials to resolve structure–property relationships in disordered oxide interfaces.

title: Route-dependent crystallization of Ni–P metallic glasses enabling a nanotwinned supersaturated Ni(P) solid solution
abstract: Tailoring crystallization pathways of metallic glasses plays a key role in designing nanocrystalline materials with novel structures. However, the fundamental relationship between amorphous structure and crystallization behavior remains poorly understood. In this work, two compositionally identical Ni81P19 metallic glasses were deliberately prepared by melt spinning and pulsed electrodeposition to clarify the intrinsic relationships among amorphous structure, crystallization pathway, and crystallized products. The as-quenched glass (QG) undergoes a one-step eutectic transformation into solid solution Ni(s) and Ni₃P, whereas the as-deposited glass (DG) follows a two-step sequence, leading to the formation of a metastable nanotwinned supersaturated Ni solid solution (Ni(ssss)) with a P solubility of up to ∼14 at.%, far exceeding the equilibrium limit (∼0.32 at.%). The distinct crystallization behaviors originate from the unique amorphous structure of the DG sample, characterized by stronger electronic orbital hybridization, denser atomic packing, and a more homogeneous chemical distribution, thereby effectively suppressing P-atom diffusion and the precipitation of Ni₃P. These findings provide deeper theoretical insight into the structure–crystallization relationship in metallic glasses and offer a new strategy for designing metastable supersaturated solid solutions via amorphous-precursor engineering.

title: Interatomic potential investigation of the structural and thermodynamic properties of mixed plutonium–americium oxides
abstract: Minor actinides (MA)-bearing mixed oxides are considered for the transmutation of long-lived radioactive isotopes that result from the lifecycle and cooling of nuclear reactors. Accurate knowledge of the U – Pu – Am – Np – O thermodynamic system is necessary for the efficient and safe usage of these actinide oxides as transmutation fuel. However, experimental data is lacking for most subsystems therein, notably ternary oxides. Atomic scale calculations can be a valuable complementary tool to experiments in the production of data. The Cooper-Ruhston-Grimes (CRG) interatomic potential has proven to be a very reliable potential for simple and mixed actinide oxides, but the parametrization available in the literature yields a strongly underestimated melting temperature of PuO2. In this work, we reparametrized the CRG terms concerning Pu4+ and Pu3+ ions and obtained a potential yielding results in excellent agreement with the available experimental data. The potential was used to perform a systematical calculation of the structural and thermal properties of the (Pu, Am)O2 – x system with a Pu content from 0 to 100% and x in [0.0, 0.1] over a large range of temperatures. The results obtained with the reparametrized potential constitute important complementary data for CALPHAD models and higher-scale models describing the behaviour of nuclear fuels in operation.

title: Optimizing intrinsic strength–plasticity synergy for refractory high entropy alloy by chemical bonding engineering
abstract: Developing strength‑plasticity synergy in refractory high‑entropy alloys (RHEAs) is challenging due to their vast composition space and intrinsic low ductility. Here, we demonstrate a machine learning‑assisted bond engineering method to improve plasticity while maintaining high strength at both room temperature and 1200 °C, using the WMoTaNbV system as a model. Through statistical correlation of bonding states with intrinsic mechanical properties and electronic structure analysis, ductile bonding characteristics (bonding states near the Fermi level and low –ICOHP) and strengthening bonding characteristics (opposite features) were identified. By machine learning‑guided bond distribution regulation, the W₂₃Mo₂Ta₃₅Nb₅V₃₅ alloy was designed and experimentally validated, achieving a high room‑temperature yield strength of ∼1.52 GPa, an ultimate compressive strength of 2.8 GPa, and a fracture strain of ∼24 %, which far exceeds all the literature reports. The bonding mechanism responsible for strengthening and toughening was further analyzed via in‑situ tensile experiments and atomistic simulations. This bond‑directed design strategy goes beyond conventional composition‑based screening by revealing the electronic origin of the strength‑plasticity balance, providing a rational basis for fine‑tuning mechanical properties in RHEAs.

title: Solid-state recycling of aluminum chips into high-performance crossover alloys via electroless Cu plating: Oxide elimination and doubled tensile strength
abstract: Recycling of aluminum (Al) chips via direct solid-state compaction reduces energy use, material losses and greenhouse gas emissions compared to scrap-remelting, but current solid-state recycling is limited by oxide films on chips, hampering wider use. To resolve this fundamental challenge, we developed an electroless copper (Cu) plating approach for solid-state recycling of aluminum chips. The plated ∼1.3 μm-thick Cu coatings prevent chip oxidation, producing oxide-free internal interfaces. This avoids the fracture and delamination typical of conventional solid-state compaction. It also promotes recrystallization, precipitation of interconnected Q′ and θ′ phases and slip band strengthening. The peak-aged Cu-coated chip-based alloy show nearly twice the strength of uncoated references, at improved strain hardening and uniform elongation. This new plating-based recycling approach not only recycles Al chips into high-performance alloys, but it creates a novel type of microstructure and sustainable material class.

title: Atomic size mismatch effects on irradiation-induced defect evolution in Nb-Zr-Ti-V multi-principal element alloys
abstract: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) generally exhibit high radiation tolerance because the substantial lattice distortion associated with atomic size mismatch and chemical disorder may enhance the migration energy barriers. The atomic size mismatch effects are less understood because of the complex coupling among defect production, chemical redistribution, and structural instability under irradiation. Here, a Nb-Zr-Ti-V alloy with a body centered cubic structure is used as a model system to elucidate the role of atomic size mismatch in irradiation-induced defect evolution under helium ion irradiation. First-principles density functional calculations show that Frenkel pairs associated with smaller Nb and V atoms have significantly lower formation energies than those associated with oversized Zr, indicating that increasing Nb and V contents enhances early-stage vacancy availability under irradiation. This defect-formation tendency is consistent with the experimentally observed earlier appearance of detectable helium bubbles in Nb/V-rich alloys. Under irradiation, coupled vacancy and interstitial fluxes toward bubbles produce inverse Kirkendall-like radiation-induced segregation, with V enrichment near bubble interiors and pronounced Zr accumulation in the surrounding matrix. The Zr enrichment near bubbles triggers a Bain-path-related BCC→FCC (FCT) transformation and the formation of plate-like radiation-induced precipitates. These precipitates act as strong defect sinks, enhancing vacancy trapping and helium bubble growth and establishing a positive feedback loop between precipitation and bubble evolution. These results highlight atomic size mismatch as an important bubble size-related descriptor that couples with local chemical effects to influence irradiation tolerance in BCC MPEAs.

title: Bayesian identification of fibrous insulation thermal conductivity towards design of spacecraft thermal protection systems
abstract: The design of spacecraft thermal protection systems (TPS) requires accurate knowledge of thermal transport properties across wide ranges of temperature and pressure. For fibrous insulation, conventional measurement techniques in laboratory settings are typically limited to temperatures much lower than what is reached in atmosphere entry scenarios. Moreover, it is often the case that only temperature measurements are available, meaning that the thermal conductivity of the insulation must be indirectly inferred as an inverse problem. We propose a Bayesian framework using information field theory (IFT) to reconstruct the thermal conductivity of high-temperature fibrous insulation from sparse experimental data. Under IFT, the conductivity is represented as a Gaussian process, and the physics is enforced via a physics-informed prior over the temperature derived from the heat equation. Bayes's rule produces an infinite-dimensional posterior distribution that quantifies uncertainty about the conductivity which can be evaluated in extrapolation regimes. We apply the method to Opacified Fibrous Insulation with both synthetic and experimental data to reconstruct the thermal conductivity beyond the experimental regime. The inferred conductivities are validated against reference data and then propagated into high-fidelity digital twins of flexible TPS performance under Mars and Earth entry trajectories. The results show that IFT yields accurate predictions with quantified uncertainty, enabling robust TPS sizing in regimes inaccessible to direct measurement.

title: Dislocation-Density interactions and binary junction population formation and evolution in BCC refractory metals with random low and high angle grain-boundaries
abstract: Refractory body-centered cubic (BCC) metals, such as molybdenum (Mo), are desirable for aerospace and nuclear applications due to their thermo-mechanical behavior under extreme conditions pertaining to high temperatures and strain-rates. However, the behavior of BCC aggregates remains difficult to predict and fundamentally understand due to inherent complex and unique dislocation interactions, non-planar dislocations and cross slip, and the accumulation and annihilation of dislocation populations and densities. This study, therefore, presents a validated microstructurally based dislocation-density crystal plasticity (DCP) framework that is integrated with a nonlinear finite-element approach, to surmount the limitations of single or discrete dislocations to investigate the formation and evolution of mobile and immobile dislocation densities and dislocation junction densities in BCC molybdenum (Mo) for the formation and evolution of <001> dislocation-density junctions that are unique to BCC structures. Interaction tensors based on Frank’s energy rule are used to predict the formation of junction populations, and these predictions underscore how <001> junctions are significant obstacles to dislocation density mobility, and how they contribute to strain hardening, and evolve to junction density formation, annihilation and strain softening. A detailed examination of molybdenum aggregates with random low and high angle GB misorientations underscored significant differences in these dislocationdensity interactions and dislocation- junction density formation. This proposed framework can be used to fundamentally understand and predict large strain deformation and failure of BCC aggregates due to unique BCC dislocation-densities interactions that lead to dislocation-junction formation and evolution.

title: Machine-learning-guided molecular dynamics simulations of point defect evolution in β‑Ga2O3 during ion implantation and annealing
abstract: In beta-gallium oxide (beta-Ga2O3), Ga-ion implantation and annealing induce abundant point defects. To overcome conventional Wigner-Seitz (WS) defect analysis limitations, a defect identification algorithm based on similarity matching and DBSCAN clustering is developed for beta-Ga2O3. It distinguishes lattice atoms from defects at high concentrations and identifies eight Ga interstitial configurations (Gaia to Gaih). Comparing SRIM and MD data highlights electronic stopping effects: neglecting them overestimates ion range and defect concentration. Across five fluences (1 to 5 x 10^14 cm-2), 1373 K is the optimal recovery temperature. Multiscale analyses using hydrostatic stress, PRDF, and defect concentration reveal defect evolution. Ga interstitials (Gai) occupy tetrahedral and octahedral sites, driving a defect-mediated phase transition from beta- to gamma-Ga2O3. Increasing fluences reduce beta-phase recovery and increase gamma-phase transformation irreversibly. Oxygen interstitial (Oi) migration is sensitive to annealing temperature, which enhances O-sublattice recrystallization.

title: Predicting co-segregation in alloys with solute-solute interactions
abstract: The co-segregation of impurities in systems with multiple solute species has been widely recognized as an effective strategy for tailoring material properties. However, reliable predictions of co-segregation behavior remain a significant challenge for alloy design in these systems. In this work, we develop an extended dual-solute (DS) segregation framework to semi-quantitatively predict co-segregation behavior with solute-solute interactions, including both homoatomic and heteroatomic contributions. A machine-learning workflow is first established to predict the pairwise segregation energy to construct the DS segregation energy spectra that intrinsically include both types of solute-solute interactions. The resulting spectral information is then used to determine the upper and lower bounds of segregation for individual solute species. When applied to magnesium-based ternary systems constructed by alloying Mg with any two of the 11 candidate solute species (Ag, Al, Ca, Co, Cu, Gd, Nd, Ni, Pb, Pd, and Zn), the extended DS segregation framework is successfully validated by hybrid molecular dynamics/Monte Carlo simulations and experimental results available in the literature. Furthermore, we introduce a design strategy to promote co-segregation by incorporating additional solute species that exhibit attractive interactions with existing solutes, thereby enabling enhanced co-segregation even in the presence of strong site competition. These results underscore the critical role of solute-solute interactions in governing co-segregation behavior and provide a predictive pathway for the design and optimization of alloys.

title: Revealing the shock-induced complex phase transformations of tin and their impacts on spallation
abstract: Spallation, a critical mode of dynamic fracture, remains a central focus in the study of material response under extreme conditions. While widely studied in common metals, the spallation of tin (Sn), a group IV element exhibiting multiple solid phases along the shock-Hugoniot, presents significant challenges due to its complex pressure–temperature phase diagram. Such complexity hinders both experimental characterization and the development of reliable interatomic potentials for atomistic simulations. Consequently, the phase transition pathways and their influence on spallation in Sn remain poorly understood. In this work, we employ non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations using a first-principles accuracy machine learning potential to simulate the dynamic response of Sn at strain rates down to ∼6×109s−1, which is comparable to experiments. Our simulations successfully capture critical behaviors such as shock-induced phase transitions and melting, and reproduce their experimental shock pressures. Meanwhile, the results clearly elucidate the β-to-bct transition pathway, revealing a two-stage mechanism mediated by an intermediate simple-hexagonal phase. Furthermore, we identify two distinct dynamic behaviors along the loading-unloading thermodynamic pathway: shock-induced kinetic metastable cold melting below the equilibrium melting point and phase-transition-mediated release amorphization. These behaviors are shown to originate from the large differences in the slopes of the melting lines between adjacent solid phases. Overall, the findings provide atomistic-scale evidence directly linking phase transformations to spallation failure, offering new insights into the fundamental physics of dynamic fracture in Sn.

title: Junction-governed diffusion kinetics and nanovoid formation in three-dimensional grain boundary networks
abstract: In polycrystals, grain boundaries (GBs) are widely accepted as potential diffusion pathways and crack-initiation sites. GBs always form network structures in three-dimensional (3D) materials including regular GB planes, triple junctions (TJs), and high-order junctions (HJs), and thus the influence of these components on the mechanical behavior of polycrystals should be understood. In this study, we used molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with a new on-the-fly GB component identification method to investigate dynamic behaviors such as atomic diffusion and nanovoid formation under uniaxial tensile loading in body-centered cubic (bcc)-Fe polycrystals. Our results show that the local atomic diffusion ability of the HJ is the highest among the GB components, followed by those of the TJ and GB. Uniaxial tensile loading simulation results suggest that junction-rich regions containing multiple HJs and TJs act as hotspots for nanovoid formation. Stress concentration at HJs provides the driving force for vacancy/nanovoid formation, and high atomic diffusivities of TJs and HJs facilitate vacancy transport and aggregation. The obtained results for the atomic diffusion ability and nanovoid formation of the GB components are comparable to previous experimental observations. The present study contributes to a deeper, fundamental understanding of the mechanical behavior of 3D GB networks and highlights the GB network topology as an important factor in controlling the mechanical properties of nanopolycrystals.

title: Physics-informed process-structure-property prediction model for additively manufactured metallic parts
abstract: Establishing process-structure-property (PSP) relationships is essential for elucidating how process parameters affect microstructural evolution and their influence on mechanical properties in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). However, prediction of mechanical properties coupled with microstructural evolution remains challenging due to complex thermal histories inherent to LPBF, in addition to time- and cost-intensive efforts for analyzing subsequent heat treatment effects. While conventional data-driven methods have attempted to predict mechanical properties directly from process or structure parameters, they often fail to characterize PSP relationships. Recent rapid advances in artificial intelligence techniques enable new approaches that combine machine learning with physics-informed modeling to overcome these limitations. Here, we propose a physics-informed process-structure-property prediction (PSPP) model for LPBF-fabricated metallic parts by integrating conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic models (cDDPM) with physics-informed neural networks (PINN). The cDDPM reconstructs high-fidelity microstructures under heat treatment conditions, while the PINN accurately predicts tensile behavior from microstructural features. Furthermore, the PSPP model successfully identifies optimum heat treatment conditions for maximizing mechanical performance with a low prediction error (≤ 6.1%). Therefore, this PSPP framework is expected to be widely applicable to other additive manufacturing techniques for dramatically reducing design cycles and experimental costs.

title: A dual-scale chemical fluctuation nanostructure enables CoCrFeNiPd high entropy alloy with exceptional mechanical properties at ultralow temperatures
abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as promising structural materials that exhibit remarkable improvements in strength, plasticity, and fracture toughness at extremely low temperatures. In this study, a dual-scale chemical fluctuation nanostructure was constructed in a CoCrFeNiPd HEA, which exhibits remarkable mechanical performance at ultralow temperatures. The dual-scale nanostructure consists of 10 nm-level large chemical fluctuations (L-CFs) and 1–3 nm small chemical fluctuations (S-CFs), as characterized by small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and 3D atom probe tomography (APT). The nanostructure endows the alloy with a yield strength of 943 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 2240 MPa, and a fracture elongation of 55% at 15 K. Notably, the alloy maintains stable plastic flow without pernicious serrated deformation that is prevalent in other HEAs at low temperatures. In-situ neutron diffraction and TEM results show that ultralow temperatures stabilize the chemical fluctuation nanostructure, promote dislocation multiplication, and enable the synergistic operation of multiple deformation mechanisms, thereby avoiding avalanche-like dislocation motion and achieving the simultaneous enhancement of strength and ductility. This work provides a promising paradigm for designing high-performance alloys for ultralow-temperature applications by constructing multiscale chemical fluctuation nanostructures.

title: Room-temperature plastic deformation of single crystals of Mg17Al12 with the body-centered cubic α-Mn (A12) type structure
abstract: The deformation behavior of single crystals of Mg 17 Al 12 has been investigated by micropillar compression at room temperature as a function of crystal orientation and specimen size. Three slip systems, {110}<111>, {110}<001> and {110}<110>, are identified to operate in crystal orientations in the middle of the stereographic triangle, close to [ 1 ‾ 11] and [001], respectively. The latter two slip systems are identified in the present study for the first time. The averaged CRSS values obtained for micropillar specimens in the size range of 1.5 to 10.6 μm do not vary significantly with slip system, and they are 295, 325, and 300 MPa for {110}<111>, {110}<001>, and {110}<110> slip, respectively. While the specimen size dependence of yield stress is negligibly small for {110}<001> and {110}<110> slip, that for {110}<111> is comparatively large. The bulk CRSS values estimated by the extrapolation of the size-dependent yield stress are 200±35, 305±50, and 280±55 MPa for {110}<111>, {110}<001>, and {110}<110> slip, respectively. As predicted by DFT (density functional theory) calculations, there are some stacking faults of sufficiently low energy, leading to two- and three-fold dissociation for the dislocation with b (Burgers vector)=1/2<111> carrying {110}<111> slip and the dislocation with b=[110] carrying {110}<110> slip, respectively. The deformation behavior of Mg 17 Al 12 is compared to that of isostructural α-Mn, in particular, in terms of the existence of low-energy stacking faults and the resultant dislocation core dissociation/spreading.

title: Emerging relaxor behavior induced by quenched random fields in Bi1/2K1/2TiO3‒Bi1/2Li1/2TiO3 solid solutions with cation vacancies
abstract: Bi 1/2 K 1/2 TiO 3 (BKT)-based solid solutions are promising lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics for electromechanical and energy storage applications. In this study, we investigate the structural, dielectric, and polarization properties of the ceramics of Bi 1/2 K 1/2 TiO 3 ‒Bi 1/2 Li 1/2 TiO 3 solid solutions [Bi (1+ δ )/2 K (1− x )(1−3 δ )/2 Li x (1−3 δ )/2 V δ TiO 3, BKT‒BLT] containing A-site vacancy ( V ) to elucidate the impacts of the Li + substitution for K + and the introduction of A-site vacancies on relaxor behavior. The temperature dependence of relative permittivity reveals that, upon cooling, the characteristic behavior of BKT, i.e., the temperature ( T )-induced spontaneous relaxor-to-ferroelectric phase transition, disappears in BKT‒BLT. Moreover, the E -induced irreversible relaxor-to-ferroelectric phase transition is hampered by increasing the contents of Li + ( x ) and A-site vacancies ( δ ). Interestingly, even a small amount of A-site vacancies can effectively reduce the freezing temperature ( T f ) and stabilize the ergodic relaxor phase with dynamic polar nanoregions (PNRs). The reduction of T f becomes more significant under the coexistence of Li + ions and A-site vacancies due to the simultaneous introduction of quenched random stress and electric fields arising from local structural distortions and local charge imbalances. As a result, BKT‒BLT exhibits slim P - E hysteresis loops with enhanced maximum polarization ( P max ), suppressed remanent polarization ( P r ), and superior energy storage properties compared with BKT. These findings establish a strategy for designing high-performance lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics by engineering quenched random fields in the BKT-based perovskites for energy storage applications.

title: Laser powder bed fusion of a newly designed Fe-based bulk metallic glass with enhanced soft magnetic properties
abstract: Additive manufacturing of Fe-based bulk metallic glasses (BMGs) is hindered by their limited glass-forming ability (GFA) and by devitrification during repeated thermal cycling in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), which degrades soft magnetic performance. Here, we investigate the LPBF processability of a newly designed Fe–Si–B–Nb–Ni alloy exhibiting enhanced GFA (critical casting thickness ≈1 mm) without the addition of P, Co, or rare-earth elements. A systematic study combining varied energy densities, time delays, and double-scanning strategies is conducted to establish processing–structure–property relationships. Multiscale characterization (X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry, electron backscatter diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, atom probe tomography, and X-ray computed tomography) reveals that the improved GFA suppresses micron-scale crystallization across a broad processing window, yielding amorphous fractions above 87% and fully XRD-amorphous states under optimized remelting conditions. Atom probe tomography confirms chemical randomness irrespective of scan strategy, whereas calorimetry and nanoindentation mapping demonstrate that double scanning reduces structural heterogeneity through enhanced relaxation of the amorphous phase. This relaxation increases resistance to devitrification during subsequent thermal cycles. The resulting as-built specimens exhibit coercivities as low as 44 A m⁻¹, i.e. over an order of magnitude lower than previously reported for P-, Co-, and rare-earth-free Fe-based MGs processed by LPBF, while maintaining stable specific saturation magnetization. At high amorphous fractions, coercivity becomes weakly correlated with residual crystallinity and more sensitive to porosity and structural heterogeneity. These results demonstrate that synergistic alloy and scan-strategy design can control structural relaxation and crystallization pathways in LPBF-processed MGs, providing a mechanistic foundation for manufacturing high-performance soft magnetic components.

title: Experimental Measurement of Polycrystalline-Average Grain Boundary Segregation using X-Ray Diffraction
abstract: We advance a framework for measuring the polycrystalline-average grain boundary segregation in binary alloys by taking advantage of the underlying physics of X-ray diffraction. By first theoretically detailing alloy thermodynamics and structural characteristics suitable to this method, we survey a large range of binary systems and identify numerous candidates where this approach is viable. Selecting Ni-Pd as a model system, we then outline necessary experimental conditions and perform this measurement on two Ni-Pd alloys over a range of temperatures, resulting in quantitative grain boundary segregation data for this system. We validate these measurements with transmission electron microscopy, highlighting the quantitative viability of using X-ray diffraction to measure segregation. The resulting experimental framework provides a pathway to greatly expand the volume of experimental data on grain boundary segregation.

title: Field inhomogeneous distributions and local percolations in Ag-BaTiO3 ceramic-metal composites: The role of microstructural variability
abstract: This work investigates how composition and microstructural variability influence the dielectric properties of xAg–(1–x)BaTiO 3 ceramic-metal composites (denoted as CerMet) through combined modelling/experimental approach. Virtually generated microstructures predict different percolation ranges depending on microstructural modifications. To check such effect, a range of compositions with x ≤ 20 vol.% were synthesized using single-step or two-steps sintering to ensure compositional integrity and similar BaTiO 3 grain size. During the consolidation, Ag undergoes melting, migration, and infiltration, generating intricate metal–ceramic connectivity. The permittivity exhibits percolation-like increases near critical compositions around ∼5, ∼11.5, and >20 vol.%, reaching a maximum value of εᵣ ≈ 17,000 at 20°C with tan δ ≤ 2% (at 10 kHz) for x = 11.5 vol.%. The high permittivity compositions selected for X-Ray tomography and detailed microscopic analyses revealed 3D microstructures with specific features, where field concentration (“hot spots”) occurs. These results demonstrate how metal melting during sintering governs microstructural evolution and variability and the important role of the elongated and tortuous filler structures in increasing the CerMet effective permittivity towards giant values towards the percolation limits.

title: Helium-mediated dislocation loop rafting in tungsten
abstract: Ordered microstructures, although visually striking, often form at the expense of mechanical robustness. Dislocation loop rafts are representative ordered defect structures that have been widely reported under neutron and heavy-ion irradiation. However, their formation and evolution under conditions in the presence of helium atoms remain insufficiently understood. Here, in-situ sequential He+/Kr2+ irradiations were conducted to clarify the role of He in dislocation loop rafting in tungsten. A non-monotonic dependence on He concentration is identified: low He concentrations (10–1000 appm) markedly delay raft formation, whereas an accelerated raft nucleation emerges in the bubble-formation regime (≥ 2000 appm). Real-time TEM observations and quantitative analyses demonstrate that the delayed rafting originates from He-induced constraints on loop diffusivity and suppression of Burgers vector rotation, thereby increasing the loop density and elastic interaction strength required for rafting. In contrast, the accelerated raft nucleation in the bubble-formation regime is attributed to the attractive elastic interactions between He bubbles and dislocation loops, which promote loop accumulation near bubbles and facilitate earlier raft nucleation. Furthermore, there is a direct interaction between dislocation loops and bubble-growth-induced punched-out dislocation networks, which further enhances loop clustering and raft formation. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into He-mediated loop rafting and defect self-organization in irradiated tungsten.

title: Robust out-of-plane ferroelectricity in Aurivillius ultrathin films through local chemical antisite
abstract: Layered Aurivillius-phase ferroelectric thin films exhibit excellent fatigue endurance, attracting significant interest for non-volatile memory applications. However, their spontaneous polarization restricts their use in modern vertical architectures. This study utilizes three-layer Aurivillius-phase Bi4Ti3O12 as a model system. A chemical solution method with non-stoichiometric modulation enables the controlled introduction of localized antisite transformations between B-site (Ti4+) and A-site (Bi3+) ions. Bi ions occupying Ti sites eliminate perovskite units, disrupting antipolar ordering and remarkably enhancing out-of-plane ferroelectricity. Polarization vector analysis, piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM), and P–E hysteresis loop measurements confirm the enhanced out-of-plane polarization. The antisite-modified Bi4Ti3O12 films exhibit well-defined ferroelectric domains and a remnant polarization (Pr) of ∼2.2 μC/cm2, representing a 7.8-fold enhancement over the pristine Bi4Ti3O12 films. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that oxygen vacancies are critical for maintaining insulating properties and ferroelectric polarization in Bi4Ti3O12 with antisite transformations. This work demonstrates a novel strategy for controlling ferroelectric orientation in layered oxides via local chemical antisite engineering, providing valuable insights for designing out-of-plane polarized films for next-generation high-performance memory devices.

title: A general synthesis strategy for volatile-element-based compounds: Achieving near-zero thermal expansion and advanced microwave absorption in Yb2Fe17 and its nitride
abstract: The synthesis of ytterbium (Yb)-based intermetallic compounds via conventional physical methods has been substantially hindered by the pronounced volatility of ytterbium, impeding both fundamental magnetic studies and practical implementations. This study develops an in-situ confined reduction-diffusion (IC-RD) strategy coupled with compaction-encapsulation technology, effectively mitigating the evaporation of ytterbium. This method successfully yields high-purity Yb2Fe17, which is subsequently converted into Yb2Fe17N3-δ via nitridation. Neutron powder diffraction (NPD) analysis reveals a near-zero thermal expansion (near-ZTE) behavior in Yb2Fe17, characterized by an ultralow volumetric thermal expansion coefficient (αv) of 1.6 × 10-⁷ K-¹ within the 100-250 K temperature range. Furthermore, nitriding significantly enhances the magnetic properties, leading to a higher magnetic ordering temperature and large saturation magnetization in Yb2Fe17N3-δ. When incorporated into a paraffin composite, Yb2Fe17N3-δ exhibits outstanding microwave absorption performance, achieving a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of -50.5 dB at 3.37 GHz in the S-band (2-4 GHz), along with a maximum effective absorption bandwidth (EABmax) of 5.96 GHz at a minimal thickness of 1.4 mm. This study not only establishes a viable synthetic pathway for compounds containing highly volatile elements, but also opens avenues for designing materials with tailored structural and magnetic properties, as well as advancing thin-layer broadband microwave absorbers.

title: Refractory high-entropy alloy films with synergistic effect of suppressing interfacial interdiffusion and modulating surface electronic structure
abstract: Simultaneously suppressing interdiffusion and regulating surface electronic structure remains a key challenge for high-temperature functional thin films. A refractory high-entropy alloy thin film with a composition of W25Re20Os45Ta5Mo5 was fabricated and applied to the thermionic cathodes. Owing to sluggish diffusion and chemical disorder, the RHEA film overcomes the stability and functionality limitations of conventional single-component films by inhibiting interdiffusion and promoting surface electron redistribution, thereby enhancing both thermal stability and emission performance. Compared with Os-coated cathodes that undergo phase transformation within 4 h at 1150°Cb, the W25Re20Os45Ta5Mo5 coated cathode maintains phase stability for up to 16 h at the same temperature. At 1050°Cb, the RHEA-coated cathode achieves an emission current density of 33.55 A/cm², 29.2% higher than that of Os-coated cathodes, which are the most widely used M-type cathodes, while reducing the evaporation rate to 1.71 × 10-9 g•cm-2•s-1, representing a decrease of 62.16%. First-principles calculations show that the diffusion energy barrier between RHEA and W is significantly higher than that between Os and W. The high-entropy surface lowers Ba and O diffusion barriers, while XPS confirms stable metal-O-Ba adsorption states that promote rapid reconstruction of Ba–O dipoles. Notably, Atomic-scale analysis by the three-dimensional charge density reveals that chemical disorder induces intrinsic surface charge heterogeneity: electron-rich regions (W, Ta, Mo) and electron-deficient sites (Re, Os) collectively drive charge redistribution, promoting more electron transfer to the Ba-O dipole and reducing the work function. These findings provide a generalizable design principle for stabilizing interfaces and regulating electronic structures through refractory high-entropy design.

title: Plasticity enhancement via β-relaxation modulation in metallic glasses: Energy engineering
abstract: The large-scale structural applications of metallic glasses (MGs) remain challenging, partly due to the limited plastic deformability induced by structural relaxation. Here, we employ high-pressure annealing (HPA) to implement a potent ‘energy engineering’ strategy to surmount this limitation. By leveraging the interplay of pressure and temperature, we successfully drove La(Ce)-based MGs into a rejuvenated high-energy state. As exemplified by the La65Al10Ni25 and (La0.7Ce0.3)65Al10Ni25 systems, the near-room-temperature (323 K) plasticity was enhanced from 0.88% to 3.48% and from 0.39% to 3.81%, respectively. Central to this work is the establishment of a robust quantitative correlation spanning the thermodynamic energy state, β-relaxation dynamics, and macroscopic mechanical response. Atomistic simulations unveil that this plasticity enhancement originates from the HPA-induced structural heterogeneity, specifically characterized by “high-density clusters embedded in a low-density matrix”. This unique ‘hard-soft’ composite architecture effectively amplifies the intensity of β-relaxation and suppresses strain localization, ultimately resulting in significant plasticity improvement. The quantitative “thermodynamics–kinetics–plasticity” linkage established herein provides a generalizable physical criterion for predicting and optimizing the mechanical performance of metallic glasses.

title: Interstitial carbon tuning of low-angle grain boundary and dislocation activity in a bulk near-α titanium for ultrahigh ductility
abstract: Near-α titanium alloys are critical for aerospace applications due to their excellent high-temperature and cryogenic performance, yet their room-temperature strength–ductility trade-off remains a persistent limitation. Here, we demonstrate that interstitial carbon effectively tailors the microstructure of a bulk near-α Ti-8Al-1Mo-1V-0.23C alloy (Ti811-C), producing elongated α grains decorated with thin grain-boundary β plates and a high fraction of low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) with slight carbon segregation. The obtained alloy exhibits ultrahigh ductility (∼29.7%) together with a substantial increase in yield strength (∼1018 MPa). Microstructural characterizations reveal that carbon stabilizes LAGBs through solute pinning and dislocation-locking interactions of 〈a〉 and 〈c+a〉 dislocations. Interstitial carbon selectively increases the critical resolved shear stress of basal and prismatic 〈a〉 slips, thereby promoting activation of extensive 〈c+a〉 slips. The combination of multiple slip systems and the high fraction of LAGBs facilitates cross-slip and dislocation interactions, effectively suppressing strain localization and stabilizing strain hardening. Besides, the LAGBs act as barriers that strengthen the alloy while maintaining strain compatibility through dislocation transmissions; they also emit dislocations in early deformation and serve as prolific dislocation sources, markedly improving ductility. This work highlights a hierarchical boundary-engineering strategy enabled by interstitial carbon, offering a new pathway to overcome long-standing strength–ductility limitations in near-α titanium and other HCP structural alloys.

title: Influence of SiO2 addition on the voltage stability of PTCR ceramics
abstract: The rise of E-mobility leads to intensive research into power electronics. Increasing onboard voltages of 800 V to 1200 V pose a challenge to electrical components like PTCR thermistors, which are applied as self-regulating heating elements, current limiters, or temperature sensors in battery electric vehicles (BEV). PTCR materials are characterized by a positive temperature coefficient of resistance (PTCR). However, the PTCR effect is limited by the breakdown field strength E BD at which PTCR materials lose their self-regulating ability. A critical factor to enhance the E BD of PTCR ceramics is the addition of a flux such as SiO 2 . In this study, the effects of the SiO 2 addition on the potential barrier and microstructure are discussed and their influence on voltage stability is evaluated assuming the validity of the Heywang-Jonker model. We developed an estimate for the average grain size with the volume weighted d V 50 and proofed its feasibility as an estimate for the average grain size along the conduction path in the Heywang-Jonker model. However, while we present a ceramic with a maximum E BD of 1118 V·mm -1 at w SiO 2 = 0.9%, we show that for w SiO 2 > 0.9% the practical voltage stability in form of the E BD is decoupled from the assumptions made by the Heywang-Jonker model. We prove that the deterioration of the E BD for w SiO 2 > 0.9% contradicting our results for the Heywang-Jonker model is founded in the destabilizing field enhancing effect of increased inhomogeneities in the ceramics.

title: Core-shell-matrix heterostructures enable high strength and ductility of titanium alloys
abstract: The nanoscale lamellar microstructures (LM) in titanium alloys impart exceptional strength but often suffer from brittleness. Conventional bi-modal (BM) microstructures introduce equiaxed αp to improve ductility, but this compromises strength and induces strain localization due to the large hardness mismatch between αp and the nano-lamellae. In this work, a tri-modal (TM) heterostructure with a Core–Shell–Matrix configuration (equiaxed αp–nanoscale ultrafine lamellar–microscale coarse lamellar) is proposed in the commercial Ti-5Al-5Mo-5V-3Cr-1Zr (wt.%) alloy. This architecture effectively suppresses strain localization and leverages enhanced heterogeneous deformation-induced (HDI) strengthening, promoting sequential activation of deformation across three distinct regions. As a result, the TM structure exhibits ∼120 MPa higher strength than the strength-oriented LM and ∼100% greater uniform elongation than the ductility-oriented BM structure. The TM heterostructure is formed via micro-regional composition modulation, which induces different phase transformation pathways between ultrafine and coarse lamellae. The high strength stems from the refined and strengthened soft αp phase within the TM architecture, which establishes a unique strain path and an enhanced HDI effect. Meanwhile, the excellent ductility is attributed to the extraordinary geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) accommodation capability and the dispersed potential crack nucleation sites, which collectively sustain HDI work hardening. This work demonstrates a scalable, cost-effective heat treatment strategy for achieving superior mechanical properties in commercial titanium alloys, offering broad applicability across alloy systems.

title: Hydrogen effects on the cyclic creep deformation mechanisms of 310s austenitic stainless steel
abstract: Hydrogen effects on cyclic plasticity of austenitic stainless steels represent a critical issue for fatigue design, as constitutive behavior is essential to assess both global and local mechanical responses of structures. In this work, the effect of solute hydrogen on cyclic hardening and cyclic creep deformation of AISI 310S, uncharged and hydrogen-charged (∼113 wppm), was investigated prior to crack initiation. To elucidate hydrogen–plasticity interactions under cyclic loading, a consistent mechanical database covering a range of mean stress σ m and maximum stress σ max levels was established under stress-controlled tension-compression ratcheting at 300 K (0.05 Hz) and compared with static creep. Internal stresses were quantified by partitioning the flow stress into back stress X and effective stress σ eff , and dislocation structures were characterized by quantitative TEM. The tensile plastic strain history, governed by σ max , reveals three deformation regimes, each distinctly affected by hydrogen. In Regime 0 (low σ max ), hydrogen promotes planar slip and homogeneous dislocation distributions, yielding high plastic strain reversibility and suppression of cyclic creep. Consistent with reduced stacking fault energy and inhibited cross slip, hydrogen increases the threshold stress σ th for the onset of cyclic creep. In Regime I (σ max > σ th ), the cyclic creep rate follows ln(dε r /dt) ≈ K(σ max /μ) + B, where μ is the shear modulus; hydrogen decreases the slope K, attributed to enhanced plastic strain reversibility and delayed formation of polarized dislocation walls. In Regime II (high σ max ), well-developed dislocation cell structures dominate, and the influence of hydrogen becomes less pronounced. Across Regimes I and II, the cyclic creep rate scales uniquely with the back-stress amplitude X a , independent of hydrogen content, indicating that fluctuations of long-range internal stresses govern ratcheting. This finding reflects the ability of cyclic loading to progressively destabilize the dislocation structure; hydrogen mitigates this effect primarily through enhanced short-range pinning.

title: Extending stable potential window by multi-principal element passivation in complex alloys
abstract: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), or complex alloys, offer expanded compositional degrees of freedom for designing corrosion-resistant alloys with extended electrochemical stability. However, how this compositional multiplicity can be translated into multi-principal element passivation (MPEP), capable of transcending the stability limits imposed by single-element-dominated passivation, remains a central question. Here, we demonstrate this transition through a comparison between a five-component CoCrFeMnNi alloy and its four-component CoCrFeNi counterpart in 0.1 M Na2SO4 (pH 4). The CoCrFeMnNi alloy exhibits a markedly higher breakdown potential (∼1500 mV vs. Ag/AgCl) than CoCrFeNi (∼1000 mV), demonstrating a widened protective window. Correlative atomic-scale structural and chemical characterizations identify that CoCrFeMnNi forms multi-principal element passivation involving Cr, Mn, and Fe, whereas CoCrFeNi remains restricted to Cr-based passivation. In addition, we propose three potential contributions to this transition: (i) staggered oxidation thermodynamics enabling sequential elemental activation, (ii) inter-element activation bridging oxidation across potentials, and (iii) valence-buffering effect that stabilizes the film under extreme anodic conditions. These findings suggest MPEP as a mechanism for designing alloys with extended stable windows.

title: In-situ formation of nanoscale Hf dispersoids enabling exceptional strength-ductility synergy and superior thermal stability in Mo alloys
abstract: Dispersion-strengthened molybdenum (Mo) alloys commonly suffer from severe performance degradation stemming from dispersoid coarsening or severe lattice misfit between the matrix and dispersed precipitates, which triggers interfacial debonding and premature intergranular fracture. Herein, we propose an in-situ nano-dispersion strengthening strategy by employing HfB2 as the Hf source for generating intragranular nanoparticles. Unlike conventional oxide-dispersion-strengthened Mo (ODS-Mo) with oxide particles preferentially segregating at grain boundaries, the present Mo-Hf alloy features ultrafine metallic Hf nanoparticles with an average diameter of ∼54 nm, approximately 84% of which are uniformly distributed inside Mo grain interiors. Combined first-principles calculations and experimental characterizations verify an ultra-small lattice misfit of only 0.04% and a low interface energy of 1.28 J/m2 for the Mo/Hf heterointerfaces. Such coherent interfacial architecture effectively suppresses interface-initiated cracking and endows intragranular Hf nanoparticles with outstanding thermal stability. Benefiting from this tailored intragranular nano-dispersion microstructure, the Mo-Hf alloy maintains exceptional tensile properties even after prolonged thermal annealing at 1000 °C for 100 h, achieving an ultimate tensile strength of 741 MPa and a tensile elongation of ∼24% at 400 °C. This work provides a feasible pathway to design high-performance Mo alloys balancing high strength, good ductility and exceptional thermal stability for high-temperature applications.

title: Combination of ultra-high strength, enhanced thermal conductivity, and large negative thermal expansion in La(Fe, Si)13 alloys via in-situ forming multi-phase
abstract: Negative thermal expansion (NTE) materials have been attracting considerable attention for their unique response to temperature. NaZn13-type (1:13) La(Fe, Si)13 alloys are considered as promising candidates, but lengthy synthesis, high brittleness, and poor thermal conductivity limit their application. Herein, an ultra-strong negative thermal expansion B-doped La(Fe, Si)13 alloy is developed via in-situ forming multi-phase with 1:13 phase as the matrix. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the 1:13 phase is thermodynamically favored over the α-Fe and LaFeSi phase upon boron doping. As-cast B-doped alloy exhibits a large NTE behavior (αl = −26.9 × 10−6 K−1, 166–247 K) around TC. Meanwhile, the semi-coherent interface between 1:13 phase and α-Fe/Fe2B enhance both compressive strength (up to 1.2 GPa, a 260% increase) and toughness (maximum strain exceeds 3.0%). Thermal conductivity is also enhanced significantly by ∼150% over the traditional single-phase alloy. Moreover, the NTE temperature range is further engineered to room temperature via interstitial hydrogen, and hydrogenation sample exhibits a nearly zero thermal expansion behavior with αl = −0.2 × 10−6 K−1 (104–244 K). Consequently, this work successfully overcomes the key challenges of La(Fe, Si)13 materials and provides a new NTE alloy with outstanding comprehensive performance.

title: Intra-regional strain partitioning within initial austenite regions in medium Mn steels
abstract: Metastable austenite (γ) plays a critical role in determining the mechanical response of advanced steels. However, despite the wide recognition of interphase strain partitioning between γ and the constituent phases, the evolution of strain heterogeneity within the initial γ regions during deformation remains poorly understood. Here, using in situ scanning electron microscope tensile tests combined with microscopic digital image correlation, we systematically investigate the grain-scale spatiotemporal evolution of microstrain in intercritically annealed medium Mn steels with and without 0.1 wt.% V, with particular focus on the initial γ regions where martensite (α′) forms during deformation via strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT). We reveal a dual strain partitioning behavior, in which intra-regional strain partitioning within the γ/α′ regions is more pronounced than interphase strain partitioning between the ferrite (α) and γ/α′ regions. We further show that the initial γ grains exhibit crystallographic orientation-dependent deformation responses, with high-Schmid-factor grains favoring stronger intragranular-dominated plasticity, whereas low-Schmid-factor grains deform mainly through intergranular accommodation, thereby establishing an early local strain contrast. This strain contrast is then amplified by SIMT and redistributed by interface-mediated strain transfer, leading to pronounced intra-regional strain partitioning. V microalloying further intensifies this strain partitioning by promoting SIMT and increasing phase mechanical contrast. These findings demonstrate that, beyond the conventionally emphasized interphase strain partitioning, intra-regional strain partitioning within the initial γ regions is a key mesoscale deformation feature in medium Mn steels, extending the current understanding of deformation heterogeneity in γ-containing advanced steels.

title: High-energy {134¯1} twin boundaries and hierarchical twinning behavior in a near-α titanium alloy under biaxial loading
abstract: Uniaxial mechanical tests, although widely used, are inherently limited in capturing the complex stress states experienced by structural materials in service. In this work, the mechanical response and deformation mechanisms of an industrial TA31 near-α titanium alloy under biaxial tensile loading were systematically investigated using a tailored cruciform specimen. True stress–strain responses under biaxial tension were obtained via an inverse analysis method combining digital image correlation (DIC) and finite element (FE) simulations. Under biaxial tension, the alloy exhibits markedly intensified plastic anisotropy, and both principal directions sustain substantially higher stress levels than in uniaxial tension. Microstructural analyses reveal that {101¯2} tensile twins are activated under both loading conditions, contributing to the accommodation of plastic deformation. Notably, a rarely reported high-energy {134¯1} twin boundary is identified in high-strain regions of biaxially deformed specimens. With increasing plastic strain, these {134¯1} twin boundaries act as preferential nucleation sites for secondary {101¯2} twins. The subsequent propagation of secondary twins along the high-energy interfaces promotes detwinning of the primary {134¯1} twins and results in the formation of interfaces approaching the crystallography of stable {101¯1} twin boundaries. These findings demonstrate that the unique stress state associated with biaxial tension enables the activation of energetically unfavorable twins and triggers hierarchical twinning processes in near-α titanium alloys. This study provides new insights into the strain accommodation mechanisms mediated by high-energy twin boundaries under biaxial loading conditions.

title: Probing the role of 3D intergranular interactions in local subcoercive switching of textured piezoelectric ceramics
abstract: The electromechanical responses of individual grains embedded in ferroelectric ceramics are modulated by local boundary conditions imposed by neighboring grains. In this work, in situ far-field high-energy X-ray diffraction microscopy data were collected for a strongly textured manganese-doped lead-magnesium-niobate-lead-zirconate-titanate ceramic manufactured by templated grain growth. Domain variant volume fractions were estimated for hundreds of grains before and after applying a subcoercive electric field and combined with spatial information to correlate local subcoercive switching behavior with grain neighborhood characteristics. Subcoercive switching was associated with the extent to which a grain's as-poled domain state deviates from that of a perfectly-aligned single crystal, likely reflecting contributions from local features that cannot be resolved with this technique (porosity, grain boundary phases, local composition variations). Competition was observed between grain orientation and intergranular interactions, with the former observed to be less important than the latter when grain volumes were considered. Larger misorientations within the tape-casting plane and reduced ferroelastic switching among near-neighbors were associated with reduced subcoercive switching, together implying a coordinated intergranular switching mechanism. Collectively, these findings emphasize the role of intergranular interactions in modulating local electromechanical response, offering insights into factors responsible for deviations in textured ceramic response relative to single crystals.

title: Segregation-induced structural reconfiguration and chemically actuated migration of grain boundaries in multi-principal element alloys
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) exhibit complex structural and chemical evolution under thermomechanical stimuli, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms coupling solute segregation, GB structural reconfiguration, and migration remain poorly understood. In this work, we employ hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations combined with a first principles-accurate interatomic potential to investigate segregation-induced grain boundary dynamics, using a commercial Au–Ag–Cu alloy as a model system. Our results show that inhomogeneous Ag segregation consistently drives GBs toward lower-energy structural reconfigurations, including a reversible faceting–defaceting transition regulated by solute saturation. These transformations arise from the synergistic reduction of elastic strain energy and interfacial energy, which reshapes the local elastic fields at GBs and in turn controls the spatial partitioning of solutes. The GB dynamics exhibit two distinct modes depending on the distribution of Ag on either side of the boundary: one-side-dominant segregation creates a chemical potential imbalance, driving directional GB migration and eventual merging with phase boundaries; whereas segregation on both sides stabilizes GB within the Ag-rich precipitates. On this basis, we further propose a structure-chemistry interplay mechanism governing the evolution of asymmetric tilt GBs: the intrinsic structural asymmetry dictates the initial segregation preference, while local chemical potential imbalances provide the key driving force for the chemically actuated GB migration.

title: Precipitates suppress the deformation-induced phase transformation in FCC-phase multi-principal element alloys
abstract: The phase transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect is a potent mechanism that simultaneously enhances the strength and ductility of materials. In this study, L12 precipitates were introduced into low stacking fault energy (SFE) FCC-phase TRIP-type multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) to investigate their influence on the FCC→HCP deformation-induced phase transformation through uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature. The L12 precipitates significantly enhance the strength of the alloy. Their presence inhibits the formation and propagation of stacking faults (SFs), thereby suppressing the FCC→HCP transformation. This phenomenon arises from the combined effect of two factors. Firstly, the dispersed distribution of L12 precipitates generates high-SFE zones that segment the FCC matrix and reduce the dislocation channel width. This increases the critical stress required for the formation of the first SF loop, thereby inhibiting SFs formation, thus preventing the subsequent generation of the HCP phase. Secondly, the higher SFE of the L12 precipitates relative to the matrix causes propagating SFs to be effectively pinned, thereby restricting their motion. The present work elucidates how coherent L12 precipitates suppress the transformation process, providing a mechanistic basis for tailoring metastability in TRIP-type MPEAs through nanoscale precipitation engineering beyond conventional compositional design.

title: Editorial Board
Opportunities and challenges of megahertz X-ray synchrotron radiography for in situ materials science applications due to high dose rate
abstract: Characterising ultra-high-speed dynamic events in the bulk of the material requires high-frame-rate imaging, combined with X-rays capable of penetrating the material. Megahertz radiography with synchrotron radiation was explored, showing strong potential for capturing dynamic damage events. In situ tensile tests were performed on fibre-reinforced polymer composites to image transverse crack dynamics. Challenges of this experimental technique were highlighted and complemented with plausible strategies. The first challenge stemmed from the limited buffer capacity of the high-speed camera, which was addressed by designing two triggering strategies based on electrical conductivity and load drops. The second challenge concerned dose effects due to the high photon flux required for ultra-high-speed radiography, which led to a degradation of the specimen by thermal effects. Dose calculations were performed, and a heat transfer model was developed to quantify the dose rate effect. Increasing beam energy and enhancing cooling were proposed to mitigate the heat load, providing actionable insights for future ultra-high-speed radiography experiments across a wide range of applications.

title: Elevated rolling contact fatigue resistance of gradient dislocation structured martensitic bearing steel
abstract: Gradient dislocation cell structures induced by cyclic torsion treatment (CT) have been shown to enable superior fatigue resistance in soft single-phase alloys. Here, we introduce a hierarchical gradient dislocation hierarchy, characterized by tens-nanometers low-angle dislocation wall boundaries at the top surface, into an ultra-high strength martensitic M50 bearing steel via CT. The resulting gradient dislocation structured M50 exhibits remarkably improved endurance life under alternating asymmetrical multiaxial non-proportional rolling contact fatigue, achieving a fatigue life approximately 2.5 times that of its counterpart. This superior contact fatigue resistance essentially arises from the gradient hierarchy of massive strong-and-stable low-angle boundaries. The presence of these boundaries not only reduces cyclic plastic strain, but also mediates a strain-delocalized mechanism through confining dislocation slip and progressive self-patterning within nanosized dislocation walls. Consequently, the formation of white etching regions and micron-scale spalling pits is significantly retarded and confined to the subsurface layer.

title: Large magnetovolume effect in multifunctional ferromagnet MnSb driven by unconventional magnetostructural coupling
abstract: Magnetostructural coupling plays a crucial role in numerous types of quantum materials and functional magnetic materials. Here, we investigate the magnetostructurally active ferromagnet MnSb, whose derivative compounds Mn 1 + x Sb are strong candidates for magnetocaloric applications. We reveal an unusually large spontaneous magnetostriction effect in MnSb, resulting in a relative unit cell expansion of up to 1% and an extended temperature region of negative thermal expansion of the crystallographic a axis. This magnetovolume effect is exceptional not only because of its magnitude, but also because the volume increase begins in the paramagnetic phase and exhibits unconventional linear scaling with the short-range ferromagnetic correlations as the temperature is lowered, before switching to quadratic scaling with the long-range-ordered magnetic moment below the transition. We explain this exceptional behavior through unusual trilinear couplings among the lattice strain and domains of distinct magnetic order parameters. Heat capacity measurements also provide new thermodynamic information about MnSb, including determination of the Debye and Einstein temperatures to be 164 and 296 K, respectively. These findings greatly expand our understanding of MnSb and provide insights into the fundamental materials physics of magnetostructural coupling in the presence of short-range magnetic correlations, with potential for broad applicability.

title: Crystallographic transformation of UO2 to U4O9, U3O7, and U3O8
abstract: The oxidation of UO 2 plays a critical role in the performance and long-term behaviour of nuclear fuel, yet the crystallographic nature of the intermediate uranium oxides and the mechanism of their formation remains poorly understood due to their complex structures and the lack of suitable single-crystal samples. In this work we investigate the oxidation of epitaxial [ 0 0 1 ] UO 2 thin films using in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction, enabling direct observation of structural evolution throughout oxidation. We show that oxidation proceeds topotactically from UO 2 to U 4 O 9 , U 3 O 7 , and U 3 O 8 , with the U 4 O 9 and U 3 O 7 phases forming as multi-domain single crystals. Comparison with calculated reciprocal space maps identifies the U 4 O 9 structure as the β phase, while the U 3 O 7 phase exhibits complex domain behaviour and additional superstructure reflections indicate a lower symmetry than that in present structural models. The final transformation to U 3 O 8 is accompanied by a large volume expansion and pronounced loss of crystalline coherence, although a clear topotactic relationship between ( 0 0 1 ) UO 2 and ( 1 3 0 ) U 3 O 8 is retained. The identification of these topotactic relationships allow us to build a mechanistic understanding of the transformations between phases. These results provide insight into the structural mechanisms governing the oxidation and spallation of UO 2 and establish a route to accessing single-crystal U 4 O 9 and U 3 O 7 via controlled oxidation.

title: Leveraging the polymorphic phase transition for high piezoelectricity in barium titanate-based lead-free piezoceramics
abstract: Growing environmental concerns over the toxicity of lead-based piezoelectrics have driven the urgent need for high-performance, lead-free alternatives. In this work, we employ a coupled A-/B-site phase-transition engineering strategy to induce room-temperature (RT) coexistence of multiple phases, enhancing structural flexibility and enabling a continuous polymorphic phase transition (PPT). This approach yields an ultrahigh piezoelectric coefficient (d33) of 829 ± 30 pC·N−1 in a designed quaternary system: (1‒x‒y‒z)Ba(Hf0.16Ti0.84)O3‒x(Ba0.70Ca0.30)TiO3‒yBa(Sn0.11Ti0.89)O3‒z(Ba0.60Sr0.40)TiO3 [abbreviated as (1‒x‒y‒z)BHT‒xBCT‒yBSnT‒zBSrT, with the optimal composition at x = 0.24, y = 0.20, z = 0.16]. Atomic-resolution Z-contrast imaging reveals the nanoscale coexistence of rhombohedral (R), orthorhombic (O), and tetragonal (T) phases, establishing a continuous pathway for polarization rotation. Phase-field simulations further demonstrate that these multiphase nanodomains are interconnected via high-density interphase boundaries, which collectively reduce both the interphase energy barrier and polarization anisotropy. These findings highlight dual-site regulation of near-room-temperature phase-transition convergence as a promising strategy for enhancing the piezoelectric performance of BaTiO3-based lead-free ceramics.

title: High-performance Fe-based superalloys designed via large language models and knowledge graphs
abstract: Fe-based superalloys are indispensable in high-temperature load-bearing components, yet simultaneous optimization of strength and ductility remains difficult due to the reliance on empirical design. Herein, a closed-loop design methodology is developed for Fe-based superalloys and experimentally validated by integrating large language model-driven knowledge extraction, knowledge graph-based semantic descriptors, multimodal property prediction, Bayesian active learning, and experimental verification.
