Composition-, processing-, and property-related entities and relations are extracted from the literature, organized into a materials knowledge graph, and encoded into semantic descriptors using domain-adaptive RoBERTa pretraining and graph representation learning. After fusion with structured descriptors, the surrogate models achieve an R2 of 0.96 for tensile strength prediction and improve elongation prediction from R2 values of 0.74 to 0.79. Bayesian optimization enables efficient exploration of the design space and leads to a new Fe-based superalloy with a room-temperature tensile strength of ∼1200 MPa, a total elongation of ∼47.5%, a strength-ductility product exceeding 50 GPa·%, and a yield strength of ∼900 MPa at 700 °C. The methodology provides an effective route for multi-objective alloy design and accelerated discovery in metallic material systems.

title: A transport-based framework for solidification cracking in Ni-based superalloys processed by laser powder bed fusion
abstract: Solidification cracking remains a persistent barrier to laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processing of solid-solution-strengthened (SSS) Ni-based superalloys and is commonly attributed to carbide formation, liquation-type failure, or elemental segregation. In this work, the cracking behavior of three SSS Ni-based superalloys—Inconel 625 (625), Inconel 617 (617), and Haynes 230 (230)—is examined under comparable LPBF conditions to evaluate the origins of their cracking susceptibility. Carbides were present in both 625 and 230, yet cracking behavior differed significantly. MC-type carbides in 625 remain discrete and preserve liquid connectivity, whereas Cr-rich M23C6 carbides in 230 form at cellular triple junctions that bottleneck the interdendritic liquid network, influencing cracking through liquid connectivity rather than as an independent cause. Alloy 617 exhibited anomalous segregation without resolvable secondary phases yet cracked mildly, indicating that extensive carbide formation is not a prerequisite for cracking. To rationalize these observations, a transport-limited framework is proposed in which cracking occurs when terminal-liquid feeding cannot accommodate solidification-induced strain; among the mechanisms evaluated, this framework is most consistent with the physical constraints imposed by LPBF solidification. Transport-based crack-susceptibility indexes incorporating permeability, viscosity, and solidification kinetics distinguish the alloy hierarchy; permeability ratios Krat increased from approximately 7 (625) to 11.5 (617) and 14.5 (230), with corresponding increases in the μ-weighted mushy zone risk index (CSIMZRM). These results are consistent with transport-limited liquid feeding as a rate-limiting contributor to solidification cracking in LPBF-processed SSS Ni-based superalloys, providing a physically grounded basis for alloy and process design.

title: UNi4Mn: A non-centrosymmetric uranium intermetallic exhibiting room-temperature ferromagnetism
abstract: We report UNi 4 Mn, a non-centrosymmetric uranium intermetallic exhibiting room-temperature ferromagnetism with a Curie temperature (T C ) of 336 K. This behavior arises from localized Mn 2+ moments and enhanced 5 f -3 d hybridization. Differential thermal analysis indicates congruent formation at 1185 °C. The compound crystallizes in the cubic MgCu 4 Sn-type structure (Pearson symbol cF 24, space group F- 43 m ) with Mn atoms fully ordered on the 4 c site, as determined by X-ray and neutron diffraction. Magnetization measurements yield an effective magnetic moment (μ eff ) of 5.6 μ B per formula unit and a saturation magnetic moment (μ sat ) of 4.85 μ B per formula unit, consistent with localized Mn 2+ behavior. Neutron diffraction reveals magnetic moments only on the Mn sites, while U and Ni atoms remain nonmagnetic; Mn moments order ferromagnetically and align along the cubic face diagonal. Density functional theory calculations reproduce the ferromagnetic ground state of UNi 4 Mn and its Ce analogue CeNi 4 Mn, and confirm the Pauli-paramagnetic character of UNi 5 . The calculations further show that enhanced 5 f -3 d hybridization strengthens exchange interactions, leading to Dirac-like electronic features and a pseudogap at the Fermi level, with potential implications for spintronic and quantum devices. To our knowledge, UNi 4 Mn represents the first uranium-based intermetallic combining room-temperature ferromagnetism with non-centrosymmetric symmetry, providing mechanistic insight into how chemical ordering, hybridization, and local coordination govern magnetic exchange in actinide intermetallics.

title: Isothermal annealing effects on β-relaxations and crystallization behaviors in amorphous GeTe
abstract: A secondary (β) relaxation process is the dominant source of atomic dynamics below T g in many glass forming systems. Recent studies reported the presence of β-relaxations in amorphous phase-change materials (PCMs). They showed that suppressing β-relaxation via annealing in Ge 15 Sb 85 can effectively slow down its crystallization kinetics. Yet, when Sb is replaced by Te, a similar annealing protocol has little effect on the Te-rich alloy Ge 15 Te 85 , which is a good glass former. Here, we investigate amorphous GeTe that is a Sb-free PCM, but with faster crystallization kinetics than Ge 15 Te 85 . GeTe is a typical PCM, i.e., crystallizes very rapidly. Using powder mechanical dynamic spectroscopy, we observe a clear reduction of the excess-wing in the loss modulus upon isothermal annealing of amorphous GeTe, indicating a suppression of its β-relaxation. Combining ultrafast calorimetric analysis and time-resolved optical reflectivity measurements shows that, whereas as-deposited GeTe exhibits stochastic crystallization behavior, annealed samples crystallize more slowly but also with reduced stochasticity. Synchrotron X-ray scattering experiments reveal increased Peierls-like distortions in the amorphous structure after annealing, and demonstrate that, even if annealing introduces nucleation sites, it nonetheless slows down crystallization kinetics. These finding suggests that, in the annealed GeTe, crystallization is limited by crystal growth rate, which is retarded through a process likely associated with the suppression of β-relaxation.

title: Post-partitioning treatment increases both yield strength and local formability in QP steel
abstract: The low cost and excellent strength-formability combination of quenched and partitioned steels have enabled improvements in automotive safety and lightweighting. Despite this, the presence of fresh martensite in their microstructures has been identified as a key factor limiting further formability improvements. Prior work has shown that the hardness contrast of fresh martensite with its surrounding matrix phases leads to decohesion and microcrack nucleation during deformation. In this study we evaluate the efficacy of a post-partitioning treatment in tempering the fresh martensite and reducing its tendency for microcrack nucleation. To this end, mechanical properties are studied across different scales (i.e., using hole expansion tests, uniaxial tensile tests, nanoindentation); and connected to characterization of microstructural constituents by scanning electron microscopy, synchrotron X-ray diffraction, dilatometry, and scanning transmission electron microscopy. The results reveal that post-partitioning treatment can indeed decrease the hardness of fresh martensite, increasing the local formability and yield strength. The increase in local formability is primarily achieved by fresh martensite tempering which reduces the hardness mismatch at phase boundaries, increasing the strain required for microcrack nucleation. On the other hand, an additional increase in the yield strength is observed which is due to increased austenite stability from additional carbon partitioning, and to a lesser degree, bainitic transformation. The potential for post-partitioning treatment to improve mechanical properties in steels beyond the one studied here is discussed in terms of microstructural and compositional factors.

title: Enhancement of Li-ion storage performance induced by out-of-plane ordering occupation in MoxV4-xC3Tz o-MXenes derivated from MoxV4-xAlC3 o-MAX phases
abstract: A series of MoxV4-xAlC3 (x = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0and 2.5) o-MAX phases have been synthesized, in which the ordered atomic occupation is firstly systematically investigated: out-of-plane ordered occupation for x = 2.0 and preferentially ordered occupation for x = 1.0, 1.5, and 2.5, which is inherited into MoxV4−xC3Tz (x = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5) o-MXene. The best Li-ion storage performance has been achieved in MoxV4-xC3Tz o-MXene for x = 2.0, attributed to faster charge-transfer kinetics and more efficient Li-ion diffusion. Combined with XPS analysis and theoretical Bader charge calculations, a reversible redox mechanism caused by Li-ion adsorption/desorption are found in MoxV4-xC3Tz (x = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5) o-MXenes anodes. By tuning the Mo/V-ratio, the o-MXene for x = 2.0 exhibits stronger orbital hybridization and up-shifted p-band center of its -O surface functional terminals, enhanced Li adsorption energy, promoting its excellent Li-ion storage performance.
keywords: Li-ion storage These two authors contribute equally to the work

title: Impact of interstitial carbon on local lattice distortions in CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys
abstract: Here, we explore component-dependent local lattice distortions in polycrystalline, equiatomic, face-centered cubic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys and their modifications induced by dilute interstitial carbon. Multi-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy combined with reverse Monte Carlo analysis reveals that the Cr component experiences the most substantial local distortions, independent of the temperature of prolonged annealing treatments (993 K or 1373 K) and the nominal carbon content (0 to 0.8 at.%). The static disorder around Cr atoms was found to increase markedly and monotonically upon carbon alloying, whereas Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni demonstrate weaker and non-monotonic tendencies. The carbon-induced lattice distortions extend over several coordination shells, indicating the early stages of carbide-related local configurations specifically around Cr absorbers. First-principles density functional theory and finite-temperature molecular dynamics simulations confirm the preferential occupation of Cr-rich interstitial sites by dilute carbon. These results provide decisive hints towards the atomistic origin of the non-monotonic diffusion behavior previously reported for carbon-doped CrMnFeCoNi alloys, and are noticeable for understanding the carbon-induced phase transitions in compositionally complex systems.

title: Solid oxide cells degradation by Nickel oxidation: A phase field study of oxide growth and its mechanical impact
abstract: Solid Oxide Cells are highly efficient energy conversion devices that can be damaged by various system failures. Specifically, the porous hydrogen electrode, which is a cermet consisting of Nickel and Yttria Stabilized Zirconia (Ni-YSZ), can deteriorate when exposed to oxidizing atmosphere at high temperature. Ni oxidation induces volumetric expansion which is partially accommodated in the pores of the cermet. This constrained swelling imposes mechanical strain on the YSZ backbone that can compromise its integrity. In this study, a conventional cermet was oxidized under air at 700◦C for different times to characterize the kinetics and features of Ni oxidation and the fracture of YSZ. A novel tri-material phase-field model, incorporating oxidation-induced strains, was developed to simulate Ni oxidation within the complex electrode microstructure. The model was validated on different cermet microstructures to reproduce the kinetics of oxidation in the different electrode layers and the YSZ mechanical loading after oxidation. The material parameters governing oxidation (Ni diffusion in NiO) and stress state (oxide growth strain) were identified through the model calibration. A correlation between oxidation and microstructural features was identified, revealing that Ni coarsening slows oxidation kinetics, and enabling pre-simulation DoO estimation with a microstructure descriptor. Simulations revealed localized high tensile stresses at several YSZ necks, matching experimental crack initiation timescales and validating a first step towards oxidation-induced damage prediction.

title: Microstructural stability and mechanical behavior of an ODS-inspired, positively phase-separating Fe–Sr ferritic alloy
abstract: Ferritic steels are widely used because of their low cost but often suffer microstructural degradation and loss of strength during elevated-temperature exposure. Oxide dispersion-strengthened (ODS) alloys offer improved thermal stability but conventionally rely on solutes with strongly negative enthalpies of mixing with Fe to form stable oxide dispersions. Here, a contrasting strategy is explored using the positively phase-separating Fe–Sr system. Fe–Sr alloys containing 1–4 at.% Sr were synthesized by high-energy mechanical alloying, producing supersaturated solid solutions that undergo thermally activated redistribution during annealing. Atom probe tomography reveals the formation of a hybrid nanoscale architecture comprising partially oxidized Sr-rich clusters, unoxidized Sr enrichment, grain-boundary segregation, and residual Sr retained within the Fe matrix. This mixed chemical state differs fundamentally from the predominantly oxide-based dispersions of conventional ODS alloys and stabilizes the nanocrystalline structure over an intermediate temperature range. At higher temperatures, composition-dependent abnormal grain growth emerges, indicating a localized breakdown of grain-boundary pinning. Bulk Fe–1Sr exhibits substantially greater resistance to irreversible thermal degradation than Alloy 430 and mechanical performance broadly comparable to an Fe–Ni–Zr ODS alloy. Fe–1Sr also softens substantially at elevated temperature but recovers its original strength upon cooling, suggesting the potential for forming without quenching or additional heat treatment.

title: Microstrain and its effect on magnetization reversal in sintered Nd-Fe-B magnets
abstract: The coercivity of sintered Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets remains significantly lower than the magnetocrystalline anisotropy field of the Nd₂Fe₁₄B phase. This discrepancy, known as Brown’s paradox, limits the full exploitation of their intrinsic magnetic potential. Although strategies including grain refinement, grain boundary diffusion and reconstruction have proven effective in enhancing coercivity, the intrinsic origin of this severe coercivity degradation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that pervasive intragranular microstrain is a critical crystallographic factor governing coercivity degradation in Nd-Fe-B magnets. Multiscale characterization reveals the presence of a gradient microstrain within 2:14:1 grains, which decays from the near-boundary region toward the grain interior within 200 nm. Additionally, nanoscale regions exhibiting severe lattice distortion are identified near interfaces, with local strain values reaching approximately 3%. First-principles calculations demonstrate that lattice strain significantly weakens the magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant K, giving rise to intragranular K-deterioration zones. Micromagnetic simulations further demonstrate that these zones substantially reduce the nucleation field for reversed domains, thereby promoting preferential nucleation and leading to pronounced coercivity degradation exceeding 40%. Quasi-in-situ combined experiments further reveal a direct correlation between microstrain distribution and demagnetization behavior: grains exhibiting large gradient microstrain and severe interfacial lattice distortions show significantly reduced resistance to demagnetization and undergo preferential magnetic reversal. This work identifies microstrain as a key factor in the coercivity degradation of sintered Nd-Fe-B magnets. Controlling and engineering microstrain may therefore provide a key strategy for developing high-performance permanent magnets.

title: Editorial Board

Atomic-scale insights into the degradation and recovery mechanisms of Ni-rich lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC811) cathodes: A combined density functional theory (DFT) and experimental study
abstract: The Ni-rich LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2 (NMC811) has attracted significant attention in response to the growing demand for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Nevertheless, NMC811 tends to undergo structural degradation, especially when stored in moisture environments. In this study, the mechanisms of moisture-induced degradation and oxygen-driven recovery in NMC811 are investigated by correlating the experimental results with Density Functional Theory (DFT) simulations. The water adsorption energy (Eads), charge density differences (CDD), and electron localization function (ELF) confirm that moisture-induced degradation is triggered by the formation of Li+/Ni2+ intermixing, thereby causing sluggish electrochemical kinetics. The Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) results further reveal increased magnetic disorder, reduced crystallinity, and increased cation mixing in moisture-degraded NMC811. Consequently, the electrochemical performance of moisture-degraded NMC811 decreases. Furthermore, DFT simulations were employed to model the recovery energy in oxygen and nitrogen atmospheres, respectively, within the moisture-degraded NMC811 structure. The partial density of states (PDOS) analysis confirms more effective recovery energy in an oxygen atmosphere, attributed to hybridization between O2–2p (oxygen) and Ni-3d (NMC811) orbitals across the Fermi level. The effective recovery in an oxygen atmosphere is further illustrated by the charge transfer between the oxygen molecule and NMC811’s surface transition metals in CDD and ELF. These DFT findings are validated by enhanced electrochemical performance, EPR analysis, and XRD results, which confirm a reduced cation mixing and a more ordered layered structure in oxygen-recovered NMC811. This study links theoretical simulations and experimental findings to provide a comprehensive understanding of degradation and recovery mechanisms in NMC811 cathode.

title: Distinct twin boundary migration regimes governed by disconnection core structure
abstract: Grain boundary migration governs microstructural evolution in crystalline materials, directly influencing mechanical properties such as strength and thermal stability. Disconnections, which are line defects formed at grain boundaries in response to local curvature, have been identified as critical carriers of boundary migration. Here, we investigate the glide of unfaulted disconnections (UFDs) on a Σ3(111) coherent twin boundary in aluminum at elevated temperatures using molecular dynamics simulations combined with the Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) method. Our results reveal a striking bifurcation in migration behavior depending on the disconnection core structure. UFDs with a pure edge Burgers vector migrate via a thermally activated double-kink mechanism, exhibiting a migration velocity that increases monotonically with temperature. In contrast, UFDs containing a screw dipole component possess an energy barrier approximately eight times lower, and their core structure undergoes a continuous transformation during glide, giving rise to stochastic, bidirectional motion with no systematic temperature dependence. These findings demonstrate that the disconnection core structure fundamentally dictates the migration mode and kinetics of twin boundaries, offering new mechanistic insights into disconnection-mediated grain boundary migration.

title: Competing lead-driven defect regulating mechanisms and their impact on polarization and piezoelectricity in ferroelectric perovskite ceramics
abstract: Lead-based ferroelectric ceramics are promising materials for high-temperature piezoelectric applications. However, their thermal stability is often limited by lead volatility and defect-induced conduction. This work elucidates the effect of excess PbO on the evolution of defects and polarization behavior of BiFeO3-PbTiO3-Ba(Zr,Ti)O3 ceramics. By employing detailed experimental characterization and first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that minor fluctuations in the level of excess lead induces significant variations in the crystal and defect structures. These variations are shown to subsequently trigger a shift in the rhombohedral-tetragonal-pseudocubic (R-T-Pc) phase boundary and a relaxor ferroelectric phase transition from the ergodic to nonergodic state. The presence of a moderate level of excess PbO is shown to suppress the formation of lead and oxygen vacancies, thereby enhancing ferroelectric stability, whereas the incorporation of an excessive level of Pb promotes Pb4+ formation and lattice distortion. This system simultaneously achieves an enhanced piezoelectric response (d33 ∼ 260 pC/N) and temperature stability, with a d33 variation of less than 8% from room temperature to 218.6°C. This work therefore provides new insights into defect regulation mechanisms, providing theoretical guidance for the design of lead-based perovskite ceramics with superior high-temperature piezoelectric properties.

title: Secondary twinning and twin–twin interaction mechanisms of {112¯1} deformation twins in rhenium
abstract: Deformation twinning plays a central role in the plasticity of hexagonal close-packed (hcp) metals, and twin–twin interactions together with secondary twinning can strongly influence their mechanical response. Yet these phenomena remain insufficiently understood, especially for the less common { 11 2 ¯ 1 } extension twins. This study investigates these mechanisms in single-crystal rhenium using in-situ transmission Kikuchi diffraction tensile testing along the [0001] axis. We observe two distinct secondary twinning phenomena. First, native secondary twins form abundantly within primary twins, independent of twin interaction sites. Their nucleation is rationalized by their high Schmid factor and the energetically favorable dissociation of basal dislocations at primary twin boundaries. Second, specific twin-twin interactions trigger a distinct secondary variant selection producing a crossing-like morphology. While these twin crossing configurations violate classical geometric criteria, we show that variant selection is governed by the local stress state and plausibly facilitated by the dissociation of non-basal dislocations. These findings establish a stress- and dislocation-based framework for secondary twinning in { 11 2 ¯ 1 } extension twins, offering new insights into deformation anisotropy of hcp metals.

title: Defect engineering enables dislocation-mediated room-temperature plasticity in boron carbide
abstract: Achieving room-temperature plasticity in strong covalent ceramics remains a fundamental challenge because the directionality of covalent bonding inhibits dislocation nucleation and glide and restricts the number of operable slip systems. Boron carbide, despite its exceptional hardness, is a prototypical example of such intrinsic brittleness. Here, using large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with a machine-learning force field, we demonstrate that Al doping reconfigures the deformation landscape of the boron-rich B₁₃C₂ by activating dislocation-mediated plasticity. To overcome the challenge of dislocation analysis in this low-symmetry crystal, we introduce a coarse-grained mapping in which each B12 icosahedron is represented by a single node, converting the icosahedral network into a distorted face-centered-cubic lattice that is compatible with standard dislocation-identification algorithms. Comprehensive shear simulations reveal that at 6.6 at.% Al, six low-barrier 90° partial dislocation systems are activated at 300 K, satisfying the Taylor–von Mises criterion for arbitrary plastic deformation in polycrystals. Large-supercell MD simulations further capture the nucleation and growth of well-defined dislocation loops, providing direct atomistic evidence of sustained plastic flow in this icosahedral ceramic. In contrast, undoped boron carbide retains only a single active slip system and fails in a brittle manner through localized amorphous-shear-band formation. We further identify ∼3.3 at.% Al as a near-critical threshold, below which slip multiplicity and dislocation mobility become insufficient to robustly support polycrystalline ductility. These results establish a quantitative design principle—maximizing the number of accessible low-barrier partial dislocation systems rather than minimizing strength alone—that can guide the development of damage-tolerant superhard ceramics beyond boron carbide.

title: Co/NbC Heterojunction for accelerating the bidirectional reaction kinetics in lithium-sulfur batteries
abstract: The implementation of high-efficiency catalysts on sulfur hosts has emerged as a predominant approach to address the sluggish kinetics on the cathode side of lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries. However, integrating highly efficient catalysts with sulfur hosts to enable rapid conversion of active materials remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report a heterojunction catalyst consisting of Co/NbC embedded within hollow N-doped carbon polyhedra (Co/NbC@HNC). The Co/NbC interface induces charge redistribution and reconstructs the d orbitals of Co and Nb, resulting in differentiated interactions with LiPSs. The Co side provide Co–S chemical bonding via d-p orbital hybridization, whereas the NbC side strengthens electrostatic attraction toward LiPSs through interfacial polarization. This optimized configuration effectively lowers the energy barrier for sulfur redox and enables accelerated bidirectional kinetics. Accordingly, Co/NbC@HNC-based sulfur host delivers an excellent specific capacity of 1277 mAh g−1 when discharging at 0.1 C with an impressive decay rate of 0.063% per cycle over 600 cycles. Our work may provide a design rationale for heterojunction-based catalysts for advanced Li-S batteries.

title: Defect Energy Formalism for CALPHAD thermodynamics of dilute point defects applied to intrinsic point defects in Mg2Si
abstract: Accurate prediction of point defect thermodynamics is essential for controlling material functionalities. In semiconductors and insulators, even dilute defects can govern carrier transport, recombination, and ionic conductivity, thereby influencing the performance of thermoelectric, photovoltaic, and solid-state ionic devices. While first-principles methods can determine defect energetics, their integration with macroscopic thermodynamic frameworks such as CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) remains limited. This gap has led to empirical CALPHAD models in which Gibbs energy parameters are fitted to available data, restricting predictive capability, especially for semiconductors with dilute defects where thermochemical, non-stoichiometry, and phase-fraction measurements are scarce.We recently introduced the Defect Energy Formalism (DEF), a first-principles-based, dilute-limit adaptation of the compound energy formalism (CEF) for modeling point defects within CALPHAD, eliminating the need for adjustable empirical parameters. Here, we apply DEF to interstitial, antisite, and vacancy defects in anti-fluorite Mg2Si and examine the resulting thermodynamic stability and properties of non-stoichiometric Mg2Si. We outline a general procedure for extracting and calibrating first-principles defect energetics from the literature, reconciling reference energy conventions between DFT and CALPHAD, and integrating them into the CALPHAD-DEF framework. This enables the direct construction of DEF models for any material–defect system from existing first-principles and bulk thermodynamic data. Finally, we demonstrate DEF’s flexibility by progressively increasing model complexity by adding competing defects and defect-induced entropy effects to assess their impact on defect concentrations, validate predictions against standard Arrhenius-type predictions, and discuss defect behavior under non-equilibrium conditions shaped by kinetic barriers or synthesis constraints.

title: Complex He diffusion pathways induced by elemental diversity in refractory high entropy alloy MoNbTaVW
abstract: The performance of plasma-facing components in nuclear fusion reactors is limited by radiation-induced degradation, particularly helium accumulation and transport. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown enhanced irradiation tolerance, yet the physical origin remains debated. We argue that conventional barrier-based models cannot fully explain helium cavity growth and migration observed in HEAs. Therefore, we explore a new framework for studying helium diffusion by investigating its pathways in a body-centered cubic refractory HEA (MoNbTaVW), a medium-entropy alloy (MoNbTa), and reference Ta, using ion implantation, isochronal annealing, transmission electron microscopy, elastic recoil detection analysis, and atomistic simulations. We show that increased elemental diversity leads to increased tortuosity of helium diffusion pathways, yielding persistent local mobility but strongly reduced long-range net displacement. Atomistic simulations reveal that helium preferentially probes local potential-well volumes associated with elements of lower local valence-electron density (V, Nb, Ta), resulting in highly tortuous trajectories characterized by short step lengths and frequent directional changes. This pathway-level confinement explains the experimentally observed coexistence of large local helium cavities and limited long-range transport in the damage-peak region. These results provide a trajectory-based perspective for understanding diffusion in HEAs under irradiation.

title: Self-adaptive wide-temperature lubricating nickel matrix composites with a single SiC additive
abstract: Achieving reliable wide-temperature lubrication remains a fundamental challenge for self-lubricating metal matrix composites. Conventional multi-lubricant strategies often suffer from mechanical degradation and lubricant depletion due to oxidation during thermal cycling. Here, we introduce a single SiC additive in a NiCr matrix to trigger an in-situ reaction during spark plasma sintering. Partial dissolution of Si into Ni lowers the stacking fault energy and promotes the formation of a hard Ni2Si phase, which enhances high-temperature load-bearing capacity and mechanical strength. Simultaneously, it generates nanoscale graphite that ensures low-temperature lubrication without notably compromising mechanical properties. Moreover, Si oxidizes to form a protective SiO2-rich scale that shields graphite from oxidation at elevated temperatures. Consequently, the composite maintains friction coefficients below 0.26 from room temperature to 700 °C and retains lubricity even after 100 h at 700 °C, with a yield strength of 1276 MPa and 16% compressive strain. This work achieves self-adaptive wide-temperature lubrication via a single SiC precursor, overcoming the traditional trade-off between lubrication and mechanical integrity.

title: Dendrite growth kinetics and grain structure anisotropy of ultrahigh temperature W25Ta25Mo25Nb25 high-entropy alloy
abstract: The dendrite growth kinetics of the W25Ta25Mo25Nb25 refractory high-entropy alloy were explored by electrostatic levitation technique under radiative heat transfer and spontaneous nucleation conditions. As liquid undercooling increases, dendrite morphology and crystallographic orientation exhibit a new transition. The first preferential growth of 〈100〉 dendrites at low undercooling originates from solid‒liquid interfacial energy anisotropy, while the formation of 〈100〉 single grain at high undercooling is governed by pronounced atomic attachment kinetic anisotropy. The synergistic effect of these two anisotropies induces tip splitting, thereby forming fractal seaweed and doublon branches with mixed-orientation within the moderate undercooling regime. The threshold undercooling for exclusive single grain growth and the critical velocity distinguishing thermally and kinetically controlled growth are derived as about 450 K and 10 m/s, respectively. The grain size is reduced by one order of magnitude, which stems from the remelting and fragmentation of inherently unstable seaweed-like and doublon branches.

title: Atomic-scale solute redistribution during high fluence neutron irradiation of a zirconium cladding alloy
abstract: In this study we have used a combination of atom probe tomography and (scanning) transmission electron microscopy to investigate solute redistribution under high fluence neutron irradiation in a Zr-Nb-Sn-Cu-Fe experimental fuel cladding alloy. The bulk samples were exposed to neutron irradiation in the BOR-60 reactor up to 33.5 dpa. By mapping solute distributions and quantifying solute compositions in carefully defined regions of irradiated materials, we show that during irradiation Fe and Cu are gradually depleted from second phase precipitates, grain boundaries and interfaces present in the unirradiated state, forming characteristic bands of enrichment at arrays of microstructural defects on the basal plane. In-solution Sn and Nb concentrations in the unirradiated material are depleted to form Sn bands that are spatially out-of-phase with Fe and Cu bands, and Nb clusters which agglomerate and coarsen with longer irradiation exposure. The compositions of both the original β-Nb second phase precipitates and the irradiation-induced Nb clusters converge on ~Zr-35%Nb after heavy irradiation. These results provide new insights into solute redistribution during irradiation. The significant microchemical variations observed at high doses can be used to refine mechanistic understanding of the coupled irradiation and corrosion processes of cladding under in-reactor conditions.

title: Hierarchical defect coupling leading to glass-like phonon thermal conductivity and infrared spectrum shielding in cation-deficient Nd(2-2x)/3CaxTiO3
abstract: The quest for ceramic oxides with ultra-low phonon conductivity and high infrared spectrum reflectance is crucial for the development of advanced thermal insulation materials. While there are various methods to manipulate phonon thermal conductivity to achieve extremely low values, strategies for suppressing radiative conductivity at high temperatures remain limited. In this study, we propose a hierarchical defect coupling approach for Nd(2–2x)/3CaxTiO3 ceramics to tailor both phonon and radiative conductivity. After characterizing the microstructure, we observe dense twin grain boundaries in all samples, a natural phenomenon in perovskite-type Nd(2–2x)/3CaxTiO3 oxide ceramics. Through defect engineering, in situ generation of a nano-chessboard structure was achieved in the Nd0.6Ca0.1TiO3 by introducing varying concentrations of cation vacancies into CaTiO3. The emergence of a strain field is observed surrounding the nano-chessboard structure, and this surrounding strain field significantly contributes to the enhanced stability of the Ca-depleted zones. This approach results in a hierarchical defect coupling, ranging from 0-dimensional point defects to 2-dimensional heterogeneous interfaces, in Nd(2–2x)/3CaxTiO3. Nd0.6Ca0.1TiO3 exhibits high infrared reflectance due to refractive index fluctuations, promoting scattering between multiple interfaces and photons, thereby suppressing the radiant energy from directly penetrating the entire material. Simultaneously, phonon thermal conductivity gradually decreases with increasing cation vacancy concentration and boundaries of nano-chessboard structure, leading to a glass-like phonon thermal conductivity with high infrared reflectance in Nd0.6Ca0.1TiO3. Atomistic simulations confirm a strong scattering probability between 0-dimensional point defects and phonons, effectively hindering phonon transport. Consequently, we successfully achieve the coupling of both low thermal conductivity and infrared spectrum shielding ability in cation-deficient Nd0.6Ca0.1TiO3 through hierarchical defect coupling. Our findings offer an innovative and practical strategy for tuning materials with low thermal conductivity and outstanding infrared spectrum shielding properties.

title: Sluggish recrystallization in additive manufactured stainless steels explained with in-situ EBSD
abstract: Additive manufactured alloys exhibit sluggish recrystallization kinetics compared to their conventionally processed counterparts, requiring higher homologous temperatures and extended annealing times to achieve full recrystallization. The metallurgical mechanisms advanced so far include front pinning by second-phases (oxides or other particles) or solute drag. We collect multi-scale and time-resolved in-situ EBSD to capture recrystallization in directed energy deposited 304L stainless steel at 950 ° C. By fitting classical kinetics models and the microstructural path method to these unique datasets, we reveal that recrystallization is characterized by early but sparse nucleation and early grain impingement. The recrystallization front is particularly tortuous and advances with intermittent, stop-and-go motion. After excluding particle pinning and solute drag effects by means of complementary ex-situ annealing and thermodynamics modeling (diffusion and dissolution), we show that the dislocation cell networks inherited from rapid solidification and thermal cycling pin the recrystallization front. This leads to intermittent front motion governed by the topology of the dislocation cell networks. These findings suggest that post-build heat treatments should be designed not only to overcome stored strain energy barriers but also to disrupt or progressively relax the thermally stable dislocation-cell network inherited from additive manufacturing. More broadly, the mechanism is expected to be relevant to other low- to medium-stacking-fault-energy FCC alloys that develop persistent cellular dislocation structures during processing.

title: Phase field crystal modeling of subgrain coarsening
abstract: Recovery of plastically deformed metals involves several stages of substructure evolution during which dislocation entanglements and networks become increasingly organized, thereby lowering the stored energy in the material. Central to recovery is the formation and evolution of subgrains, which is also recognized as a recrystallization precursor. In this paper, subgrain coarsening is investigated by means of phase field crystal (PFC) simulations. PFC enables tracking subgrain evolution with atom-scale spatial resolution and over extended time scales, beyond the reach of alternative methods such as molecular dynamics simulations. Different subgrain models are devised to investigate various relevant conditions for subgrain coarsening, both with and without the presence of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs). The results show that subgrain coarsening initially takes place by sub-boundary dissolution and rearrangement. At later stages, the coarsening is dominated by subgrain boundary migration—somewhat similar to normal grain growth—but with instances of subgrain coalescence. Lattice rotation within the subgrain network is demonstrated to occur gradually under the formation of intra-subgrain orientation gradients. The results also reveal that a presence of HAGBs is not a prerequisite for subgrain coarsening, even if involving coalescence, contrary to the classical assumption. Subgrain coarsening is, in fact, shown to proceed more efficiently without any HAGB influence in all of the investigated scenarios.

title: A spectral-model analysis of grain boundary segregation in Cu-Ni alloys: roles of enthalpy, entropy, and statistical coupling
abstract: Understanding grain-boundary segregation in Cu–Ni alloys has been hindered by conflicting reports: dilute-limit radiotracer experiments suggest pronounced segregation, whereas atomistic simulations and indirect measurements often indicate little to no segregation. Here, we combine EBSD-based boundary identification with atom probe tomography to directly quantify grain-boundary chemistry in a Cu–9 at% Ni alloy. No measurable Ni enrichment is observed at any boundary type or annealing temperature, providing a firm experimental benchmark for concentrated Cu–Ni alloys. To reconcile these findings with dilute-limit measurements, we employ a spectral model that captures the full distribution of segregation energies and its statistical reshaping under varying global compositions. The model shows that, in the ultra-dilute limit, segregation behavior is strongly influenced by the lowest-energy portion of the spectrum, leading to enhanced segregation at low temperatures. The trends of the model are consistent with those observed in radiotracer experiments, though these experiments still show much more boundary enrichment than expected purely thermodynamically. In contrast, at bulk-relevant compositions, solutes occupy a broader range of boundary sites, and the net segregation factor approaches unity. Using both bivariate joint distributions and a generalized Gaussian copula formulation, we further demonstrate that segregation behavior is primarily governed by the structure of the enthalpy spectrum, while entropic contributions and enthalpy–entropy coupling play a secondary role and do not significantly alter the predicted trends.

title: Redox thermodynamics and hydrogen production of ferrite-based multi-cation oxides for thermochemical water splitting
abstract: Thermochemical water splitting (TWS) is a sustainable route for large-scale hydrogen (H2) production. However, its practical efficiency remains around 5.25%, mainly due to excessively high reduction temperatures (Tred) and limited thermodynamic performance of conventional redox materials. Recently, ferrite-based oxides have gained renewed interest owing to their relatively low Tred and high H2O-to-H2 conversion. While a poly-cation oxide (PCO, Fe0.25(NiCoMg)0.75Oy) has emerged as a promising material, the redox thermodynamics of its constituent cations remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the FexM1-xOy system (M = Ni, NiCo, CoMg, and NiCoMg) by mapping redox trajectories that describe the coupled evolution of reaction enthalpy (ΔhO) and entropy (ΔsO) as a function of oxygen non-stoichiometry (δ). This analysis shows that moderate ΔhO values combined with a large ΔsO span enable low Tred or a small temperature swing (Tswing) for a given oxidation temperature. In addition, a small ΔsO change per unit δ during the redox cycle allows a larger oxygen exchange capacity within a given Tswing. Experimental validation demonstrates that Fe0.35(NiCoMg)0.65Oy achieves an H2 yield of 6.39 mL g-1 per hour, exceeding previously reported PCO by twofold and CeO2 by fourfold under identical conditions. Further oxidation-state analysis confirms that the H2 yield is governed by the effective Fe redox swing during cycling, rather than by Fe concentration. This work identifies the δ-dependence of ΔsO as an additional thermodynamic descriptor for accessing large oxygen exchange capacity under limited Tswing.

title: Mechanisms of free surface and pre-grain-boundary wetting transitions in the Sn-Fe system
abstract: We investigate the wetting transition mechanism of liquid Sn on solid Fe from 650 to 950 °C. At 650 °C, rapid Fe-Sn IMC formation results in slow wetting of the solid/vapor (S/V) interface (free surface) and prevents diffusion at the liquid/solid (L/S) interface. No evident grain boundary grooves are observed at either interface. At 950 °C, under dissolutive conditions with minimal solid solution formation, rapid free surface wetting (FSW) and the pre-grain-boundary wetting (pre-GBW) transition occur concurrently. Significant GB grooves form at both interfaces. On the free surface, the capillary flow of Sn into GB grooves enhances wetting. At the L/S interface, in-situ observation experiments and phase field simulations confirm that the substantial Sn segregation, driven by a large GB-to-L/S interface energy ratio (σGB/σLS), initiates a pre-GBW transition (a precursor state towards complete GBW) and promotes the development of columnar grains. Beyond thermodynamic energy considerations, we propose that suppressing rapid L/S solidification is kinetically critical for rapid FSW and complete GBW. The immediate formation of intermetallic compounds or solid solutions pins the liquid front, thus slowing FSW and preventing complete GBW. In dissolutive systems, CR (the solidification composition range) determines the formation of solid solutions while CL (the solubility of the substrate metal within the liquid metal) controls its onset. Systems with a large CL or a wide CR resist interfacial solidification, thereby promoting rapid FSW and complete GBW. For such systems, CL and CR correlate as CR ≈- (0.96–0.98) CL + (94.91–95.97).

title: Defect physics and iron substitution in tremolite: A first-principles study of a complex silicate
abstract: Complex silicate minerals exhibit chemically diverse and structurally intricate frameworks, yet the mechanisms governing their defect formation and defect-mediated properties remain poorly understood. Here, using first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate intrinsic point defect formation and Fe substitution in tremolite, a representative Ca–Mg amphibole. We find a pronounced sublattice dependence of defect formation: framework cation vacancies are energetically costly and weakly site-dependent, whereas oxygen vacancies are strongly site-sensitive and become thermodynamically accessible under p -type conditions. A central finding is that charge compensation universally governs defect stabilization, dictating distinct electrostatic pathways for intrinsic versus extrinsic defects. While intrinsic antisite defects are stabilized through donor–acceptor pairing with native oxygen vacancies, extrinsic Fe dopants trigger a reversed compensation logic, pairing preferentially with native acceptors to form highly stable neutral defect clusters. Crucially, the activation of these extrinsic compensation pathways is governed by local hydration and redox conditions. This environment-dependent pathway selection controls the Fe 2 + / Fe 3 + ratio, providing an atomic-scale origin for the intervalence charge transfer and systematic color variations (from pale green to dark brown) observed in natural amphiboles. More broadly, these results establish charge compensation as a unifying principle for defect formation in complex silicates and demonstrate that transition-metal doping via intrinsic compensation networks is a more effective approach for property tuning than the manipulation of isolated intrinsic defects.

title: Decoupling 2H and 3R polymorphs in A5B19 La–Mg–Ni-based superlattice hydrogen storage alloys for enhanced cycling stability
abstract: Rare-earth–Mg–Ni-based superlattice alloys are promising anode materials for nickel–metal hydride batteries. However, the role of crystallographic polymorphs in their insufficient long-term cycling stability remains unclear due to the frequent coexistence of 2H and 3R phases. Herein, we obtain phase-pure 2H and 3R A5B19 polymorphs of La0.57Sm0.21Y0.10Mg0.12Ni3.62Al0.17 alloys via controlled annealing, respectively, and study the effect of crystallographic polymorphism on defect chemistry and subunit-level structural compatibility on electrochemical and gas-solid hydrogen storage properties. The 3R polymorph is thermodynamically stabilized at 950 °C, whereas the 2H polymorph preferentially emerges as the equilibrium polymorph at 1025 °C via recrystallization annealing. Both polymorphs show capacities exceeding 390 mAh g−1, but the 2H polymorph demonstrates superior cycling stability, with a capacity retention of 63.8% after 500 cycles, exceeding that of the 3R polymorph by 6.1%. In contrast, the 3R polymorph shows enhanced rate capability and low-temperature performance. Comprehensive microstructural and kinetic analyses reveal that the performance divergence originates from the interplay between crystallographic configuration and defect-mediated transport. The 3R polymorph, characterized by finer grains and higher defect density, facilitates faster hydrogen diffusion and charge transfer. Conversely, the 2H polymorph exhibits larger grains, lower geometrically necessary dislocation density, and more coordinated volume evolution among [A2B4], [AB5]-1, and [AB5]-2 subunits, which effectively mitigates strain accumulation and suppresses pulverization. This work highlights the critical role of subunit-level structural compatibility in governing cycling stability and provides new insights into the structure–degradation relationship in superlattice hydrogen storage alloys.

title: Atmosphere-dependence and mechanistic origin of preparation-induced martensite transformation in 17-4 PH stainless steel fabricated by laser powder bed fusion
abstract: This work resolves the observed atmosphere dependence on phase constitution in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of high-nitrogen 17-4 PH stainless steel (EOS GP1) and identifies the mechanism responsible for previously reported discrepancies. The results demonstrate that both nitrogen and argon atmospheres yield a nearly fully austenitic structure under optimal processing parameters. Microstructural differences, previously attributed to processing atmosphere, are demonstrated to arise not from processing itself, but from atmosphere-dependent susceptibility to preparation-induced martensitic transformation (PIMT). Characteristic features of PIMT-formed martensite are summarized to facilitate its recognition. A mechanistic framework is established to explain this atmosphere-dependent behavior by linking melt pool geometry, thermal history, residual stress heterogeneity to PIMT susceptibility. Finally, a distinct PIMT mechanism governed by the chemical composition is proposed, based on a review of prior studies on high-nitrogen 17-4 PH steels. Together, these findings reconcile contradictory reports in the literature and highlight the necessity of depth-resolved, multi-technique characterization when interpreting microstructures in metastable austenitic alloys processed by LPBF.

title: Dual-orientation growth enabling multiple stable interfaces in directionally solidified Gd2Zr2O7/GdAlO3 eutectic ceramics
abstract: Interfaces, including grain boundaries (GBs) and phase boundaries (PBs), govern the mechanical properties and stability of materials. It is a challenging yet feasible method for introducing them to tailor the mechanical properties of high-temperature materials. In this work, we introduced coherent GBs and multiple PBs into Gd2Zr2O7(GZO)/GdAlO3(GAP) eutectic ceramics via directional solidification. Both phases exhibited dual preferred growth orientations: [101], [010] for GAP, and [101], [001] for GZO. This results in five distinct stable interfaces, consisting of four PBs and one GB in GAP. The coherent GAP GB exhibited a near-zero volumetric strain (0%) and low strain energy (<0.05 J/m²). The four PBs showed closely matched volumetric strains (∼6.1%) and ultra-low strain energies (<0.025 J/m²). Such a balanced, low-energy state enabled the stable coexistence of all interfaces. The resulting multi-interface structure significantly enhanced the fracture toughness through extrinsic toughening mechanisms such as crack bridging, deflection, and bifurcation. This study demonstrates that low-energy interface structure design offers a promising pathway for developing advanced high-performance ceramics.

title: Systematic investigation of composition–microstructure–property relationships in the HCP Ti-Zr-Hf model system
abstract: Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP) alloys are used in structural materials applications for extreme environments such as those involving cryogenic conditions, or for nuclear cladding. However, the alloy design space explored for HCP compositionally complex alloys, namely High-Entropy or Medium-Entropy Alloys (hereafter referred to as HEAs) has been limited. Here, we propose the Ti-Zr-Hf ternary system as an ideal model for developing single-phase HCP HEAs and systematically investigate its composition-microstructure-property relationships. CALPHAD thermodynamic calculations predicted, and experimental results confirmed, that a stable single-phase HCP solid solution forms over a wide compositional range. The as-cast microstructure exhibited a systematic evolution dictated primarily by Hf content: high-Hf content alloys formed coarse dendritic structures via diffusion-dominant transformations, whereas low-Hf alloys formed fine acicular structures through diffusionless martensitic transformations. This change with Hf content is rationalized by a compositional dependence of the Continuous Cooling Transformation (CCT) kinetics. Nanoindentation revealed a strong solid-solution strengthening effect, with hardness generally increasing from 4.3 GPa in Ti-rich compositions to 5.5 GPa in high Hf-content alloys. Notably, the equiatomic TiZrHf alloy demonstrated an exceptional synergy of high yield strength (1140 MPa) and superior ductility (elongation >16%). Post-deformation analysis revealed that this is governed by the Twinning-Induced Plasticity (TWIP) effect, via the activation of {10-12} extension twins, confirmed by a characteristic misorientation angle of ∼86° across twin boundaries. Comparing alloys of contrasting c/a ratio at fixed Ti content further revealed a transition from twinning- and stacking-fault-mediated plasticity to confined planar slip, consistent with the reduced {10-12} twinning shear and enhanced slip accessibility that accompany a higher c/a ratio; the as-cast morphology, by contrast, modulates the magnitude of the work-hardening response rather than the operative deformation mode. This work establishes the Ti-Zr-Hf system as a cornerstone for developing high-performance HCP HEAs.

title: Modeling the impact of twin boundaries on the deformation of nanotwinned metals: A dislocation dynamics approach
abstract: The impact of twin boundaries (TBs) on the microstructure evolution and plastic deformation mechanisms of face-centered cubic (FCC) metals has been extensively studied since the discovery that nanotwinned materials exhibit a favorable combination of high strength and ductility. In this work, a dislocation-twin boundary interaction model for copper is incorporated into a three-dimensional discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) framework. This approach is applied to systematically investigate the orientation effects on the deformation of nanotwinned copper, utilizing a multilayer twinned structure (MTS) with a twin thickness of 160 nm. The simulation results show that the stress–strain response of MTSs under uniaxial loading depends significantly on the orientation of the loading axis. When the loading axis is perpendicular or parallel to TBs, geometric confinement constrains dislocations to slip within single- or multi-layer twin lamellae on glide planes inclined to the TBs. When the loading axis is inclined to the TBs, in contrast, the highest resolved shear stress acts on glide planes parallel to the TBs, preferentially activating twinning dislocations. These dislocations glide unimpeded, which defines the soft deformation mode. If the hard mode dominates the deformation mechanism, microstructures with a single-layer confined slip lead to significant hardening behavior, while microstructures with multilayer confined slip maintain stable plastic flow and do not lead to hardening. Finally, by incorporating dislocation-mode-specific critical resolved shear stresses — physically motivated thresholds reflecting the distinct resistance of hard mode Ⅰ, hard mode Ⅱ, and soft-mode dislocation–TB interactions — we extend Schmid’s law to predict the orientation-dependent yield stress of MTSs.

title: Simultaneous control of phase stability and crystallographic texture for low-modulus biomedical β-type Ti–Cr–Al alloys by in-situ-alloying LPBF
abstract: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) offers not only geometric freedom, but also a unique route to co-design composition-based phase stability and crystallographic texture, which are critical for realizing low-modulus Ti alloys. In this study, we fabricated Ti–Cr and Ti–Cr–Al alloys by the in situ alloying of elemental powders and programmed single-crystal-like textures (<100>, <110>, or <111> // build direction (BD)) via tailored scanning strategies. By employing processing conditions that yielded a melt pool depth far greater than the layer thickness, compositionally uniform builds were achieved through multiple remelting events. In Ti–12Cr (mass%), which has relatively low β-phase stability, the ω phase was observed despite not being detected in its solution-treated-and-quenched counterpart. This observation suggests that the LPBF-specific thermo-mechanical history, including a tensile residual stress of 353 MPa, may have contributed to ω-phase formation. The addition of Al suppressed the formation of ω, resulting in a single-phase β matrix. Furthermore, scan-strategy-dependent textures were consistently observed across all the compositions. The elastic modulus showed pronounced orientation-dependent anisotropy, reaching ∼60 GPa along <100> in a Ti–12Cr–3Al composition, whereas the BD-parallel yield strength approached 800–1,000 MPa depending on the texture, producing elastic admissible strains that surpass those of reported LPBF-fabricated Ti–6Al–4V. Based on these findings, we propose an additive manufacturing process-aware design framework in which alloy composition, LPBF-specific thermo-mechanical history, and crystallographic texture contribute collectively to phase stability and directional mechanical properties in metastable β-Ti alloys.

title: Atomistic study of grain boundary-mediated {101¯1} twinning in magnesium
abstract: The mechanisms underlying twining in hexagonal close-packed (hcp) metals are inherently complex owing to their crystallographic characteristics. In this work, we uncover a grain-boundary (GB)-mediated {101¯1} twinning mode through molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of [21¯1¯0] textured polycrystalline Mg samples. We demonstrate that two types of [21¯1¯0] tilt GBs can act as sources for {101¯1} twinning. The first is the faceted-GBs with a faceted structure featuring an intervening sequence of {101¯1} coherent twin boundary (CTB) segments and basal/pyramidal (B/Py) interfaces. The second is the dissociated-GBs containing subgrains with {101¯1} CTB segments and B/Py interfaces. The transformation of a 4-layer B/Py interface into a four-layer twinning disconnection (b4 TD) triggers this GB-mediated {101¯1} twinning. The twinning shear associated with this GB-mediated {101¯1} twin is shown to be consistent with that of compression twinning.

title: Editorial Board
An experimentally informed model of meso‑scale architecture of CeO2 hierarchical catalyst: the role of structural hierarchy of Ru-decorated Co-doped CeO2 in propane oxidation
abstract: In this study original approach for modeling of the mesoscale architecture of hierarchical catalyst has been presented. Data from TEM, HRTEM, SEM, SAED, and ET were used to inform the construction of model of texture of hierarchically structured CeO2 particle via crystallographic modelling approach. The model allowed to explain the exceptional activity of Ru/CeO2 hierarchically structured catalyst (T50= 130°C, Ea = 33 kJ/mol), and its enhanced self-regenerative action. While the architecture of CeO2 catalyst is imprinted in the crystallographic structure of the Ce(HCOO)3 catalyst precursor, the driving principle for texture formation is geometric fitting of ceria crystallites along the directions of similarity of structural motifs of both materials. Structural elements dissimilarity is behind formation of channels that allow rapid diffusion of gaseous thermolysis products that leads to development of highly porous catalyst that exposes (110) CeO2 facets inside the porous volume, which poses compromise between activity and stability. Doping hierarchical ceria by cobalt ions changes the architecture and increases activity of the catalyst but decline of activity is seen when specific texture is lost for highly doped samples. Structural hierarchy facilitates self-regenerative property of Ru-decorated CeO2 system due to fostering redispersion of Ru inside the porous volume of macroparticle during variable conditions of catalytic process. The presented approach for synthesis and modelling of hierarchically structured oxides opens possibility of knowledgeable design of materials showing synergistic properties.

title: Tailoring tensile properties of Al88Ni10MM2 metallic glass by in-situ precipitation of FCC-Al nanocrystals under controlled cooling rates
abstract: Amorphous alloys offer unique opportunities for tailoring microstructures via non-equilibrium processing; however, precise control of nanoscale crystallization during rapid solidification remains challenging without post-solidification heat treatments. Herein, we demonstrate that in-situ precipitation of FCC-Al nanocrystals in an Al 88 Ni 10 MM 2 (MM: Ce-rich misch metal) metallic glass can be effectively controlled solely by tuning the cooling rate during melt-spinning. By systematically varying the wheel speed from 40 m/s to 10 m/s, corresponding to cooling rates from 2.5 × 10⁶ K/s to 4.0 × 10⁵ K/s, we achieve a substantial increase in the number density of FCC-Al nanoprecipitates from 2.15 × 10²¹ to 1.55 × 10²² m⁻³, while maintaining a nearly constant nanocrystal size (∼5–6 nm). To elucidate the governing nucleation kinetics, nucleation delay times were quantified using flash differential scanning calorimetry and employed to construct Time-Temperature-Transformation and Continuous-Cooling-Transformation diagrams. Statistical analysis of nucleation temperatures enables direct estimation of nucleation rates under different cooling conditions, revealing that reduced cooling rates significantly enhance nucleation kinetics, leading to dense in-situ precipitation. In contrast, crystal growth remains strongly diffusion-limited under rapid solidification conditions, thereby constraining precipitate coarsening. Consequently, we establish a cooling-rate-dependent framework for decoupling nucleation and growth during melt-spinning, enabling high-density nanocrystal formation without significant size evolution. Mechanical testing, including ribbon bending and cyclic tensile experiments, confirms that such controlled in-situ nanocrystallization simultaneously enhances both tensile strength and plasticity, addressing one of the long-standing challenges in metallic glass research. This work provides a processing strategy for cooling-driven microstructural design in metallic glasses, offering a pathway to bypass conventional annealing treatments while achieving enhanced mechanical performance.

title: Covariant formula for the driving force for interface migration
abstract: Interfaces of crystalline materials are strongly affected by the anisotropy of interface energy. A key quantity in this context is the interface stiffness tensor, which characterizes the response of the interface energy to changes in interface orientation and plays a role in determining the driving force for interface migration. The latter is expressible via contraction of the stiffness tensor and interface curvature tensor. Practical computations involving tensors necessarily rely on their individual components. In this work, an explicit component-wise expression is derived for the contraction of the stiffness and curvature tensors, valid in arbitrary coordinate systems. Within this formulation, to get the driving force, the curvature tensor is contracted with the pullback of a stiffness-related tensor – originally defined in three-dimensional Euclidean space – onto the interface manifold. This covariant treatment establishes a physically consistent foundation for three-dimensional computational models involving interface stiffness.

title: Anisotropic deformation behavior of LPBF fabricated Co35Cr25Mn15Ni15Fe10 with low stacking fault energy studied by in situ neutron diffraction
abstract: Stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT, FCC→HCP) is a crucial deformation mechanism that enhances ductility in alloys with low stacking fault energy (SFE), particularly in high-entropy alloys (HEAs). In this study, a low-SFE Co₃₅Cr₂₅Mn₁₅Ni₁₅Fe₁₀ HEA was fabricated via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) to systematically investigated coupled effects of crystallographic orientation and grain size on SIMT during tensile deformation, using in situ neutron diffraction. <100>-oriented grains (D0) are found to facilitate dislocation dissociation through a higher accumulation rate of SFs during plastic deformation. In contrast, <111>-oriented grains (D45) exhibit an enhanced dislocation multiplication rate, leading to increased flow stress. However, D90, <110>-oriented grains, reveals grain size plays a more critical role in tailoring deformation mechanism than special orientation for low SFE alloy. D90 exhibits the highest phase fraction of martensitic after deformation attributed to the decreased apparent SFE by larger grain size. Anisotropic deformation mechanisms result in pronounced variations in mechanical properties: the highest ultimate tensile strength of 788 MPa is attributed to accelerated dislocation multiplication, while the SIMT activity contributes to extensive uniform plastic deformation, yielding a total elongation of 64.8%. These findings provide mechanistic insights into the deformation behavior of low‑SFE alloys and have broad implications for microstructural design—particularly through controlled orientation and grain size—toward achieving exceptional mechanical properties.

title: Quantitative characterisation of γ′ precipitation and its role in governing robust properties in the Alloy 925 material system
abstract: This work quantitatively investigates the γ′ precipitation behaviour and mechanical properties of the Alloy 925 (UNS N09925) material system to elucidate its resilience to compositional variations and aging treatments. Using advanced characterisation techniques, it is shown that both composition and aging parameters have a distinct influence on the volume fraction and size of γ′ precipitates during production-relevant heat treatments, including one-step aging at 720–760°C and subsequent second aging steps at 621–635°C. Quantitative analysis of the γ′ volume fraction, implementing a novel analysis procedure for high-energy X-ray diffraction data proposed in this work, shows that minor changes to the Ti and Al contents result in changes of up to 2 vol.% in the γ′ phase during aging. In addition, the introduction of a second aging step at lower temperatures increases the γ′ fraction by approximately 2.5 vol.%. Small-angle X-ray scattering captures not only the progressive coarsening with increasing temperature and time during one- and two-step aging, resulting in precipitate diameters ranging from 4 to 22 nm, but also the compositional effect on precipitate size. The experimentally obtained quantitative data for the γ′ precipitates allow the prediction of the yield strength increase associated with precipitation strengthening as well as the validation of precipitation kinetics modelling. Comparison with the results of hardness measurements reveals a strong correlation between the γ′ precipitation behaviour and the mechanical properties due to order-type strengthening associated with the weakly coupled dislocations mechanism.

title: Tailoring ionic conductivity in argyrodite-type solid electrolytes via simultaneous P5+/Sn4+ and S2-/I- substitutions
abstract: This work reports, for the first time, the synthesis and single crystals growth of new cubic solid solutions based on argyrodites Ag6PS5I and Ag7.23SnS5.44I0.50. The samples were obtained by directional crystallization from a melt-solution, which allowed for the production of compositionally homogeneous crystals free of impurity phases with the space group F-43 m. The structural features of the heterovalent double-ion substitution P5+ ↔ Sn4+ and S2- ↔ I- were investigated. It was established that cation transport is caused by the diffusion of silver ions along cation sublattice channels through Ag2 sites. Using impedance spectroscopy, the frequency and temperature dependencies of the ionic and electronic components of electrical conductivity were determined. It was found that an increase in the Sn content causes a sharp increase in ionic conductivity followed by a linear increase at room temperature from 2.11 × 10–2 S/cm (x = 0.25) to 4.16 × 10–2 S/cm (x = 0.75). This behavior of ion transport parameters is explained in detail in terms of the distortion of the [AgS3(S(I))] coordination tetrahedra and [AgS3] pyramids, which weakens the Ag-S and Ag-I bonds. The values of electronic conductivity at 25 °C vary within the range of ∼ 9.4 × 10–7 S/cm (x = 0.25) to 2.44 × 10–5 S/cm (x = 0.5).

title: Planar antisite defect-engineered domain structures in BiFeO3 thin films
abstract: Defects in ferroelectric materials profoundly dictate domain configurations and polarization characteristics, yet the deterministic correlation between long-range ordered defect architectures and the resulting polarization topology remains underexplored. In this study, we introduced long-range ordered planar antisite defects into epitaxial BiFeO3 (BFO) thin films. Atomic-scale observations reveal that these defects act as effective positive charge centers, generating localized electric fields that drive polarization rearrangement into unconventional tail-to-tail configurations. The localized rearrangement further triggers a large-scale redistribution of the domain structure throughout the film. Oxygen-sublattice imaging by 4D-STEM ptychography further supports the presence of oxygen vacancies at the defect core. First-principles calculations confirm that the electronic influence of these defects is highly localized. Furthermore, film-substrate lattice mismatch modulates the defect arrangement: high compressive strain (on DyScO3) promotes in-plane ordering, whereas reduced strain (on TbScO3) favors a transition to out-of-plane ordering as the film thickness increases. This work elucidates the role of long-range ordered defects in regulating ferroelectric properties and provides insights for defect-engineering strategies to tailor functional properties.

title: High crack propagation resistance of polysynthetic twinned TiAl single crystals induced by delamination cracks
abstract: Polysynthetic twinned (PST) TiAl single crystals exhibit exceptional potential for application in aero-engine blades, making the investigation of their fracture behavior highly essential. Here, the crack propagation behaviors and fracture mechanisms of PST TiAl single crystals are systematically investigated from room temperature to 900 ℃ for the first time. The results show that fracture toughness exhibits significant orientation dependence: 0°-Type II＞0°-Type I＞45°＞90°. For 0°-Type II specimens, the improved fracture resistance is primarily attributed to the activation of delamination toughening. Delamination toughening associated with cracking at γ/α2 interfaces normal to the primary fracture surface, which dramatically improves overall fracture resistance. During delamination, numerous new interfaces are created that consume energy. This effectively increases the energy release rate and contributes to the exceptional fracture toughness. Meanwhile, the TWIP effect makes the deformation of the lamellar bundles more uniform, preventing rapid fracture from local necking, and enhancing the resistance to crack propagation. In 0°-Type I specimens, the lamellar interface hinders crack growth, causing the path to deflect repeatedly. Additionally, the TWIP effect appears at the crack tip, blunting it and increasing the crack propagation resistance. For the 45° specimens, the crack propagation mode transitions from Mode I to a mixed Mode I/II. The crack shifts from the divider direction to propagate along the lamellar plane, leading to relatively low crack propagation resistance. In 90° specimens, the crack plane is parallel to the lamellar planes, allowing cracks to propagate rapidly and resulting in the weakest crack-propagation resistance.

title: Concentration-dependent suppression of thermal anisotropy in 4H-SiC by nitrogen doping
abstract: Nitrogen (N) doping is a standard and well-established strategy for achieving n-type conductivity in 4H-silicon carbide (SiC), which has enabled extensive use in power electronic devices and other emerging applications. However, the effect of N doping on thermal transport properties, especially the anisotropy behavior governing electronic devices cooling, remains poorly understood. In this work, a unified neural network potential (NNP) is developed to elucidate the atomistic origins of concentration-dependent thermal conductivity (к) anisotropy behavior in N-doped SiC. The simulation results indicate that N doping markedly suppresses the anisotropy of к. At the microscopic level, strong phonon localization and polarization disorder induced by doping atoms enhance phonon scattering and shorten phonon relaxation times. Different from the predominantly in-plane polarization of low-frequency phonons in pristine SiC, N doping enhances out-of-plane polarization components and reduces the anisotropy of к. The in-depth microscopic understanding of N doping modulated thermal transport in 4H-SiC provides significant insight into the thermal management of n-type SiC electronic devices.

title: Self-pinning and Self-climbing of skyrmion dislocations through topological characterization: Lattice mechanics of deformable quasiparticles
abstract: Skyrmions are emergent quasiparticles in ferromagnets possessing topologically identified unique dynamics, stability, and deformability. They self-assemble into skyrmion lattices whose collective behaviors are central to both fundamental understandings and spintronics applications. However, in contrast to atomic crystals, the lattice mechanics in skyrmion lattices, where lattice defect dynamics mediate macroscopic deformations, remain elusive. Here, we revealed unconventional defect dynamics in skyrmion lattices, including self-pinning and self-climbing of dislocations accompanied by large skyrmion deformations with topologically protected transitions from a single skyrmion to half-skyrmions. Our phase-field simulations demonstrate that external field dependent skyrmion deformability fundamentally alters lattice defect behaviors from conventional atom-like dislocation glide to the phenomena unique to topological quasiparticles. These behaviors are successfully revealed by topological characterization and described by strain analysis. This study not only provides critical insight into spintronics engineering for skyrmion-based devices but also establishes a foundation for a new class of mechanics, “quasiparticle lattice mechanics”.

title: Integrated molecular dynamics modelling of the full electron beam physical vapor deposition process chain in nickel thin films
abstract: ABSTRACT Electron Beam Physical Vapor Deposition (EB-PVD) is a critical technique for high-performance coatings, but modeling its full non-equilibrium process chain, i.e., from source evaporation to film evolution, remains a significant challenge. This study presents a comprehensive, integrated Molecular Dynamics (MD) framework that simulates the entire non-equilibrium EB-PVD process for nickel thin films, in which vapor composition, atomic configuration, velocity, incidence angle, and atomic flux obtained from open-boundary evaporation are directly transferred to the deposition model. The emitted vapor is predominantly monomeric, while larger clusters form during subsequent gas-phase transport. Vapor density primarily governs collision and aggregation, whereas vapor temperature controls cluster coarsening and persistence. During deposition, film morphology shifts from cluster-size controlled to substrate-controlled regimes: roughness increases with cluster size on smooth surfaces while this sensitivity is substantially reduced on rough substrates. This work provides critical atomic-level predictive insights for microstructural engineering and performance optimization in EB-PVD systems.

title: Insights into the mechanism of kink band formation: Case study on an additively manufactured BCC Ti-9V-3.5Al-5Sn-3Zr-2.5Mo-0.2O alloy
abstract: Slip localization, leading to planar slip bands in many high-strength engineering alloys, often results in deleterious effects, such as shear band formation, limited ductility, and premature failure. Such premature failure in body-centered cubic (BCC) alloys has been reported to be obviated by the formation of kink bands, which tend to enhance ductility and toughness. Examples of such systems include metastable β-titanium alloys, Nb-based alloys, and Nb-Hf-based refractory high-entropy alloys. While observations of such kink bands are extensive in the published literature, there is a poor understanding of their formation mechanism, especially in the early stages. The present study delves into the mechanistic details of kink band formation during tensile deformation of an additively processed metastable β Ti-9V-3.5Al-5Sn-3Zr-2.5Mo-0.2O (wt. %) (ATI Titan 23™) alloy. Dislocation slip mediated {112} and {110} planar slip bands form. Subsequent interactions between slip bands, or between slip bands and grain boundaries, lead to progressive lattice rotation, eventually resulting in kink band formation. These details have been correlatively characterized by combining electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The interplay between slip localization into planar slip bands and subsequent interaction between non-parallel slip bands forming kink bands leads to local hardening, resulting in exceptional tensile fracture strains exceeding 30% at yield strengths greater than 750 MPa, in the as-built metastable β ATI Titan 23™ alloy, without necessitating any post-processing such as hot isostatic pressing.

title: Ferroelectric domain-wall dynamics in point-defects elastic fields: A phase-field study
abstract: Domain walls (DWs) in ferroelectrics introduce distinct electrostatic and elastic features into an otherwise single-domain state, and their electric field–driven dynamics significantly influence device performance. Lattice defects are ubiquitous in materials and strongly interact with DWs; however, their effects remain complex and are not yet fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that specific strain components induced by point defects govern the fundamental DW dynamics. A systematic examination of individual strain tensor components using a phase-field framework enables the construction of DW energy landscapes in the presence of defects, providing a unified description of DW stability and mobility. Furthermore, the spatial variation in the simulated DW velocity is explained by the gradient of the defect-induced energy landscape, and the threshold electric field associated with defect pinning is estimated from the maximum pinning force acting on the DW.
