Additionally, we demonstrate that the relationship between the energy landscape and the threshold electric field can be approximated using the stress distributions near the defect and the DW. This study provides fundamental insights into the role of lattice defects and establishes a systematic framework for understanding defect-affected DW dynamics.

title: Stress partitioning, variant selection, and anisotropic elastic response during martensitic transformation in Fe–Ni–C alloy under constant tensile stress
abstract: Determining how the anisotropic transformation strain of martensite affects internal stress redistribution under external loading has long been a challenge in experimental research, due to the difficulty in distinguishing between the a-axis and c-axis of martensite. Here, by employing in situ neutron diffraction during cryogenic cooling under a constant tensile stress, we successfully resolve the crystallographic orientation-dependent lattice strain responses of martensite variants in an Fe-24Ni-0.3C (wt.%) alloy. Remarkably, we find a striking dichotomy: under a 120 MPa tensile stress, variants with the c-axis (the Bain compression axis) aligned close to the loading direction (LD), specifically, 〈001〉α'//LD and 〈101〉α'//LD grains, exhibit a substantial increase in interplanar spacing compared to the non-loaded reference. In contrast, variants with the c-axis perpendicular to LD, such as 〈100〉α'//LD and 〈110〉α'//LD grains, show almost no change. This provides direct evidence that the external tensile stress is preferentially accommodated by specific variants according to their transformation eigenstrain components. The resulting internal elastic energy difference further increases the total driving force disparity among variants, thereby promoting variant selection beyond what would be expected from the Patel–Cohen criterion alone. With the externally applied tensile stress increasing, the variant selection became more pronounced, ultimately leading to the disappearance of tetragonality‑related peak splitting in the diffraction patterns of deformation-induced martensite. These findings not only reveal a previously unreported anisotropic elastic response of martensite but also establish a clear causal link between the crystallographic orientation of variants and their stress-partitioning behavior during the transformation.

title: Modelling thermal expansion of pure metals and steels
abstract: A new approach is proposed for modelling thermal expansion based on a modified Bose–Einstein (BE) distribution function in which the phonon population n* depends on a temperature-dependent phonon frequency ω*. The corresponding characteristic temperature θ* (θ* = ħω*/kB) is assumed to decrease exponentially with temperature, thereby accounting for intrinsic anharmonicity. Since both the phonon population n* and the lattice volume V are governed by the asymmetric interatomic potential, the variation of n* with θ* is assumed to be correlated with the temperature dependence of V. Accordingly, the change of V with temperature T, expressed by the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE), is assumed to scale with the variation of n* with θ*, such that the CTE is proportional to the derivative of n* with respect to θ*. The resulting three-parameter model, which also incorporates electronic and magnetic contributions, is validated using experimental data for 21 elements from groups 4 to 11 of the periodic table. All datasets are reproduced with satisfactory accuracy. Analysis of the fitting results shows that, for elements belonging to the same group and sharing the same crystal structure, one model parameter can be treated as constant, while another parameter is demonstrated to correlate with the Einstein temperature. The model further provides an accurate description of the thermal expansion behaviour of cementite, C–Mn steels, and both ferritic and austenitic stainless steels.

title: Irradiation-driven recrystallization in fusion-grade tungsten: A mesoscale, microstructure-aware model
abstract: Tungsten (W) is the leading candidate material for plasma-facing components in fusion reactors. However, its upper operational temperature is limited by premature grain coarsening due to recrystallization processes. Irradiation adds further complexity to the process by generating defect clusters and transmutation products that alter the driving forces and kinetics of grain boundary motion. Designing W alloys with better high-temperature resistance is a necessity for the further development of advanced fusion energy devices. However, the challenges associated with understanding all the physical processes that take part in recrystallization under irradiation, plus the poor general reproducibility of W microstructures with sufficient fracture toughness, makes this an extremely difficult task. In this work, we develop a physics-based, mesoscale framework that couples crystal plasticity, stochastic cluster dynamics, and discrete grain boundary dynamics to model the co-evolution of plastic deformation, irradiation damage, and grain evolution in fusion-grade tungsten polycrystals. The approach enables simulations on realistic microstructures with arbitrary grain size and misorientation distributions, without recourse to mean-field simplifications. The model captures (i) the spatial heterogeneity of dislocation density distribution during hot working; (ii) irradiation-induced defect accumulation under fusion conditions, and (iii) the buildup of chemical and elastic driving forces for grain boundary migration and microstructural evolution. Our simulations reveal an incubation period followed by rapid irradiation-assisted recrystallization characterized by Avrami exponents close to unity, which are consistent with experimental observations. Parametric studies demonstrate the dominant influence that temperature has on thermally activated grain-boundary mobility, a weak dependence on plastic strain, and a pronounced retardation of recrystallization by rhenium segregation arising from neutron transmutation. Under fusion energy irradiation conditions, our framework predicts a substantial reduction in the effective recrystallization temperature relative to unirradiated microstructures. However, within the current modeling framework, the incorporation of transmuted Re counteracts this drop and may even elevate the thermal limit by increasing the activation energy for grain boundary migration. By providing quantitative projections of recrystallization kinetics and in-service recrystallization temperatures, this work demonstrates the potential of integrated mesoscale tools to assess the lifetime and operational envelope of W-based plasma-facing materials under fusion conditions.

title: Double-peak age strengthening of magnetostriction in heterogeneous Fe-Ga alloy
abstract: Artificial aging is a powerful approach to strengthen most structural alloys owing to the precipitation of mechanically harder particles, and a large portion of structural alloys exhibit a “harder-to-softer-to-harder” transition when extending the aging time, an effect known as “double-peak age strengthening”. Beyond this, here we report a “double-peak age strengthening” effect of functional properties—magnetostriction (magnetic-field-induced elastic strain), well corresponding to two successive microhardness softening states, as exhibited in a proof-of-principle reference Fe73Ga27 alloy. During the isothermal aging process, the body-centered-cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution undergoes concurrent ordering of the matrix and successive precipitations of Ga-depleted tetragonal L60 and Ga-enriched ω/M (ω is a hexagonal phase; M is a monoclinic Fe13Ga9-type phase) nanoparticles with extending aging time. The first magnetostriction peak arises from the nucleation of coherent L60 nanoprecipitates, following which the magnetostriction drops due to the formation of ω nanoprecipitates as well as the phase-transition-induced dislocations. The second peak appears when the coherent M nanoparticles precipitate and the phase-transition-induced dislocations are reduced, prior to the formation of incoherent L60/L12 phases. Upon reaching these two critical conditions, the saturation magnetostriction is nearly 3 times higher than that of the solution-treated counterpart. Such double-peak age strengthening effect of magnetostriction was observed at a metastable phase-transition state, which may provide more freedom for tuning the functional properties of heterogeneous alloys.

title: High-temperature EBSD reveals the link between ferroelastic switching, martensitic transformation, and lattice correspondences in zirconia ceramics
abstract: Three different lattice correspondences have been reported in the martensitic transformation from tetragonal to monoclinic phases in zirconia ceramics. Each of these transformation pathways implies a different amount of strain in the transformation, which points to a conflict between experimental data (which shows all three) and the usual criteria for correspondence selection (which predicts only one, that having the minimum atom displacement or minimum interfacial strain). This work provides primary experimental evidence supporting recent computational results that point to correspondence C as the unique pathway between austenite and martensite phases in zirconia. We achieve these results by high-temperature EBSD experiments, which point to ferroelastic switching of the tetragonal phase as a necessary intermediate step allowing the formation of martensite that appear as belonging to correspondences A or B. These variants are in fact the result of a two-step process involving re-orientation of the parent phase in combination with martensitic transformation through lattice correspondence C and can only be observed if ferroelastic switching is an active mechanism.

title: Beyond averaging: δH, a chemical heterogeneity descriptor for single-phase formation prediction in multicomponent alloys
abstract: A new dimensionless descriptor for single-phase microstructure prediction in multicomponent alloys (MCA) and high-entropy alloys (HEA) is proposed: the normalised dispersion of binary mixing enthalpies, δ H . This descriptor quantifies the internal heterogeneity of chemical interactions among constituent element pairs —a contribution that classical descriptors do not capture, as they rely on weighted averages that mask the coexistence of strongly attractive and repulsive pairs. Combined with the atomic size mismatch parameter δ , the pair δ H – δ significantly outperforms the Ω – δ reference criterion established by Yang and Zhang (2012), with an improvement of +3.16 percentage points in cross-validated accuracy (83.16% vs 80.00%) and +0.063 in the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (0.663 vs 0.600), validated on an experimental dataset of 1675 alloys from three independent sources spanning binary to nonary compositions (McNemar test, p = 0.006). Although δ H and δ are moderately correlated at the global level (Spearman ρ = 0.27), partly because both tend to increase with compositional complexity, the significant improvement of δ H – δ over any univariate classifier confirms that δ H contributes predictive information that δ alone does not capture. The critical threshold δ H ≤ 1.1 has a direct physical interpretation: the solid solution is stable when the heterogeneity of binary chemical interactions does not exceed 1.1 times the mean thermal energy available at the solidification temperature.

title: Corrigendum to “Intra-regional strain partitioning within initial austenite regions in medium Mn steels” [Acta Materialia 319 (2026) 122658]
Effect of Al on microstructural evolution and hot corrosion behavior of AlxCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy coatings fabricated using laser directed energy deposition
abstract: High-temperature chlorine- and sulfate-containing environments, such as those encountered in waste incineration and chemical processing, cause severe degradation on structural alloys through the coupled action of molten-salt attack and active oxidation. Here, the hot-corrosion behavior of 304 stainless steel coated with AlxCoCrFeNi2.1 (x = 1.0–1.8) high-entropy alloy (HEA) using the laser directed energy deposition (L-DED) technique in a 75 wt.% KCl–25 wt.% Na2SO4 molten salt at 650°C for up to 168 h was investigated. Increasing the Al content progressively transforms the coating’s as-deposited microstructure from an FCC-dominated dendritic structure with BCC interdendritic regions to a nearly single-BCC constitution, accompanied by a columnar-to-equiaxed grain transition associated with enhanced constitutional undercooling. Results show that the hot-corrosion resistance varies non-monotonically with the Al content, first deteriorating and then improving markedly. The BCC-dominated Al1.8 exhibits the lowest mass gain, with single-stage near-parabolic kinetics, whereas those with lower Al show near-linear, two-stage kinetics that are indicative of progressive scale breakdown. The improved resistance of Al1.8 originates from a coupled stabilization mechanism. At the surface, high Al content promotes a compact Al2O3-dominant scale that resists chloride-induced degradation and maintains its protective integrity during the mixed-salt exposure. At subsurface, stable single-BCC microstructure minimizes FCC/BCC interphase-boundary diffusion pathways and suppresses selective internal corrosion. Nevertheless, intermediate-Al coatings that are also BCC-dominated in the as-deposited state undergo FCC re-precipitation during exposure at 650°C, consistent with the calculated phase stability at this temperature. The resulting FCC/BCC heterogeneity promotes degradation pathways similar to those observed in inherently dual-phase coatings. These findings highlight that phase type alone does not determine hot-corrosion resistance. Surface-scale chemistry and service-temperature phase stability must be considered concurrently when designing HEA coatings for extreme environments.

title: Why does Re anti-segregate from the grain boundaries in Ni?
abstract: Abstract In virtually every polycrystalline material with more than one elemental constituent, grain boundaries (GBs) offer preferential sites for minority elements to occupy; the phenomenon of GB segregation is ubiquitous. Here, in stark contrast, we report a rare observation of “antisegregation” in a clean binary alloy of Ni-Re. In addition to being unusual, this observation also runs counter to prior density functional theory predictions, which suggest that rhenium should segregate to GBs in Ni. From first principles, we demonstrate that this discrepancy originates from a magnetic effect. Whereas the zero-Kelvin calculations that are typical for assessing GB segregation energies are appropriate for the low-temperature, ferromagnetic state of Ni, GB segregation is a high temperature phenomenon where the system is paramagnetic instead. This magnetic change turns out to flip the sign of the segregation tendency on average, and indeed predicts GB solvent enrichment, rather than typical solute enrichment. With a multiscale, quantum-accurate model, we apply machine learning methods to address the full, complex case of a polycrystalline system. The analysis shows that when this magnetic effect is accounted for, the experimental antisegregation is quantitatively predicted with accuracy. Our findings call for a broader focus on magnetic disorder as a critical factor in GB segregation science and high-temperature alloy design.

title: Pressure-induced local structural heterogeneity in a metallic glass
abstract: Heterogeneity is an intrinsic hallmark of glasses, inherited from supercooled liquid fluctuations and dictating their relaxation dynamics, thermodynamic stability, and phase transformation behavior. How atomic-scale heterogeneity of disordered glasses responds to non-thermal external perturbations, however, remains poorly understood. Here, using diamond anvil cell high-pressure processing combined with ex-situ flash differential scanning calorimetry and in situ high-pressure pair distribution function (PDF) measurements, we demonstrate that room-temperature high-pressure compression enhances local heterogeneity by "frustrating" the disordered short-range atomic configurations in an Au-based metallic glass, contrasting with the prevailing expectation of pressure-induced homogenization. PDF analysis reveals pronounced disordering signatures of local structure above ∼20 GPa. In recovered glass samples, the irreversible structural disordering causes a significant broadening of β-relaxation spectra and accelerated crystallization kinetics, while the glass transition temperature remains nearly unchanged. These results establish high pressure as a motif-selective thermodynamic tool, rather than a global, structure-averaging field, to tune the potential energy landscape and widen the local activation-barrier spectrum in kinetically frozen glass state without requiring thermal activation or long-range diffusion.

title: Development of a Zr-based bulk metallic glass with excellent industrial producibility and high fracture toughness
abstract: Bulk metallic glasses with superior mechanical properties represent a class of advanced engineering materials. However, most metallic glasses developed in the laboratory exhibit poor industrial producibility, as well as low fracture toughness or ductility under industrial conditions. In this study, we successfully developed a new Zr-based bulk metallic glass ((Zr58Ti2Cu16Ni12Nb2Al10) Y0.2) combining excellent industrial producibility and high fracture toughness via the thermodynamic-guided multi-element engineering strategy. The Zr-based alloy can achieve a fully amorphous structure in 15 mm-diameter rods via high-vacuum suction casting and 3.5 mm-thick plates via industrial die casting, which outperforms the current commercial Zr-based bulk metallic glasses such as Vit-106 (an amorphous dimension of 2.5 mm thickness for industrial die casting). Meanwhile, the suction-casting glass sample exhibits a fracture toughness up to 139 MPa·m1/2, together with an impact toughness of as high as 14.75 J/cm2, a large compressive plasticity of 19.5%, exceeding all previously reported beryllium-free Zr-based bulk metallic glasses. Furthermore, a fracture toughness of up to 60 MPa·m1/2 is achieved in the industrial die-casting sample, and is about 50% higher than that of commercial Vit-106 bulk metallic glasses (∼40 MPa·m1/2). Finally, we demonstrated the potential of industrial applications of the bulk metallic glass by fabricating a variety of defect-free components with complex shapes, such as hinges of foldable phones and flexsplines of harmonic gear drives.

title: Grain boundary stability dictates the rate-limiting deformation process in nanocrystalline metals
abstract: Nanocrystalline metals can exhibit both dislocation-mediated and grain boundary (GB)-mediated plasticity, making it difficult to identify the rate-controlling unit process. Here, we vary GB structural stability in Ni- and Pt-based films through deposition route and alloying, and determine the governing deformation mechanisms by coupling transient activation-parameter measurements with simultaneous in situ transmission electron microscopy observations. Despite having comparable mean grain sizes, the films with different nonequilibrium GB states separate into two reproducible mechanical regimes. In the grain-coarsening regime, rapid stress-assisted grain growth influences the plastic flow rate, and the measured activation volume is small (∼4-5 b ³ in Ni and 3-4 b ³ in Pt). In the stable-grain regime, the plastic flow rate is controlled primarily by dislocation activity, and the measured activation volume is larger (∼7-12 b ³ in Ni and 6-10 b 3 in Pt 90 Au 10 ). The measured activation volumes for the stable-grain condition agree quantitatively with atomistic predictions for GB dislocation nucleation, whereas the smaller values measured during grain coarsening are attributed to diffusion-assisted GB motion. These results show that, in addition to grain size, GB structural stability is a key variable influencing which localized process controls plastic flow in nanocrystalline face-centered cubic metals.

title: Revealing the effects of dealloying on hydrogen evolution reaction catalysis by distribution of relaxation times analysis
abstract: Dealloying is an efficient method to improve the electrochemical catalytic activity of alloys and intermetallics. During dealloying, the formation of nanopores is combined with the changes of the alloy composition, element chemical states, etc. All of these developments may improve the catalytic activity of the materials. Though several mechanisms have been proposed, it remains unknown which mechanism plays the most important role for a given reaction. As a consequence, it is difficult to design a nanoporous metal with both an ideal porous structure and the optimal chemical composition. Herein, we use the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy coupled with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis to reveal the dominant role that dealloying plays in catalyzing the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). It was found that dealloying the Ni70Cu30 alloy resulted in the formation of nanoporous D-Ni70Cu30 with high HER catalytic activity. Low HER overpotential (55 mV at 10 mA⋅cm−2, 163 mV at 100 mA⋅cm−2) and a low Tafel slope (44 mV⋅dec−1) were obtained on D-Ni70Cu30. The DRT analysis showed that dealloying played different roles when the applied potential varied. At low potential, dealloying improved the HER by enhancing the intrinsic catalytic activity of the alloys, while at high potential, dealloying improved the HER kinetics by providing more active sites.

title: Frank-type stacking faults in 4H-SiC: A unified crystallographic, thermodynamic, electronic, and optical framework
abstract: Frank-type stacking faults (FSFs) are among the most important extended defects in 4H-SiC, yet their crystallographic classification, transformation mechanisms, electronic structures, and optical properties remain incompletely understood. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation of FSFs in 4H-SiC through the integration of high-angle annular dark-field high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF HR-STEM), photoluminescence (PL) mapping and spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. By rigorously applying Frank’s original crystallographic definition, we resolve long-standing ambiguities in the intrinsic/extrinsic classification of FSFs and demonstrate that the widely discussed (3,2) FSF is intrinsically classified despite involving an insertion-mediated formation process. Direct atomic-scale observations further reveal structural connectivity among the standard (5,2), (4,2), and (4,1) FSFs, providing experimental support for one possible crystallographic evolution pathway linking these faults. Investigations of non-standard FSFs show that identical Zhdanov notations can correspond to either intrinsic or extrinsic fault configurations depending on their crystallographic topology. DFT calculations establish, for the first time, comprehensive stacking-fault energies and electronic band structures for both standard and non-standard FSFs. While most FSFs exhibit conventional 3C-like quantum-well states, the (1,1) and (2,1) FSFs display distinct 2H-like electronic characteristics associated with dominant K-point split-off states. Finally, direct HR-STEM/PL correlation and first-principles calculations identify the characteristic PL emission wavelength of the standard (4,1) FSF as 459 nm, demonstrating that the long-accepted 424 nm assignment is inconsistent with both experimental and theoretical evidence. These results establish a unified crystallographic, thermodynamic, electronic, and optical framework for FSFs in 4H-SiC.

title: The thermodynamic and crystallographic origins of hysteresis in NiTi–Nb shape memory alloys
abstract: Achieving wide thermal hysteresis in NiTi-based shape memory alloys is critical for coupling and sealing applications. Yet, the physical mechanisms governing this behaviour in NiTi–Nb remain disputed, which has limited the application of predictive design principles to wide-hysteresis alloys. In this study, a systematic series of NiTi–Nb alloys were investigated using differential scanning calorimetry and in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction to separate the effects of microstructure and crystallography. Crucially, this study demonstrates that the characteristic hysteresis widening is not driven by the presence of β -Nb phase. Instead, a synergistic thermodynamic mechanism is identified, whereby Nb additions decouple the transformation temperature from crystallographic compatibility. Unlike binary NiTi, where lowering the transformation temperature naturally improves compatibility, Nb additions maintain a large lattice incompatibility even as the martensite start temperature is suppressed to low levels. At these low temperatures, the transformation entropy is intrinsically low; consequently, the system requires a significantly larger undercooling to generate the necessary driving force to overcome the strain energy barrier, resulting in a larger thermal hysteresis width. Additionally, Nb was found to enhance phase homogeneity and suppress intermediate R-phase formation. These findings provide a new, physically grounded criterion for the design of wide-hysteresis shape memory alloys.

title: High-throughput screening of oxidation kinetics in a combinatorial library of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr(-Al)-based superalloys
abstract: A combinatorial library of one hundred Ni-Co-Fe-Cr(-Al)-based superalloys is synthesized from blends of four basis alloys via powder-blown directed energy deposition: Ni-based INCONEL® 625, Co-based HAYNES® 25, Fe-based stainless steel 316L, and a commercial Ni–Co–Cr–Al–Y bond coat. One hundred total alloys across four monolithic 5×5 alloy arrays are each oxidized in air at 870 or 950 °C for up to 9 days. Oxide scales are characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) to quantify phase fractions and infer growth kinetics. Parallelized alloy fabrication and oxidation enable semi-automated XRD measurement and pattern refinement, accelerating characterization by ∼5× relative to serial mass gain or cross-section thickness measurements. This scalable experimental framework screens a large quaternary composition space using a logarithmic-growth kinetic constant, K0, as a quantitative metric for oxide scale evolution. XRD-derived K0 shows good agreement with a traditional cross-section approach; correlations between K0 and composition also reproduce established oxidation trends in superalloys. At 950 °C, Al additions reduce K0 and oxide scale thickness (after 9 days) by up to an order of magnitude. The transition between Type II and Type III oxidation occurs at ∼5 at. % Al, and a total concentration of Al + Cr ≥ 29 at. % is recommended for alumina-forming superalloy coatings. A Gaussian process regression (GPR) surrogate model is constructed to predict oxidation-resistant compositions, identifying an optimized alloy candidate near binary IN625 + 40 wt. % Ni–Co–Cr–Al–Y; corresponding to an overall composition of Ni–20Cr–9Co–5Al–5Mo–3Fe–2Nb (wt. %).

title: Multiscale insights into the important roles of grain orientation and boundary in hydrogen embrittlement of a Ni-based bicrystal superalloy
abstract: Hydrogen embrittlement of a Ni-based bicrystal superalloy was investigated across multiple scales to elucidate the important roles of grain orientation and grain boundary (GB). Slow strain rate tensile testing combined with multiscale characterization reveals a pronounced orientation dependence of hydrogen trapping behaviour and hydrogen-induced fracture evolution. The [001] orientation exhibits higher hydrogen uptake with a relatively dispersed distribution, whereas the [012] orientation shows a lower hydrogen content but stronger segregation at the γ/γ′ interfaces. The GB serves as an additional hydrogen trapping site and represents the most hydrogen-enriched region. Correspondingly, for the [001] orientation, the initial damage is governed primarily by hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity (HELP), whereas hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE) mainly contributes to crack opening and propagation at later stages. For the [012] orientation, preferential interfacial hydrogen segregation promotes the decohesion of γ/γ′ interfaces and Mode I brittle cracking dominated by HEDE, whereas HELP mainly contributes to subsequent crack propagation. Notably, preferential slip activity in the [001]-oriented grain continuously transports hydrogen towards the GB, where hydrogen re-enrichment, dislocation pile-up, and local stress concentration synergistically accelerate intergranular fracture. Overall, hydrogen embrittlement in this alloy system is governed by the interplay of crystallographic orientation, interfacial characteristics, and deformation-induced hydrogen redistribution, rather than by the total hydrogen content alone.

title: Cryogenic plasticity enhancement of additively manufactured refractory high-entropy alloys via dislocation junctions
abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are promising for structural applications in extreme environments. However, their cryogenic deployment has been fundamentally constrained by reduced plasticity that results from insufficient dislocation multiplication and severe strain localization. Here, we report an additively manufactured (AMed) Nb40Ta25Ti15Hf15Zr5 RHEA produced via in-situ multi-metal alloying laser-directed energy deposition (LDED) without any post-processing. This alloy exhibits a fracture elongation of 20.5 ± 0.4 % at -196 °C, representing a 3% improvement over its conventionally recrystallized counterpart. It is found that the complex thermal cycling of AM introduces high-density dislocations and multijunctions within the alloy. These pre-existing dislocation configurations create an inherent multi-slip environment and lower the energy barrier for forming multijunction networks under the low activity of screw dislocations at cryogenic temperatures. From the initial stage of deformation at -196 °C, the multijunction networks form throughout the matrix, acting as dynamic sources for dislocation multiplication via debris-mediated mechanisms and enabling sustained planar slip, which significantly enhances the cryogenic deformability of the alloy. This work presents a cost-effective pathway for designing AMed RHEAs with exceptional cryogenic strength-ductility synergy, paving the way for next-generation structural materials tailored for extreme environments.

title: Strength retention induced by thermally stable nanoprecipitates in an additively manufactured Al-Fe-Cr-Sc-Zr alloy after long-term exposure at 400 °C
abstract: Heat-resistant aluminum (Al) alloys that are additively manufactured (AM) using the powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB) technique hold promise for elevated temperature (up to 400 °C) lightweight structural applications. However, upon long-term thermal exposure, they often suffer marked strength degradation due to precipitate coarsening via the Ostwald ripening mechanism. This work focuses on a PBF‑LB Al-Fe-Cr-Sc-Zr alloy, which retains ∼60% of its yield strength after 400 °C/200 h exposure, and presents a detailed investigation of its microstructural evolution and the mechanisms behind such retention. Results show that thermal stability is governed by the grain structure, coherent L12 particles, and Fe/Cr-rich precipitates. In particular, the unique elemental interfacial segregation in a Sc/Zr-modified θ′ composite precipitate, featuring an Fe-rich core encapsulated by Sc/Zr-segregated layers and Cr-rich terminal regions, inhibits atomic diffusion and precipitation coarsening, which, in turn, preserves strength against the Oswald ripening-induced softening. Positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy is conducted to elucidate the vacancy-mediated formation of such θ′ composite precipitates during the long-term thermal exposure.

title: Defect-mediated mechanisms of deformation-induced martensitic phase transformations in structural alloys: application to austenitic stainless steel
abstract: Deformation-induced martensitic transformations are a common feature of workhorse and advanced structural alloys, such as 300-series austenitic stainless steels, transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) steels, and emerging high-entropy alloys. Despite many decades of study, the fundamental mechanisms by which these transformations proceed have been elusive. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations combined with line defect analysis to reveal the mechanisms underlying two exemplar martensitic transformations in a 300-series-like steel: a reversion transformation from HCP ε-martensite to FCC γ-austenite and a transformation into BCC α’-austenite. Both transformations were observed to occur at twin and ε-martensite slip band intersections, in agreement with microscopy observations reported in the literature. Contrary to prevailing theories, we found that both transformations proceeded via nucleation and expansion of line defect loops (partial dislocations and disconnections) in the primary slip band. Using atomistic analysis tools, the precise Burgers vectors and line defect morphologies responsible for the transformation were characterized and correlated with nucleation and propagation of the martensitic phases. Our findings provide a pathway towards predictive models of martensitic transformations useful for alloy design and engineering predictions.

title: Achieving a superior combination of ambient and high-temperature mechanical properties in a precipitation-enhanced α+β Ti alloy via cluster-formula design
abstract: Conventional Ti alloys strictly limit the content of Al and Si to avoid ductility loss caused by the precipitation of intermediate phases, which in turn restricts the further enhancement of their ambient and high-temperature properties. This study proposes an innovative strategy based on precise composition design via the cluster formula approach, coupled with subsequent heat treatment to control intermediate phases. Starting from the cluster formula of Ti-6Al-4V, α-{Al2Ti14}12+β-{Al1V2Ti14}5, the composition was modified by increasing Al to promote α2-Ti3Al precipitation, adding Zr and trace Si to form silicides, and substituting V with a refractory element (Mo0.5Nb0.5Ta0.5W0.5) to refine α lamellae. After the 840 °C/1 h solution + 600 °C/4 h aging treatment, S1-840 exhibits a bimodal microstructure consisting of equiaxed α and the transformed β matrix. A hierarchically distributed, multi-scale precipitate structure is observed: sub-micron primary silicides and nano-sized Ti3Al are preferentially located in the primary α phase, while secondary silicides are uniformly dispersed at the grain/phase boundaries. The sample achieves an ultra-high strength level at ambient temperature (Rm∼1496 MPa, Rp0.2∼1446 MPa). After the 910 °C/1 h solution +600 °C/4 h aging treatment, S3-910 presents a fully lamellar microstructure, reaching a tensile strength of 840 MPa at 600 °C, which is superior to typical near-α high-temperature Ti alloys such as IMI 834. This study successfully realizes the controlled precipitation of strengthening phases and microstructural refinement through the cluster formula approach, providing a novel pathway for developing Ti alloys with outstanding performance at both ambient and high temperatures.

title: Structural and chemical length scales at near-stationary austenite-ferrite interfaces in a model duplex stainless steel
abstract: The structural and chemical properties of austenite/ferrite (γ/α) interfaces were investigated in a model duplex stainless steel (Fe–Cr–Ni–Mo–N) using a correlative approach combining scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and atom probe tomography (APT). Two interface types were selected based on their orientation relationship (OR): a near-Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) interface and a non-K-S interface. The near K-S interface presents a planar terrace-ledge morphology with atomically sharp structural transitions at the terraces, whereas the non-K-S interface is rough with protrusions of 3–5 nm amplitude. In both cases, the chemical transition width measured by EELS and APT exceeds the crystallographic interface width determined from STEM imaging, indicating that chemical potential perturbations extend beyond the structural discontinuity. The OR is found to have a clear effect on the solute segregation behavior: Mo and N segregate exclusively to the non-K-S interface, while Cr segregates to both interface types. Ni shows no detectable interfacial excess at either interface. The 2D APT composition maps reveal a spatially heterogeneous distribution of Cr at the near K-S interface, with a strong spatial correlation between Cr and N enrichment attributed to their attractive thermodynamic interaction. Gibbsian interfacial excess values and segregation energies are reported for all solutes, distinguishing between effective and intrinsic contributions. Thermodynamic self-consistency of the derived segregation energies is only achieved for an interface width of 1–2 nm, consistent with the chemical width from EELS. This provides an experimentally grounded estimate of the interface width directly applicable to solute drag models of γ/α interface migration.

title: Atomic-scale interface kinetics during non-equilibrium solid-vapor phase transition in crystalline metals
abstract: Understanding the kinetics of solid-vapor phase transitions at interfaces is essential for describing high-temperature material behavior under thermodynamic non-equilibrium conditions. While sublimation and evaporation rates have traditionally been characterized by the Hertz-Knudsen equation for decades, this classical framework cannot account for atomic-scale interface migration, where local non-equilibrium interface configurations lead to spatially non-uniform desorption kinetics. In this study, we establish an atomic-scale interface kinetic theory of non-equilibrium solid-vapor phase transition in crystalline metals. Atomic-resolution observations of non-uniform sublimation kinetics in the ultrathin Ag nanosheet using transmission electron microscopy reveal that transitions between different sublimation pathways are energy-dependent. The tendency toward surface energy minimization generates a net vapor flux, accompanied by variations in local energy barriers at atomic sites undergoing sublimation. By introducing surface step density as a structural state variable, we derive a rate equation for non-uniform sublimation that quantitatively predicts local atomic desorption rates along the interface. Extending this framework to nanoparticles and nanowires, we further develop a corresponding numerical model to track the resulting interface evolution, and the agreement between simulation and experiments across these nanostructures demonstrates the generality of the kinetic description and establishes a predictive framework for non-equilibrium interface migration in crystalline metals.

title: Resolving the metastable Si-XIII structure through convergent theory and experiment
abstract: Silicon allotropes have emerged as a pivotal frontier for engineering materials with tailored optical, electronic, and thermal functionalities, opening routes toward integrated photonics, energy harvesting, and quantum technologies, while avoiding rare or toxic elements. High-pressure experiments have revealed several metastable silicon allotropes, among which Si-XIII stands out. First observed more than 20 years ago, this phase has remained structurally unidentified, representing a significant gap in our understanding of elemental silicon allotropy. In this work, a convergent methodology is employed combining advanced theoretical modeling with experimental characterization to finally resolve the long-standing structural assignment of Si-XIII. We construct a structural model guided by experimental observations, validate it through first-principles optimization, and systematically test it against multiple experimental signatures. All key fingerprints of this phase — interplanar spacings, Raman frequencies, thermodynamic stability, and kinetic pathways — are consistently rationalized by our proposed crystal structure. These findings provide a crucial missing piece in the high-pressure phase diagram of silicon, demonstrate the power of integrating computational predictions with experimental validation to resolve complex structural problems in materials science, and open new avenues for the controlled synthesis and functional exploitation of metastable Group-IV allotropes.

title: Toughening of additively manufactured NiAl-28Cr-6Mo nanostructured composites by modification of the local microstructure
abstract: NiAl-(Cr,Mo) in-situ composites such as NiAl-28Cr-6Mo (at.%) exhibit a high fracture toughness due to their directionally solidified two-phase microstructure. The reinforcing (Cr,Mo)-phase hinders the crack propagation through the brittle B2-NiAl-matrix. In this study, two different morphologies with a range of achievable phase thicknesses in a NiAl-28Cr-6Mo alloy are produced by additive manufacturing. This resulted in either an isotropic, interconnected rod network or a lamellar microstructure. Due to the small size of the phases, the fracture properties of the so formed nanostructured composites are analysed locally by focused ion beam (FIB) milled microcantilevers. It was shown for the first time that an isotropic, interconnected network exhibits a maximum fracture toughness of 9 MPa√m at a (Cr,Mo)-phase thickness of 50–70 nm. In contrast, the fracture toughness of the plate morphology (6–8 MPa√m) is largely independent of the (Cr,Mo)-phase thickness. However, (Cr,Mo)-plates with a favorable crack arrester orientation demonstrate significantly higher work of fracture due to active toughening mechanisms during extended stable crack growth, compared to the rod-network morphology or plates with unfavorable orientation. It could be shown that fundamental toughening mechanisms are also active in additive manufactured NiAl-(Cr,Mo) composites even down to the size of nano-structured plates.

title: Niobium partitioning-mediated austenite decomposition in a Si-modified austenitic stainless steel during long-term thermal aging at 550 °C
abstract: Si-modified Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic steels exhibit superior corrosion resistance in liquid lead-bismuth eutectic coolant; however, their application is limited by Si-induced austenite decomposition at elevated temperatures. This decomposition arises from pronounced Si rejection during M23C6 precipitation, thereby creating a local chemical environment favorable for α-ferrite formation. Herein, Nb addition is introduced to regulate Si redistribution and modify the decomposition pathway during aging at 550 °C for up to 3000 h. Nb addition suppresses M23C6 precipitation through preferential NbC formation and promotes the formation of (Nb, Si)-rich clusters via strong Nb-Si interactions. The Nb-modified austenite decomposition proceeds via two distinct pathways: an M6C-associated γ → α-ferrite transformation at intermediate aging times (∼500 h) and a G-phase-mediated γ → G-phase + α-ferrite eutectoid transformation during prolonged aging. The (Nb, Si)-rich clusters act as chemically favorable precursors for M6C carbide and G-phase nucleation, while the partitioning of Nb and Si mainly governs the transformation kinetics. A stabilization treatment involving the formation of dispersed nanosized NbC further suppress decomposition by reducing the availability of C and Nb in the austenite matrix. These findings demonstrate that Nb addition effectively mitigates Si-induced austenite decomposition by altering precipitation sequences and local solute redistribution, providing a strategy for improving the long-term microstructural stability of Si-modified austenitic steels.

title: Twin boundary modification induced by dopant segregation
abstract: Revealing the interaction between dopants and grain boundaries (GBs) is crucial for tailoring the material properties by elemental doping. It is generally believed that the segregation behavior of dopants depends on the initial structure of pristine GBs and the effect of GB segregation is localized since the dopants only affect the arrangement of neighboring atoms. In this study, aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy observations reveal that pristine α-Fe2O3 possesses three types of (0001) coherent twin boundaries (TBs) with different displacement vectors, which evolve into the same TB after co-doping of Sr and Si. The dopant co-segregation at the TBs causes the localized TB structural transition of Fe2O3 grains, which consequently fundamentally alters the local atomic coordination and the relative alignment of the adjacent grains. First-principles calculations suggest that the spontaneous segregation of large-sized Sr atoms induces a local interfacial modification and promotes the segregation of Si atoms. These findings suggest that dopants can not only completely modify the structure of GBs but also induce collective atomic rearrangements across the interface, thereby providing insights for atomic-scale interfacial engineering.

title: Micromechanics of the sintering force in sintering by bulk diffusion
abstract: Densification in sintering originates from the relative approach of contacting particles, which is driven by the sintering force. This concept has been rigorously established for grain boundary diffusion, where the driving force is determined by the local curvature at the neck. For bulk diffusion, however, the diffusion potential is governed by the Laplace equation in the particle interior, so the driving force is inherently non-local and depends on the overall surface morphology of the particle; a rigorous definition of the sintering force has been lacking. Here, a microscopic theory of the sintering force for bulk diffusion is developed by decomposing the diffusion potential into non-densifying and densifying solutions. The sintering force takes the same form as that for grain boundary diffusion when the neck curvature is replaced by an effective curvature—a virtual curvature that would produce a chemical potential equal to the area-averaged value on the contact face. Front-tracking boundary-element simulations of two-particle sintering show that the sintering force exhibits a broad peak as a function of the contact radius and vanishes at the equilibrium shape. The effective curvature, sintering force, geometric factor, and relative velocity are presented as functions of the contact radius, so that the dynamics of sintering can be predicted from the particle geometry alone.

title: Programmable polar vortex lattices as nano-transducers for sub-terahertz coherent phonon excitation
abstract: Sub-terahertz elastic waves enable electromechanical and magnetoacoustic interactions at the nanometer spatial and picosecond temporal scales, and hold promising prospects for next-generation sensing, imaging and signal-processing techniques. However, their nanometric wavelengths impose great challenges on materials design and experimental accessibility. Here, we demonstrated that polar vortex lattices in ferroelectric thin films can act as programable transducers to generate sub-terahertz elastic waves (coherent phonons), whose frequency can be tuned by varying the film thickness. Leveraging the intrinsic nonlinearity of ferroelectrics and the multiple spatial modes of vortex lattices, higher-frequency waves are achieved via high-order harmonic generation and coherent overtones. Notably, electric-field tuning of vortex lattices enables dynamic amplitude modulation by over an order of magnitude. Moreover, the chiral vortex lattice enables frequency-selective excitation of Rayleigh and shear-horizontal waves. This behavior originates from nanoscale polarization modulations within polar vortex lattices, which induce spatially periodic stresses that are phase-matched with high-wavevector acoustic modes. Our findings shed new insights into the interplay between collective dynamics of polar topological textures and coherent phonons, opening avenues for sub-terahertz elastic-wave technologies.

title: Kinematic analysis of shear localization in lath martensite under bending based on a non-symmetric displacement gradient framework
abstract: Improving the bendability of martensitic steels requires a clear understanding of microscopic shear-band formation, because these bands often initiate cracks during bending, while the crystallographic origin of the bands remains unclear. We propose a slip-based kinematic framework for analyzing heterogeneous microscopic shear deformation in lath martensite. A non-symmetric displacement gradient representing a shear mode defined by two independent shear-plane angles (α,β) is prescribed, and the resulting slip systems are analyzed. A shear-mode slip accommodation index, Is*, is also defined to quantify the crystallographic propensity for shear deformation. Comparison with in-situ SEM/DIC observations shows that the relative magnitudes of the indices for in-habit-plane (HP) and out-of-habit-plane (OHP) shear, Is*hp and Is*ohp, respectively, govern the type of shear. The orientation of strain localization bands can be predicted by the shear-plane angle combination (α,β) that minimizes the index. When the minimum of the Is(α,β) function is relatively flat, multidirectional strain localization is predicted, consistent with experimental observations. Packet-averaged index analysis reveals that HP shear propensity varies more among packets than the case of OHP shear propensity. Packets with high HP shear propensity accommodate deformation early during bending, whereas those with low HP shear propensity likely act as stress-bearing regions. Crack initiation occurs both in HP-shear-localized regions and in low-propensity packets that sustain higher stresses. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a crystallographic basis for microscopic shear-band formation and crack initiation during bending.

title: Influence of magnetic phase transition and magnetic structure on cryogenic magnetocaloric effect in metamagnetic Ho3Si2C2 compound
abstract: The magnetocaloric (MC) properties in many rare-earth (RE)-dominated magnetic solids have been extensively investigated, aiming to identify proper cryogenic magnetic refrigerant and unveil their inherent magneto-physical properties. Here, the crystal structure, magnetic phase transition (MPT), magnetic structure, and MC effect in Ho3Si2C2 compound were systematically determined by means of the neutron powder diffraction (NPD), magnetization and specific heat measurements together with the first principal calculations. The Ho3Si2C2 compound crystallizes in an orthorhombic Pr3Si2C2-type structure (space group Cmmm) and each unit cell contains six Ho atoms locating at two (four Ho1 and two Ho2) Wyckoff positions. Long-range antiferromagnetic (AFM) transition occurs around TN of 6.8 K which originates from the polarized Ho1 atoms and the ordered moments of Ho2 atoms are negligible. A typical first-order type metamagnetic MPT has been observed in Ho3Si2C2 compound which arises from its AFM ground state to a field-aligned ferromagnetic (FM)-like state below TN. Notable reversible MC performances assessed by the magnetic entropy change and adiabatic temperature change have been realized, which are comparable to most RE-dominated cryogenic high-performing magnetic refrigerants. These studies indicate that the metamagnetic Ho3Si2C2 compound is a considerable cryogenic magnetic refrigerant.

title: Negative thermal expansion of Barium Copper Silicate
abstract: BaCuSi4O10, an artificially synthesized blue ceramic pigment, was first discovered on pottery and ceramics associated with ancient human civilizations and history. It is also known as Chinese Blue. However, its thermal expansion behavior and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this work, a joint study of synchrotron X-ray diffraction, neutron powder diffraction, extended X-ray absorption fine structure, variable-temperature Raman spectroscopy, far-infrared spectroscopy, and first‑principles calculations was employed to investigate the thermal properties of BaCuSi4O10. It exhibits anisotropic thermal expansion, with volumetric thermal expansion changing from negative to positive across 125–1100 K. BaCuSi4O10 features layered framework structures, and the in-plane contraction originates from the coupled rotation of Si4O10 rings and CuO4 units, while the interlayer expansion is closely associated with structural distortions of BaO8 polyhedra. Moreover, the anisotropic thermal expansion of BaCuSi4O10 is governed jointly by phonon contributions and elastic effects. The results show that the thermal expansion along the a axis is dominated by phonon contributions, and the thermal expansion along the c-axis arises from the combined contributions of phonons and elasticity, with the elastic contribution more prominent.

title: Simultaneous enhancement of coercivity and electric resistivity of Nd-Fe-B magnets by Tb2O3 stepwise reduction-grain boundary diffusion process
abstract: To satisfy the high-temperature and high-speed operating requirements of high-power, high-speed permanent magnet motors, Nd-Fe-B magnets are demanded to possess both high coercivity and high electrical resistivity. However, these two items are difficult to achieve simultaneously. In this work, a novel Tb2O3 stepwise reduction-grain boundary diffusion (SRGBD) process was adopted, which successfully enhanced the coercivity and electrical resistivity of Nd-Fe-B magnets from 954.8 kA/m and 124 μΩ·cm to 1874.6 kA/m and 272 μΩ·cm, respectively. Specifically, the coercivity was increased by 919.8 kA/m (96.33%) and the electrical resistivity by 148 μΩ·cm (119.35%). In comparison with existing literature reports, this process not only achieves the highest recorded increase in the electrical resistivity of magnets subjected to grain boundary diffusion treatment, but also realizes a remarkable enhancement in coercivity. Comprehensive characterizations of the magnet’s microstructure, microregional composition and magnetic domain structure confirm that this synergistic performance optimization is attributed to two key factors: the increased formation depth of the Tb-enriched 2:14:1 shell with high magnetocrystalline anisotropy field, and the simultaneous elevation of the content of RE-rich phases and high-resistivity oxide phases (CaO) within the grain boundary phases after diffusion. It thus results in the simultaneously improved output power and energy efficiency of the motor because of the combination of magnetic thermal stability enhancement and eddy current loss reduction, as theoretically confirmed by electromagnetic simulation.

title: Strain-rate dependent screw dislocation glide mechanisms in BCC refractory metals and alloys
abstract: Plastic flow in body-centered cubic (BCC) metals and dilute and concentrated alloys is governed by the motion of 〈111〉 screw dislocations, whose glide is often impeded by cross-kinks (jogs). Existing strengthening models generally attribute cross-kink depinning to defect-assisted cutting or dislocation bowing, while the strain-rate dependence of cross-kink evolution and the resulting obstacle spacing remain poorly understood at the atomistic scale. Here, we combine conventional molecular dynamics and strain-boost hyperdynamics to investigate screw-dislocation glide in pure Nb and Mo, dilute and concentrated Nb–Mo alloys, and the refractory high-entropy alloy NbMoTaW at 300 K over strain rates from 103 to 107s−1. At high strain rates, cross-kinks predominantly depin through vacancy–interstitial formation. In contrast, low-strain-rate simulations with sufficiently long dislocation lines reveal that cross-kinks formed on different {110} slip planes can migrate and interact to form super cross-kinks and cusp-like structures that act as strong pinning points. These evolved pinning structures subsequently depin through multiple pathways, including cusp unzipping via backward cross-slip and prismatic-loop formation. The same three-dimensional mechanisms are consistently observed in different alloys using both empirical and machine-learning interatomic potentials, demonstrating their robustness. Our results suggest that the effective obstacle spacing governing the critical resolved shear stress evolves from the initial equilibrium kink structure through subsequent stress-driven cross-kink migration, interaction, and depinning during deformation. These findings provide new insight into screw-dislocation strengthening in BCC alloys.
keywords: Screw dislocations in BCC metals and alloys

title: Local lattice distortion governs stochastic dislocation-twin boundary interactions in fcc alloys
abstract: Understanding how dislocations interact with coherent twin boundaries (CTBs) is critical for tailoring the mechanical response of face-centered cubic (fcc) alloys. While such interactions are traditionally described by average stacking-fault energy (SFE), this framework may break down in chemically complex alloys exhibiting strong local lattice distortion. Here, large-scale molecular dynamics simulations are employed to investigate screw dislocation-CTB interactions in CoFeNiAlx multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), with weakly distorted CoxNi1-x alloys serving as reference systems with comparable SFE ranges. In CoxNi1-x, dislocation transmission across CTBs is deterministic and well described by conventional SFE-controlled models. In contrast, CoFeNiAlx alloys exhibit a transition from deterministic transmission to stochastic competition between transmission and absorption with increasing Al content. Atomistic analysis reveals that both outcomes originate from a common constriction precursor, but the subsequent evolution depends on spatial heterogeneity in local constriction barriers. Unlike uniform alloys, constriction in MPEAs occurs locally along the dislocation line, leading to segmental propagation or trapping at the boundary. These results demonstrate that average SFE alone is insufficient to describe defect-interface interactions in distorted alloys, and a statistical description of local energy landscapes is required.

title: Microbial degradation of the passive films drives corrosion of Ti-6Al-4 V by sulfate-reducing bacteria in seawater
abstract: The excellent corrosion resistance of titanium alloys originates from the passive film that naturally forms on their surfaces. However, these materials remain highly susceptible to microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) in marine environments. Here, we investigate the mechanisms of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB)-induced MIC of titanium alloys from the perspective of passive film defect evolution. Results show that prolonged anaerobic exposure promotes the development of a defect-rich passive film enriched with oxygen vacancies, which act as preferential sites for sulfide interaction. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy combined with time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry directly reveals sulfur accumulation and structural heterogeneity within the passive film, confirming that biogenic sulfide can be incorporated into the defective film and promote its degradation. The degraded passive film exhibits significantly enhanced hydrogen evolution activity, transforming the originally inert titanium surface into a more electrochemically reactive interface and thereby accelerating MIC. Collectively, these results establish passive-film defect chemistry as a key factor that governs the SRB-induced degradation of titanium alloys. More broadly, they extend the mechanistic landscape of MIC from active metals to highly passive metallic systems by uncovering a defect-mediated degradation route that may be operative in other passivation-dependent materials.

title: Spatially resolved structural correlations at the nanoscale in phase-separated silicate glass revealed by electron total scattering analysis using 4D-STEM
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding structural heterogeneity in silicate glasses at the nanometer scale remains challenging because conventional diffraction techniques provide only a spatially averaged structural response and cannot resolve the atomic structure of individual amorphous domains. Here, spatially resolved electron total scattering is used to investigate a phase-separated soda–lime–silicate glass by combining local Selected-Area Electron Diffraction (SAED) and four-dimensional Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (4D-STEM). Electron diffraction data were processed using the ePDFMapping software package to obtain electron pair distribution functions (ePDFs). Local SAED measurements reveal two distinct phase-specific structural signatures corresponding to silica-rich droplets and the surrounding modifier-rich matrix. While both phases exhibit similar tetrahedral short-range order, they differ systematically in their medium-range organization, the most prominent feature being a shift of the First Sharp Diffraction Peak (FSDP). Spatially resolved 4D-STEM reproduces this structural contrast and directly maps its spatial distribution across individual amorphous domains at the nanometer scale through Pearson-correlation analysis of both reciprocal-space S ( Q ) and real-space G ( r ) , together with peak position and integrated-area analyses. The close agreement with SAED demonstrates that 4D-STEM provides sufficient sensitivity to resolve these phase-dependent structural signatures while enabling their spatial localization. Conventional bulk X-ray total scattering contains the structural contributions of both amorphous phases only as an averaged response, whereas spatially resolved electron total scattering separates and maps these contributions directly. These results establish spatially resolved electron total scattering as a powerful approach for probing nanoscale variations in medium-range order in heterogeneous glasses and other amorphous materials.

title: Dislocation locking versus distributed amorphization: Crystallographic dichotomy of fracture in GaSb
abstract: Gallium Antimonide (GaSb) is pivotal for next-generation infrared optoelectronics, yet its deployment is constrained by intrinsic brittleness and susceptibility to machining-induced damage. Overcoming these limitations requires a mechanistic understanding of how crystallographic orientation governs the brittle-to-ductile transition. Here, we elucidate the atomistic origins of tribological anisotropy in GaSb(010) via in situ nano-scratching and atomic-resolution STEM. We reveal a fundamental bifurcation in mechanical response: the 〈101〉 direction exhibits stick-slip instability and premature fracture, whereas the 〈100〉 direction enables stable, deep ductile flow. This divergence originates from competing subsurface accommodation pathways. In 〈101〉, the intersection of {111} twin variants facilitates the formation of sessile Lomer–Cottrell dislocation locks, creating local stress concentrations that increase crack susceptibility. Conversely, the 〈100〉 orientation shows reduced lock-like defect intersection and accommodates deformation through more distributed nanocrystallization/amorphization. This “distributed dissipation” mechanism delocalizes stress, allowing deep plastic penetration without failure. These findings prescribe a clear strategy for ultra-precision manufacturing: selecting 〈100〉 processing vectors to leverage phase transformation over dislocation locking, thereby ensuring superior surface integrity.

title: Tuning grain-boundary cohesion and chemical ordering via trace boron in BCC Ti-Al-Nb alloy
abstract: Body-centered cubic (BCC) alloys are plagued by limited ambient ductility, largely arising from the synergy of impurity-induced grain boundary (GB) embrittlement and high antiphase boundary (APB) energy inherent to the highly chemical ordering structure. Here, we report a breakthrough in overcoming this shortcoming in a Ti-22Al-25Nb (atomic percentage) alloy via trace boron microalloying. Adding 50 ppmw boron to the alloy nearly doubles the tensile elongation (from ∼10.5% to ∼20.1%) without sacrificing yield strength. A multi-scale structural reconstruction mechanism is identified to be responsible for this ductility surge. At the atomic scale, boron kinetically and thermodynamically outcompetes oxygen for GB occupancy, effectively "purifying" the interface. First-principles calculations reveal that this substitution transforms the interfacial bonding from brittle ionic nature (O-induced) to compliant metallic one (B-induced), rendering the GBs "dislocation-transparent" by eliminating the potent solute pinning effect. The addition of boron also promotes the "chemical order-to-disorder" transition, creating a chemically disordered A2-like "flexible shell" at the GBs while simultaneously triggering the intragranular structure change from chemical medium-range order (CMRO) to short-range order (CSRO). This hierarchical disordering significantly lowers the APB energy penalty, promoting cross-slip and cooperative deformation of dislocations. Our findings establish a unified "GB toughening plus matrix softening" strategy for designing ductile BCC alloys.

title: Grain boundary migration across compositional complexity: A molecular dynamics study from binary alloys to high-entropy alloys
abstract: Grain boundary (GB) migration critically influences the mechanical response of structural metals, making a mechanistic understanding of this process indispensable. GB migration in binary alloys has been extensively examined within the framework of the Cahn--L\"{u}cke--St\"{u}we (CLS) theory. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), composed of more than four principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions, have recently attracted considerable attention as next-generation structural materials because of their excellent mechanical performance, including superior high-temperature strength compared with pure metals and conventional binary alloys. However, the multicomponent nature of HEAs raises questions about the applicability of the CLS theory, and the mechanisms underlying their exceptional mechanical properties remain incompletely understood. To achieve a unified understanding of GB migration across compositional complexity from binary alloys to HEAs, we employed a combined approach integrating the CLS framework with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of GB migration. The MD simulations demonstrate that, similar to binary alloy models, GB migration resistance in the HEA model increases due to solute drag arising from dynamic elemental segregation to the moving boundary. Applying the CLS theory with a modified solute-diffusion profile to the binary alloy model leads to quantitative agreement between the simulated and predicted migration resistance. In contrast, the migration resistance in the HEA model cannot be quantitatively explained by the modified CLS theory alone, indicating the involvement of additional mechanisms. We propose that local compositional heterogeneity near the GB, which arises naturally from the compositional complexity of multicomponent alloys, constitutes an additional and distinct source of GB migration resistance unique to HEAs.

title: Insights into hydrogen-induced vacancy stability and creep in chemically complex alloys
abstract: Hydrogen (H) content modifies the creep response of Fe-based alloys by altering thermodynamics of point-defects; here we identify the electronic-structure mechanism underlying this effect. Using spin-polarized first-principles calculations combined with a cluster dynamics formulation, we establish a general framework linking H-assisted vacancy stabilization to diffusion-mediated creep in BCC Fe, FCC Fe, and chemically complex FCC Fe-Cr-Ni alloys. H-vacancy binding analysis shows that H-stabilized vacancies form at low hydrogen content in BCC Fe but require much higher chemical potentials in FCC Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloys due to broader d-bands, electronic screening, and chemical disorder. Consequently, plastic deformation mediated by diffusive processes is expected to be far more strongly impacted in BCC Fe than in FCC alloys. These electronic-controlled trends determine steady-state vacancy populations and provide a symmetry-resolved microscopic basis for H-assisted creep in ferritic and austenitic steels.

title: Editorial Board
Metalloid silicon alloying enables ultrastrong and ductile single-phase high-entropy alloys
abstract: Metallic structural materials face a long-standing trade-off between strength and ductility. Single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) high- and medium-entropy alloys (H/MEAs) with substantial lattice distortion offer a pathway to mitigate this dilemma, but achieving high strength in such alloys typically relies on scarce, expensive, and dense refractory elements. Here we introduce an alternative paradigm using Earth-abundant metalloid silicon. We have developed an Fe26Co26Ni26Cr12Si10 HEA that retains a stable single-phase FCC structure at medium-to-high temperatures, enabling continuous tuning of the grain size from ultrafine-grained (UFG) to coarse-grained regimes through simple thermomechanical processing. The fully recrystallized UFG alloy achieves a yield strength of 1027 MPa while maintaining a uniform elongation of 22.4%—a combination that surpasses the conventional strength–ductility trade-off in single-phase solid solutions. Silicon addition simultaneously elevates lattice friction stress and the Hall–Petch coefficient through severe lattice distortion and grain-boundary segregation, while the accompanying reductions in stacking fault energy and shear modulus lower the critical twinning stress. This sustains strong twinning-induced plasticity even in the UFG regime and delivers high strain-hardening ability. Our work establishes metalloid silicon alloying as a design platform for high-performance, cost-effective, and sustainable structural materials.

title: Effect of stacking complexity on deformation and fracture of hexagonal SiC polytypes: An atomistic investigation
abstract: Stacking-sequence variations in polytypic silicon carbide (SiC) provide a unique platform to isolate the influence of long-range structural order on mechanical behavior while preserving identical local tetrahedral Si–C bonding. However, the mechanistic role of stacking sequence in governing shear instability, strain localization, and fracture in hexagonal SiC remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the tensile deformation behavior along the 〈 1120 〉 direction of 2H, 4H, and 6H SiC using molecular dynamics simulations with a machine-learning interatomic potential (UF3). All polytypes show nearly identical elastic responses up to 6% strain. However, significant differences emerge near failure. To understand these differences, we examine the evolution of shear localization using von Mises strain and non-affine squared displacement. Deformation in all polytypes is governed by shear, while the degree of localization varies significantly. Shear localization severity follows the order 4 H > 6 H > 2 H . This trend mirrors the corresponding increase in Shannon entropy–based local stacking complexity, suggesting that higher local stacking heterogeneity promotes stronger strain localization in hexagonal SiC. In contrast, peak tensile stress follows the order 6 H > 4 H > 2 H and correlates with unstable stacking fault energy and theoretical shear strength obtained from generalized stacking fault energy calculations. These results demonstrate that global hexagonality governs intrinsic shear resistance and attainable peak stress, whereas local stacking complexity controls strain localization and fracture morphology.

title: Synergistic effects of soft-hard spots in Ni-Co-P nanoglass boost superior electrocatalytic activity
abstract: Metallic glasses (MGs) are advanced catalysts for sustainable energy and green chemistry, yet their rational design has been hindered by unclear structure–property relationships rooted in atomic-scale order. Herein, we overcome this fundamental challenge by engineering a series of composition-tunable Ni-Co-P nanostructured metallic glasses (NGs) via pulse electrodeposition, enabling systematic modulation of soft-hard spots and catalytic energetics. The optimized composition, Ni69Co12P19 NG (Ni69-NG), achieves exceptional hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance with an overpotential of 31 mV at 10 mA cm-2, comparable to commercial Pt/C. Through systematic analysis, we establish a direct correlation between catalytic activity and soft-hard spots. In addition to a high concentration of potential active sites in soft spots, Ni69-NG features dominant hard spots with Z9-type short-range order (SRO) and denser medium-range order (MRO) topological packing, collectively optimizing the hydrogen adsorption free energy (|ΔGH*|). Moreover, this unique local coordination environment induces favorable charge redistribution, enhancing electron density at Co sites while rendering Ni centers more electrophilic, thereby accelerating reaction kinetics. Our work not only deciphers the long-sought atomic origin of catalytic function in MGs, but also demonstrates that controlled structural disorder, particularly through SRO/MRO engineering, can enable the rational design of amorphous electrocatalysts with atomic precision.

title: Hydrogen sorption-induced tuning of magnetocaloric properties of heavy rare-earth-based Laves-phase DyCo2 for hydrogen liquefaction
abstract: Materials with magnetic phase transitions in the cryogenic temperature range are the key for efficient magnetocaloric hydrogen liquefaction. The Laves-phase DyCo 2 exhibits a significant magnetocaloric effect, but its Curie temperature ( T C ) is above the temperature window needed to magnetically liquefy hydrogen. Here the change of its T C upon hydrogen absorption was investigated. Complete hydrogenation modified T C from 139 K to 24 K, leading to 3.4 hydrogen atoms per unit cell of the crystal. Partial hydrogenation leads to two distinct T C ’s, corresponding to the parent and hydrogenated phase. Light microscopy revealed a maze-like pattern on the micron scale for the DyCo 2 phase, which is not found for the materials saturated in hydrogen, and a core–shell-like microstructure was observed in the partially hydrogenated samples, where the pattern of DyCo 2 phase is only seen on the core. The Hydrogen-sorption reactions yield a massive crystal volume increase of 21%. After thermal dehydrogenation T C was recovered, however stacking faults and chemical heterogeneities were detected by high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy, which reduced magnetocaloric performance of the dehydrogenated compound. The isothermal entropy change reached up to 21 J kg -1 K -1 in the pristine DyCo 2 when 14 T magnetic field was applied at 139 K, while the fully hydrogenated compound reached 15 J kg -1 K -1 at 24 K. Our work demonstrates the usefulness of reversible hydrogen sorption to tune the magnetocaloric properties of heavy rare-earth-based Laves-phases towards hydrogen liquefaction transition temperature range.

title: Achieving wide axial zero thermal expansion and enhanced toughness by microstructure orientation engineering
abstract: Zero thermal expansion (ZTE) alloys are highly desirable for precision applications but remain challenging due to the instability arising from the anisotropic lattice of polycrystal materials and the inherent brittleness of intermetallic compounds. Here, we develop a microstructure alignment strategy that simultaneously tames crystallographic texture, thermal expansion, and mechanical performance. As a model system, Er2Fe17Cux alloys were fabricated by directional solidification, which shows highly oriented multiphase microstructures, primarily consisting of a 2:17 matrix and α-Fe(Cu) phase. The strong 〈0001〉 texture of the 2:17 phase enables the intrinsic negative thermal expansion (NTE) along the solidification direction, which can be compensated by the positive thermal expansion of the α-Fe(Cu) phase. Concurrently, the relatively high Curie temperature of the Cu-contained alloys broadens the working temperature window of abnormal thermal expansion, together enabling a wide stable ZTE behavior (αL=3.7(6) × 10–7 K–1, 10–370 K) in the Er2Fe17Cu3 composition. In addition, the directionally solidified samples exhibit significantly improved mechanical properties, with a compressive strength and toughness reaching 1.2 GPa and 30.1 J cm–3, respectively, which are 2.5 and 2 times as high as those of the non-textured counterpart. This enhancement may be attributed to reduced internal stress distribution in the oriented alloys, as supported by finite-element simulations. Importantly, the effectiveness of this microstructural alignment strategy has also been validated in other anisotropic NTE/ZTE alloy systems. Therefore, this work demonstrates that directional solidification provides a general route to integrate crystallographic texture, enabling simultaneous optimization of thermal expansion behavior and mechanical robustness in anisotropic NTE/ZTE intermetallics.

title: Fracture induced by a martensitic grain boundary complexion transition
abstract: Sub-critical grain boundary (GB) fracture (with a stress intensity factor below the critical value) is observed in molecular dynamics simulations of a symmetric-tilt aluminum grain boundary. The mechanism driving the sub-critical fracture is revealed to be a martensitic complexion transition mediated by nucleation and propagation of a GB dislocation at the crack tip. To rationalize the observed transition, the excess free energy for the two complexions is computed as a function of stress, demonstrating that one complexion is stable at low stresses and the other is stable at high stresses. At stress levels where the high-stress complexion is metastable, the activation energy for the complexion transition was computed using nudged elastic band methods for homogeneous nucleation and Arrhenius analysis of molecular dynamics runs for nucleation at a crack tip. The resulting kinetic law indicates that the observed complexion transition would occur under stress, temperature, and flaw-size conditions relevant to aluminum structures. These results demonstrate that GBs are dynamic defects that can undergo rapid martensitic transitions under loading, possibly altering material properties (such as fracture toughness) and behaviors.

title: Volume, grain- and interphase-boundary diffusion of Ag in eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 compositionally complex alloy
abstract: Solute diffusion of Ag in a two-phase multi-principal element eutectic AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy is measured in an extended temperature interval using the radiotracer technique. Both volume and short-circuit diffusion rates of Ag are determined. Complementary ToF-SIMS and high-resolution STEM experiments with natural Ag are used to distinguish the diffusion paths in the eutectic microstructure, especially to quantify the relative contributions of interphase and grain boundaries. Furthermore, Ag diffusion is measured in single-phase FCC and B2-ordered alloys with compositions mimicking those in the eutectic material.
